questions.title: What's Actually Inside _delta_log, and What Happens When Two Writers Commit at Once
questions.prompt: Explain what's actually stored inside a Delta table's _delta_log directory -- the JSON commit files and the checkpoint files -- and how Delta Lake derives ACID transactions and time travel purely from that log. Then walk through, mechanically, what happens when two separate Spark jobs try to commit a new version of the same Delta table at nearly the same moment: how Delta decides who wins, what the loser's job experiences, and what that job needs to do about it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Every Delta table's _delta_log directory is a sequentially numbered ledger of every transaction ever committed against the table: 000000.json, 000001.json, 000002.json, and so on, one file per committed version. Each of those JSON files holds a set of actions -- add (a data file that entered the table's current state), remove (a data file that's logically no longer part of the table, though it isn't physically deleted on the spot), plus metaData and protocol actions describing schema and feature versions, and a commitInfo action recording who ran what. A reader determines the table's current state by starting from version 0 (or the nearest checkpoint) and replaying every action in order -- there's no separate 'table state' stored anywhere; the log is the source of truth, and the actual Parquet data files are just referenced by it.

That log is also exactly how time travel works. Because a remove action only marks a file as logically gone -- it doesn't physically delete it from cloud storage immediately -- you can reconstruct the table exactly as it looked at any earlier version by replaying the log only up through that version's commit file; VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF are literally doing that replay. The physical files only disappear later, when a VACUUM actually removes files that are no longer referenced by any version still inside the configured retention window.

Replaying from version 0 every time would get expensive on a long-lived table, so Delta periodically writes a checkpoint: a Parquet file (by default roughly every 10 commits) that captures the cumulative state as of that version, with a _last_checkpoint pointer file recording where the latest one is. A reader then only needs to load the nearest checkpoint and replay the handful of JSON commits written after it, instead of the whole history. ACID properties fall directly out of this design: atomicity because each version's JSON file is written as a single atomic file creation; isolation and consistency because writers use optimistic concurrency control rather than locking; and durability because both the log and the data files sit on the same durable, versioned cloud storage.

The concurrent-writer scenario is where optimistic concurrency control actually earns its name. Say two Spark jobs both read the table at version N, each independently stages new data files reflecting its own changes, and then each attempts to commit version N+1 by creating N+1.json. The underlying storage's atomic create semantics guarantee only one of those two commits can actually become N+1.json -- whichever one wins, wins outright. The losing job's commit attempt fails, but Delta doesn't just give up: it checks whether the winning commit's changes actually conflict with what the losing job was trying to do (for example, did the winner remove or modify files the loser's operation logically depended on). If there's no real overlap -- two blind appends, say -- Delta can often resolve this automatically by re-attempting the loser's commit as N+2 against the now-current state. If there is a genuine conflict -- both updated overlapping partitions, for instance -- Delta raises a concurrency exception (ConcurrentAppendException, ConcurrentDeleteReadException, and similar), and it's the losing job's responsibility to re-read the latest version of the table, recompute its intended change against that new state, and retry the commit from there. That's why high-concurrency write patterns like streaming MERGE into the same table need an application-level retry loop around the write, not just a one-shot commit.
questions.professionalAnswer:
If someone asked me to explain _delta_log in one sentence, I'd say: it's a ledger, not a filesystem listing. Every time something changes the table, Delta writes one more numbered entry to that ledger -- 000000.json, 000001.json, and so on -- and each entry just says what got added and what got logically removed. The table 'as it is right now' is nothing more than the result of reading that ledger front to back. There's no hidden state anywhere else.

That's also the whole trick behind time travel, and once you see it that way it stops feeling magical. If 'remove' in the log doesn't mean 'physically delete right now' -- and it doesn't, the file sticks around until VACUUM actually cleans it up -- then asking for version 12 of the table is just replaying the ledger up to entry 12 and stopping. Checkpoints exist purely so you're not replaying from zero every single time; every ten-ish commits, Delta snapshots the cumulative state into a Parquet file so a reader can start there instead of from the beginning.

Now, the concurrent writers question -- this is the part people get nervous about because they're picturing database row locks, and that's not what's happening. Two Spark jobs can both read the table at the same version and both go off and build their own new data files in parallel; Delta doesn't stop that. What it does enforce is that only one of them can actually win the race to write the next numbered log entry -- the storage layer itself only lets one writer successfully create that file. The other one gets told 'no, try again,' and then Delta's smart about it: it looks at whether the winning commit actually stepped on the same files the loser cared about. If it didn't -- two separate appends, nothing overlapping -- Delta can just quietly retry the loser on top of the new state and move on. If it did overlap, you get a real exception, and now it's on the losing job's code to go re-read the table and redo its write. That's the part teams miss: Delta protects the table from corruption automatically, but it doesn't protect your job from having to retry -- that logic has to live in your pipeline.
questions.example:
-- Two jobs both read the table at version 5
-- Job A: blind append
INSERT INTO sales.orders VALUES (101, '2026-10-09', 49.99);
-- Job B: MERGE touching overlapping rows in the same partition
MERGE INTO sales.orders t USING updates u ON t.order_id = u.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *;

-- If Job A's commit (000006.json) lands first and Job B's MERGE
-- depended on files Job A didn't touch, Delta may auto-resolve Job B
-- as 000007.json. If Job B's read set overlaps files Job A changed,
-- Job B instead raises ConcurrentAppendException and must retry:
--   1. re-read sales.orders at the new current version
--   2. recompute the MERGE's matched/unmatched sets
--   3. re-attempt the commit
commonMistakes: Thinking a Delta table is just a folder of Parquet files with no additional bookkeeping
Believing a 'remove' action in the log immediately deletes the physical data file
Confusing the Parquet checkpoint files with actual table data files
Assuming any two concurrent writers to the same table always conflict, or assuming they never do
Not realizing the losing writer in a conflict must detect the failure and explicitly retry, rather than Delta resolving it silently in every case
keyPoints: _delta_log is an ordered sequence of JSON commit files containing add/remove/metaData/protocol/commitInfo actions
The table's current state is derived purely by replaying the log, not stored separately
Checkpoints (Parquet, roughly every 10 commits) let readers skip replaying the full history
Time travel works because removed files are tombstoned in the log, not physically deleted, until VACUUM
Delta uses optimistic concurrency control: writers race to commit the next version, not locks
Conflict detection is based on whether file-level changes actually overlap; a losing writer must re-read and retry

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes the JSON commit log structure and its actions accurately
Explains checkpoints and why they exist
Correctly ties time travel to log replay and tombstoned files
Explains optimistic concurrency control mechanics for simultaneous commits
Explains what the losing writer experiences and must do about it
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER vs. VACUUM: Why Running Only One of Them Eventually Breaks Production
questions.prompt: A table in production gets heavy streaming MERGE traffic. Someone on the team runs OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER BY on it nightly and considers the maintenance 'handled.' Explain what OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER actually do to the table's files, what VACUUM does that OPTIMIZE does not, and why skipping VACUUM (or, in the other direction, running VACUUM with an aggressively shortened retention period) will eventually cause a real production incident.
questions.modelAnswer:
OPTIMIZE's job is file compaction: it finds the small files that accumulate from frequent small writes -- exactly what heavy streaming MERGE traffic produces, since every micro-batch tends to write a handful of small files per partition -- and bin-packs them into fewer, larger files closer to Delta's target file size. Z-ORDER BY goes a step further on top of that compaction: it co-locates rows with similar values in the specified columns within those new, larger files by sorting the data along a space-filling curve, so that each file's min/max statistics become meaningfully narrow for that column. That's what makes data skipping effective -- a query filtering on a Z-ordered column can prune out whole files instead of scanning them, which is the real performance win people are chasing when they run it. Critically, OPTIMIZE does not delete the small files it's replacing. It writes new, compacted files and marks the old, now-superseded files as logically removed in the _delta_log, but the actual bytes for those old files stay on disk -- that's necessary so that concurrent long-running readers, or any time-travel query against a recent-past version, still have something to read.

VACUUM is the only operation that turns 'logically removed' into 'actually gone.' It physically deletes data files that are no longer referenced by any table version still inside the retention window, which defaults to 168 hours (7 days). That's the step that reclaims the storage left behind by OPTIMIZE's superseded small files, and by the tombstones that every DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE statement generates. If the team runs OPTIMIZE nightly but never runs VACUUM, every single night's compaction leaves the previous day's now-orphaned small files sitting in storage forever, on top of the tombstones the day's MERGE traffic itself generated -- storage grows roughly in proportion to the table's entire write history, not its current logical size. The table itself looks healthy and well-compacted when you query it, but cloud storage costs climb steadily, and eventually the sheer number of objects accumulating under that path starts to slow down storage-layer operations like directory listings -- which is a real production incident, just one that shows up as a bill and a slow listing operation rather than a query failure.

The opposite mistake -- shortening VACUUM's retention well below the default, or disabling its safety check to force an aggressive cleanup -- is dangerous for a different reason. That retention window exists specifically to protect anything that might still be reading an older snapshot of the table: a long-running batch job that started before last night's OPTIMIZE and is still mid-execution against files that compaction has since marked removed, a Structured Streaming job reading the table as a source and relying on recent-past versions still being physically present, or anyone running a time-travel query against a version from the last few days. If VACUUM deletes a file that one of those readers is about to open, that reader doesn't get a graceful fallback -- it fails outright with a file-not-found error, because the bytes it expected to be there have actually been deleted.

The right answer is to run both, on a schedule, for the reasons they each exist: OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER on the columns your queries actually filter on, to keep file layout and data skipping healthy as new data lands, and VACUUM on a retention setting that's deliberately chosen to be no shorter than the longest-running concurrent job or time-travel need you actually have -- not simply shortened to save on storage costs without checking who might still be reading an older version.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell them 'handled' is doing too much work here, because OPTIMIZE and VACUUM solve two completely different problems and running one is not a substitute for the other.

OPTIMIZE is about making queries fast. Heavy streaming MERGE traffic throws off a lot of small files, so OPTIMIZE comes along and rewrites them into fewer, bigger ones -- and if you add Z-ORDER on top, it also sorts the data inside those files by whatever column you care about, so a query filtering on that column can skip whole files instead of scanning everything. Great for read performance. But here's the part that trips people up: OPTIMIZE doesn't throw anything away. The old small files it just replaced are still sitting in storage -- they're marked as gone in the transaction log, but the actual bytes are untouched, on purpose, so nothing that's mid-read against an older version suddenly breaks.

VACUUM is the thing that actually deletes those orphaned files -- but only the ones outside its retention window, which defaults to seven days. So if this team is running OPTIMIZE every night and never running VACUUM at all, they're accumulating a full night's worth of now-dead small files, forever, on top of whatever DELETE and MERGE already left behind that day. The table still queries fine and still looks optimized -- that's the trap, it looks handled -- but the storage bill keeps climbing, and eventually just listing everything under that path gets slow because of how many stale objects are piled up underneath it.

And I'd flag the opposite failure too, because people reach for it to save money: don't shorten that seven-day retention window to claw back storage faster. That window is the only thing standing between VACUUM and deleting a file some other job is still actively reading -- a long streaming job, a time-travel query, anything that started before last night's cleanup. Cut that window too short and VACUUM will delete a file out from under a job that's mid-read, and that job doesn't degrade gracefully, it just fails with a file-not-found error. So the actual fix here isn't 'run OPTIMIZE more' -- it's 'add VACUUM on a real schedule, at a retention you've actually thought through, not the shortest one that passes the safety check.'
commonMistakes: Believing OPTIMIZE itself deletes the small files it replaces
Treating VACUUM as optional cleanup that can be skipped indefinitely without consequence
Shortening VACUUM's retention period to save on storage costs without checking for long-running readers or streaming sources
Assuming Z-ORDER is a one-time setup rather than something that needs to be re-applied as new data continues to land
Not recognizing that unbounded small-file and tombstone growth from streaming MERGE silently inflates storage cost and slows listing operations over time
keyPoints: OPTIMIZE compacts small files into larger ones; Z-ORDER additionally clusters data for effective skipping
OPTIMIZE marks old files as logically removed but does not physically delete them
VACUUM is the only operation that physically deletes unreferenced files and reclaims storage
The default 7-day/168-hour retention window protects concurrent long-running readers and time travel
Shortening retention too aggressively risks file-not-found failures for in-flight or stale readers
A healthy maintenance routine schedules both OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, not just one of them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains what OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER actually do to the table's files
Explains what VACUUM does and that it is the only physical deletion step
Explains the real production consequence of running OPTIMIZE without VACUUM
Explains the danger of an aggressively shortened VACUUM retention period
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Choosing Between #Temp Tables, Table Variables, and CTEs Inside a Stored Procedure
questions.prompt: You're writing a complex reporting stored procedure. Partway through, you compute an intermediate result set of roughly 200,000 rows that gets referenced three separate times later in the procedure, filtered differently each time, and would benefit from its own index on one of its columns. A junior developer on your team used a CTE for it because 'that's what we always use.' Explain why that choice is likely to hurt performance here, what you'd use instead and why, and the one scenario where a table variable would actually be the better choice over a temp table.
questions.modelAnswer:
A CTE isn't a stored, materialized result at all -- it's inlined into the statement that references it, and if you reference the same CTE three separate times, SQL Server may well re-run its underlying query three separate times (unless it happens to decide to spool the result on its own, which isn't something you can rely on or control). For a 200,000-row intermediate result referenced three times with different downstream filters, that risks recomputing the same expensive logic three times over, and a CTE also can't carry its own index -- so if the column you'd filter or join on isn't already well-served by indexes on the base tables, every one of those three references pays that cost independently.

A #temp table is the right choice here. It's a real, physically-stored table in tempdb, which means two things that matter directly to this scenario: SQL Server maintains real statistics on it, so the optimizer can build a genuinely informed plan for each of the three later queries against it (rather than guessing), and you can explicitly CREATE INDEX on it -- so the column those three downstream queries filter or join on can actually be indexed, turning three potential scans into three seeks. At 200,000 rows, this is squarely the 'thousands of rows, reused more than once, might need its own index' case.

A table variable would be the better choice only when the intermediate set is small -- a handful to a few hundred rows -- and you're specifically trying to avoid statement recompilation inside a stored procedure. Historically, SQL Server assumed a table variable held exactly one row for costing purposes (pre-2019 compatibility levels, or without the newer deferred-compilation improvements), which is actually fine when the set really is tiny, but would badly under-allocate resources at 200,000 rows -- the opposite of what you want here. Table variables also aren't rolled back by an enclosing ROLLBACK, which occasionally matters for specific logging/auditing patterns, but that's a narrower reason to choose one and isn't the deciding factor in this scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the junior developer: the CTE choice makes sense as a habit, but it's working against them here specifically because of how many rows there are and how many times it gets used. A CTE doesn't actually store anything -- every time you reference it, SQL Server might just re-run the query behind it from scratch, and it has no index of its own. If we're touching this 200,000-row set three separate times with three different filters, we could be paying for that underlying computation three times, and none of those three references get to use an index on it even if one would help a lot.

My recommendation is a #temp table instead: dump that intermediate result into it once, put an index on whatever column the three downstream queries actually filter or join on, and now each of those three references gets a real seek against real statistics instead of SQL Server guessing. That's exactly the profile -- meaningful row count, reused multiple times, benefits from its own index -- where a temp table wins clearly.

I'd also tell them table variables aren't wrong, just wrong for this case -- they're great when the set is genuinely small and you're inside a procedure trying to avoid a recompile every time row counts shift. The catch is that SQL Server has historically assumed a table variable holds about one row when it's building a plan, which is totally fine for a small set but would be a disaster at 200,000 rows -- the optimizer would badly under-allocate for a set that size, and the plan quality would suffer for every one of those three references, not help it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a CTE out of habit regardless of row count or reuse pattern
Not realizing a CTE referenced multiple times may re-run its underlying query each time
Assuming a table variable always outperforms a temp table because it 'sounds lighter weight'
Putting a large, reused intermediate set into a table variable and getting a poor plan from the one-row cardinality assumption
Forgetting that only a #temp table supports an explicit CREATE INDEX statement after the fact
keyPoints: CTEs are inlined and re-evaluated per reference, not materialized or indexed
#Temp tables are physically stored with maintained statistics and support explicit indexes
200,000 rows reused three times with filtering is a textbook #temp table case
Table variables historically get a one-row cardinality assumption, poor for large sets
Table variables fit small sets inside procedures where avoiding recompilation matters most

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a CTE is inlined/re-evaluated, not materialized
Recommends a #temp table and justifies it with statistics/indexing
Explains the risk of recomputation across three CTE references
Correctly identifies the scenario where a table variable wins
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Indexed Views: Mechanics and Restrictions
questions.prompt: Explain how an indexed view actually works under the hood in SQL Server — what SQL Server materializes, how it keeps that materialized data in sync with the base tables, and why indexed views come with such a strict list of requirements (deterministic functions only, no outer joins, SCHEMABINDING, etc.).
questions.modelAnswer: A standard view is just a stored query — nothing is persisted, and every time you select from it, SQL Server substitutes the view's definition into your query and compiles a plan against the base tables. An indexed view is fundamentally different: when you create a unique clustered index on a view, SQL Server actually materializes the result set of that view's query onto disk, in exactly the structure a clustered index implies (a b-tree with the data at the leaf level, physically sorted by the clustered index key). From that point on, the view's rows exist as real, maintained data, not a re-run query. Once that materialized data exists, SQL Server has to keep it transactionally consistent with the base tables, so every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against the underlying tables also triggers maintenance of the indexed view's data as part of the same transaction — this is handled automatically and synchronously, which is why indexed views add write overhead in proportion to how many views depend on the table. The strict rules exist precisely because this maintenance has to be deterministic and unambiguous: SCHEMABINDING is required so the base tables can't be altered out from under the view's materialized structure; aggregate functions need COUNT_BIG rather than COUNT so NULL/overflow semantics are unambiguous; outer joins and subqueries are disallowed because the engine can't always determine, incrementally, exactly which materialized rows need to change when a base row changes; and non-deterministic functions (GETDATE(), RAND()) are banned because the materialized value has to be reproducible and tied only to its deterministic inputs. In short, an indexed view trades write-time cost and a narrow set of allowed constructs for read-time speed, because the expensive aggregation or join work is done once at write time instead of on every read.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about indexed views is that they flip a normal view inside out. A regular view is lazy — it's just a saved SELECT statement, and the actual work happens every time someone queries it. An indexed view is the opposite: the moment you put a unique clustered index on it, SQL Server goes and physically builds that result set on disk, like any other table, and from then on it has to maintain it in real time. So if you've got an indexed view that aggregates sales by product, every single insert or update to the Sales table also updates that materialized aggregate behind the scenes, inside the same transaction. That's the trade-off — you're paying extra cost on every write so that reads against the view are basically free, just reading pre-computed data off disk instead of re-aggregating millions of rows. The restrictions make total sense once you see it that way — SCHEMABINDING locks the base tables so nobody can change a column type underneath the materialized structure, you need COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT because the engine needs predictable, deterministic math to maintain the aggregate incrementally, and things like outer joins or non-deterministic functions like GETDATE() are blocked because the engine genuinely can't figure out, row by row, exactly how to patch the materialized result when something changes upstream. I'd tell an interviewer: use indexed views when you have an expensive aggregate that's read far more often than the base data is written — that's the sweet spot — and be honest that they're not free, they add real overhead to every write against the underlying tables.
commonMistakes: Thinking an indexed view is 'just a view with an index for faster lookup' rather than a materialized, physically stored structure
Forgetting that maintenance happens synchronously inside the write transaction, not as an async refresh job
Not knowing why COUNT_BIG is mandatory instead of COUNT or COUNT(*)
Assuming indexed views support the same join/subquery flexibility as regular views
Overusing indexed views on heavy-write tables without weighing the write-amplification cost
keyPoints: Indexed views physically materialize the result set via a unique clustered index
Base table DML synchronously maintains the indexed view's data in the same transaction
SCHEMABINDING prevents base table changes that would break the materialized structure
Deterministic-only functions and no outer joins/subqueries are required for unambiguous incremental maintenance
The performance trade-off is faster reads at the cost of slower writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains physical materialization via unique clustered index
Explains synchronous maintenance on base table writes
Connects restrictions (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, no outer joins) to the underlying reason
Identifies the read-speed vs write-cost trade-off
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: Upserting Changed Customers with MERGE INTO, Then Z-Ordering for Lookups
questions.prompt: A nightly CDC batch lands in a staging Delta table staging.customer_changes containing customer_id plus the latest attribute values for customers that are new or have changed since the last run. Write a Delta Lake MERGE INTO statement that upserts those changes into curated.customers: insert customers that don't yet exist, update attributes on customers that actually changed, and do nothing for customers that landed in staging unchanged. Then explain why you'd follow this merge with an OPTIMIZE curated.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id) command, and what Z-ordering is actually doing on disk that makes it worth running.
questions.modelAnswer:
The MERGE joins staging.customer_changes to curated.customers on customer_id. The WHEN NOT MATCHED branch handles brand-new customers with a plain INSERT. The WHEN MATCHED branch is where the 'do nothing for unchanged rows' requirement actually gets enforced: without a change-detection predicate, MERGE would blindly UPDATE every matched row every night even when nothing actually changed, which is wasted write amplification against a Delta table. Adding a predicate like (tgt.email IS DISTINCT FROM src.email OR tgt.phone IS DISTINCT FROM src.phone OR ...) to the WHEN MATCHED clause means the UPDATE only fires for rows where at least one tracked attribute genuinely differs; rows where nothing changed simply don't match any WHEN clause and are left completely untouched. IS DISTINCT FROM is the deliberate choice over <> or !=, because standard inequality comparisons involving NULL evaluate to NULL (neither true nor false) rather than true, so a column that goes from a real value to NULL (or vice versa) would silently fail to trigger an update with <> -- IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value and correctly flags that as a change.

OPTIMIZE curated.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id) is worth running afterward for two separate reasons stacked together. First, OPTIMIZE performs file compaction (bin-packing): every MERGE, even one that only touches a handful of rows, can leave behind small files from the rewritten data files, and a table accumulating many small files forces downstream readers to open, read metadata from, and close far more files than necessary. OPTIMIZE rewrites those into fewer, larger files close to Delta's target file size. Second, and this is what ZORDER BY specifically adds on top of plain compaction: Delta tracks min/max statistics per file for data skipping, and Z-ordering physically co-locates rows with similar values of the Z-order column(s) into the same files during that rewrite. For a table like curated.customers that gets queried and joined constantly on customer_id, that co-location means each file's min/max range for customer_id becomes narrow and distinctive instead of overlapping broadly with every other file -- so a query filtering or joining on a specific customer_id can skip reading the vast majority of files entirely, because Delta can prove from the file-level statistics alone that the value can't be in them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always write this kind of MERGE with the no-op case in mind first, because that's the part people forget. The ON clause joins on customer_id, WHEN NOT MATCHED just inserts the new customer -- that part's easy. The WHEN MATCHED clause is where I add a change-detection condition across the attributes I actually care about, and I specifically use IS DISTINCT FROM instead of a plain not-equal, because not-equal against NULL in SQL just evaluates to unknown, not true -- so if a customer's phone number goes from having a value to NULL, a plain <> comparison would quietly never flag that as a change. IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe version that actually catches it. With that predicate in place, rows that genuinely didn't change don't match any WHEN clause at all, so MERGE leaves them alone -- which is exactly the 'do nothing' behavior being asked for.

As for OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY afterward -- I think of that as two favors in one command. OPTIMIZE alone just compacts the small files that a nightly MERGE tends to leave scattered around into fewer, bigger ones, which cuts down on file-open overhead for anyone reading the table. ZORDER BY customer_id is the extra step that actually sorts and co-locates data by that column while it's doing the rewrite, so each resulting file ends up covering a narrow, distinct range of customer_id values instead of a little bit of everything. That matters because Delta keeps min/max stats per file, and a query or join hitting a specific customer_id can use those narrow ranges to skip almost every file in the table instead of scanning all of them.
questions.example:
MERGE INTO curated.customers AS tgt
USING staging.customer_changes AS src
ON tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND (
       tgt.email        IS DISTINCT FROM src.email
    OR tgt.phone         IS DISTINCT FROM src.phone
    OR tgt.address_line1 IS DISTINCT FROM src.address_line1
    OR tgt.loyalty_tier   IS DISTINCT FROM src.loyalty_tier
) THEN UPDATE SET
    tgt.email         = src.email,
    tgt.phone          = src.phone,
    tgt.address_line1  = src.address_line1,
    tgt.loyalty_tier    = src.loyalty_tier,
    tgt.updated_at      = current_timestamp()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (
    customer_id, email, phone, address_line1, loyalty_tier, updated_at
) VALUES (
    src.customer_id, src.email, src.phone, src.address_line1, src.loyalty_tier, current_timestamp()
);

OPTIMIZE curated.customers
ZORDER BY (customer_id);
commonMistakes: Using <> or != instead of IS DISTINCT FROM, silently missing changes that involve NULL
Omitting a change-detection predicate entirely, causing every matched row to be rewritten on every run
Forgetting the WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT branch, so brand-new customers never make it into the curated table
Running OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY on a very large table far more often than the write pattern justifies, burning unnecessary compute
Choosing a ZORDER column that doesn't match the table's actual filter/join predicates, gaining no data-skipping benefit
keyPoints: ON clause joins on the natural/primary key (customer_id)
WHEN MATCHED uses a null-safe change predicate (IS DISTINCT FROM) so unchanged rows are true no-ops
WHEN NOT MATCHED handles inserts for brand-new customers
OPTIMIZE compacts small files left behind by incremental merges
ZORDER BY co-locates rows by the given column(s) so file-level min/max statistics enable data skipping
ZORDER columns should match real, frequent query/join predicates to pay off

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct overall MERGE INTO structure
Correct null-safe no-op/change-detection predicate on WHEN MATCHED
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT clause
Explains OPTIMIZE's file-compaction purpose
Explains Z-ordering's data-skipping mechanism via file statistics
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Deploying Azure SQL with Bicep, and What a Missing Default Parameter Does in CI/CD
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep template that deploys an Azure SQL logical server, a database on that server, and a firewall rule allowing Azure services to connect, using parameters for the server name, admin login, admin password, database SKU, and the firewall rule's IP range. Then explain the real difference between a Bicep parameter declared with a default value and one declared without a default, specifically in terms of what happens when that template is deployed non-interactively from a CI/CD pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Bicep parameter declared with a default value is optional at deployment time: if the caller, whether that's a CI/CD pipeline, an az deployment command, or another module, doesn't explicitly supply a value, Bicep silently falls back to the default and the deployment proceeds without complaint. A parameter declared without a default is required: Bicep/ARM validates that every required parameter has a supplied value before the deployment is even allowed to start, and if one is missing, the deployment fails immediately at validation with an explicit 'missing required parameter' error.

That distinction matters most for a non-interactive CI/CD pipeline, because there's no human sitting at a prompt to supply a forgotten value -- whatever behavior the parameter declaration specifies is exactly what happens, with zero chance for someone to notice and type in a correction partway through. For a value like location or databaseSku, where there's a sensible standard choice most deployments should use, a default is appropriate: it lets most pipeline runs omit it entirely while still allowing an override when a specific deployment genuinely needs one. For sqlAdminLogin and especially sqlAdminPassword, the opposite is true: those should be required parameters with no default (the password additionally marked @secure() so it's never persisted in deployment history or logs), precisely because you want a hard, explicit failure forcing the pipeline to pull the value from a key vault or secure variable group every single time, rather than risk a template silently deploying with some hardcoded or forgotten placeholder credential baked into source control.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd put it: a default value makes a parameter optional, no default makes it mandatory, and the difference only really bites once nobody's around to catch a mistake -- which is exactly the situation in a CI/CD pipeline. If a parameter has a default and the pipeline doesn't pass anything for it, the deployment just quietly uses that default and keeps going. If there's no default and the pipeline forgets to pass it, the deployment refuses to even start -- it fails validation up front with a clear error instead of limping along with some guessed value.

That's why I'm deliberate about which of my parameters get defaults. Something like location or the database SKU, where there's a perfectly reasonable standard choice -- sure, give it a default, so most runs don't even have to think about it but can still override it when they need to. But the admin login and especially the admin password -- those I leave without defaults on purpose, and I mark the password @secure() on top of that. I want the pipeline to be forced to pull that value from somewhere secure every time, not accidentally succeed with a stale or hardcoded credential nobody noticed was still sitting there as a fallback.
commonMistakes: Giving sqlAdminPassword a default value (even a blank placeholder), undermining the point of requiring it explicitly each deployment
Forgetting the @secure() decorator on the password parameter, exposing it in deployment history
Using an overly broad firewall IP range instead of the 0.0.0.0-0.0.0.0 'Allow Azure services' convention
Hardcoding the database SKU instead of exposing it as a parameter
Assuming a parameter with a default still forces the pipeline to supply a value
keyPoints: A defaulted parameter is optional; the deployment silently falls back to the default if omitted
A non-defaulted parameter is required; validation fails immediately if it's missing
In non-interactive CI/CD, there's no prompt to recover from a missing required value -- it simply fails fast
Secrets like the admin password should be required (no default) and marked @secure()
Standard, non-sensitive values like location or SKU are reasonable candidates for defaults

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Bicep resources (SQL server, database, firewall rule)
Correct parameterization of server name, admin login/password, SKU, and IP range
Correct @secure() usage on the password parameter
Accurately explains optional-vs-required parameter behavior at deployment time
Explains why secrets should never have defaults in a CI/CD context

questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct anchor/recursive member structure in the query
Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ROW_NUMBER/PARTITION BY/DELETE query
Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Covering, Filtered Index for a High-Frequency Reporting Query
questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint runs this query hundreds of times per minute: SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product WHERE Color = 'Red' AND SellEndDate IS NULL ORDER BY ListPrice. Design the single nonclustered index you'd create to best serve it -- specifying key column order, included columns, and any filter -- and explain exactly how you'd confirm in the execution plan that it's actually being used as a fully covering seek rather than falling back to a scan or a key lookup.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query filters on Color (equality) and SellEndDate IS NULL, then orders by ListPrice, and selects ProductID, Name, ListPrice. I'd build the index key on Color first, since it's the equality predicate the optimizer can seek on directly, then ListPrice second, since that both satisfies part of the ORDER BY and keeps rows pre-sorted within each color -- letting the engine potentially avoid a separate sort operator entirely. ProductID and Name don't belong in the key at all; they're only ever selected, never filtered or sorted on, so they belong as INCLUDE columns, which attaches their data to the index's leaf level without making them part of the search key (keeping the key itself narrow). Finally, since this query only ever cares about currently-active products, I'd add a filter: WHERE SellEndDate IS NULL, so the index only covers the subset of rows this specific query pattern actually needs -- smaller, faster to scan, and still perfectly usable by any other query matching that same filter condition.

To confirm it's working as intended, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run the exact production query. I'm looking for a single Index Seek operator with no accompanying Key Lookup and no separate Sort operator afterward -- that combination means the index is fully covering (every selected column came straight from the index, no trip back to the clustered index) and pre-sorted for the ORDER BY. If I instead see an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup, that tells me I missed an included column the query actually needs. If I see a Sort operator after the seek, either my key column order doesn't match the ORDER BY the way I assumed, or the optimizer decided sorting was cheaper than using the index's physical order for some other reason. And if I see a Scan instead of a Seek at all, I'd first check that the filter predicate on the index exactly matches the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server will only use a filtered index when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter, and a subtle mismatch (like comparing against a variable instead of a literal in some SQL Server versions) can silently prevent that match and fall back to scanning the base table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through the query, I see one equality filter (Color), one IS NULL filter that's really describing 'currently active products' (SellEndDate), an ORDER BY on ListPrice, and three columns actually being selected. So my index key is Color first, because that's the equality predicate, then ListPrice second, because that handles the sort and keeps things grouped nicely within each color. ProductID and Name never show up in a WHERE or ORDER BY here, so I don't want them cluttering the key -- they go in as INCLUDE columns instead, just along for the ride so the index can hand back the full row without touching the base table. And since this query only ever wants active products, I'd make the whole index filtered on SellEndDate IS NULL -- there's no reason to carry the weight of retired products in an index built specifically for this access pattern.

To prove it's actually helping, I turn on the actual plan and run the real query, and I want to see exactly one operator: an Index Seek, nothing else hanging off it. If there's a Key Lookup tagging along, that tells me I forgot to include a column the query needed. If there's a Sort sitting after the seek, my key order isn't lining up with the ORDER BY the way I thought it would. And if I'm staring at a Scan instead of a Seek, my first suspicion is that the filter on the index doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server is strict about that match for a filtered index, and small mismatches are a classic reason the optimizer quietly falls back to ignoring it.
commonMistakes: Putting ProductID/Name in the index key instead of as INCLUDE columns, widening the key unnecessarily
Forgetting the ORDER BY column when choosing key column order, leaving a Sort in the plan
Leaving off the filter, indexing retired products the query never actually needs
Assuming an Index Seek alone proves full coverage without checking for an accompanying Key Lookup
Writing a filter predicate that doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause, causing SQL Server to ignore the filtered index
keyPoints: Equality predicate columns go first in the index key, ahead of sort/range columns
ORDER BY columns in the key can eliminate a separate Sort operator
Select-only columns belong in INCLUDE, not the key, to keep the key narrow
A filtered index should match the query's WHERE clause as closely as possible
Verify with the actual execution plan: single seek, no Key Lookup, no Sort = fully covering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct key column choice and order (Color, ListPrice)
Correctly places ProductID/Name as INCLUDE columns
Correctly applies the SellEndDate IS NULL filter
Describes verifying via actual execution plan (seek, no key lookup, no sort)
Explains what a Key Lookup or Sort in the plan would each indicate is wrong

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';
commonMistakes: Only fixing one of the two predicates and leaving the other non-SARGable branch in the OR
Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies both predicates as non-SARGable and explains why
Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Uses a half-open interval that correctly handles time components
Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
Clean, correct SQL syntax

questions.title: A Dashboard-Facing Delta Table Has Quietly Degraded From Small Files
questions.prompt: A Delta table feeding several BI dashboards has been append-only, ingested every 15 minutes by a streaming job for the last 8 months. Row count has only grown about 20% in that time, the query the dashboards run hasn't changed, but the same query that used to return in 3 seconds now takes 3-4 minutes. Nobody on the team has ever run OPTIMIZE or VACUUM on this table. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it, and how you'd prove the fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd confirm the symptom is really a small-file problem before touching anything, rather than assuming. Running DESCRIBE DETAIL on the table gives numFiles and sizeInBytes directly, and dividing those two gives average file size. If that number comes back in the tens or low hundreds of KB on a table this size and age, that's a hard confirmation, not a guess -- the recommended Delta file size for good query performance is generally in the 128MB-1GB range depending on table size.

The root cause is mechanical once you see the file count: a streaming job appending every 15 minutes for 8 months is roughly 23,000 micro-batches, and each micro-batch writes at least one new Parquet file, often more depending on partitioning and task parallelism. With OPTIMIZE never run, file count scales with how often the job fired, not with how much data arrived -- those are two completely different axes. That's exactly why a 20% row-count increase and a 60-80x runtime increase don't correlate: the thing that actually got worse is file count, not data volume.

Why that hurts dashboard queries specifically: the query engine has to open, read the footer of, and schedule a task for every single file, and at hundreds of thousands to over a million files that per-file overhead -- especially against cloud object storage with per-request latency -- dwarfs the actual time spent scanning 40GB of real data. The Delta transaction log itself also gets more expensive to plan against with that many file entries recorded across its history.

The fix is OPTIMIZE to compact the small files into right-sized ones, but a one-time compaction alone just resets the clock on the same problem recurring in another few months. I'd also enable delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite and delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact as table properties (or move to liquid clustering if the runtime supports it) so new small files get compacted automatically going forward instead of silently accumulating again. I'd run VACUUM afterward too, but I'd be precise about what it does: VACUUM only removes files that are no longer referenced after the retention window (default 7 days) to reclaim storage and reduce the file-listing surface -- it has no effect on query speed on its own, so running VACUUM without OPTIMIZE would not have fixed this at all.

To verify, I'd re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and show the before/after on numFiles and average file size, then re-run the actual dashboard query and compare wall-clock time and Spark UI task counts/bytes read before and after -- that's the real proof, not just a feeling that it's faster.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The row-count math is the tell for me before I even open a notebook -- rows grew 20%, runtime grew 60-80x, so whatever's slow isn't proportional to data volume, which means it's probably proportional to something else: file count. I'd go straight to DESCRIBE DETAIL and look at numFiles versus sizeInBytes, because dividing those two gives me average file size, and if that number is sitting in the tens or hundreds of KB on a table this old, that's my answer right there.

What actually happened is pretty mechanical: this table's been fed by a streaming job every 15 minutes for eight months, and every one of those roughly 23,000 micro-batches wrote at least one new file. Nobody ever ran OPTIMIZE, so the file count scaled with how often the job ran, not with how much data came in -- those are two completely different axes, which is exactly why the row-count growth and the slowdown don't match.

Why that kills a dashboard specifically: every query has to open, read the footer of, and schedule a task for each of those files, and at over a million files that per-file overhead swamps the actual work of scanning 40GB of data. The transaction log itself has also gotten heavier to plan against with that many file entries.

The fix is OPTIMIZE, but I wouldn't stop there -- a one-time compaction just resets the clock on the same problem recurring. I'd turn on autoOptimize.optimizeWrite and autoCompact (or move to liquid clustering if the runtime supports it) so this doesn't quietly come back in another eight months. And I'd be careful not to conflate this with VACUUM -- VACUUM is a storage cleanup step that removes files no longer referenced after the retention window, it has zero effect on query speed, so running it alone wouldn't have fixed anything here.

To prove it worked, I'd show the before/after on numFiles and average file size directly, and then the actual dashboard query time, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming row-count growth explains the slowdown and never checking file count or average file size at all
Running VACUUM expecting it to speed up queries, when it only reclaims storage after the retention window
Running OPTIMIZE once but never enabling auto-optimize/auto-compact, so the problem quietly returns in a few more months
Choosing a Z-ORDER column that doesn't match the dashboard's actual filter columns, which doesn't address the core small-file issue
Jumping straight to resizing the cluster instead of looking at file layout first
keyPoints: DESCRIBE DETAIL's numFiles and average file size is the correct diagnostic signal, not row count
Root cause: many small files from frequent streaming appends that were never compacted
OPTIMIZE compacts files and improves query speed; VACUUM only reclaims storage after retention and doesn't touch query speed
Prevent recurrence with autoOptimize.optimizeWrite/autoCompact or liquid clustering
Verify with before/after numFiles, average file size, and actual query wall-clock time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses DESCRIBE DETAIL / file count and size to confirm the small-file problem
Correctly explains the root cause (frequent small appends never compacted)
Prescribes OPTIMIZE as the fix
Distinguishes OPTIMIZE's query benefit from VACUUM's storage-only benefit
Proposes prevention (auto-optimize) and concrete before/after verification

questions.title: Autoloader Started Silently Skipping Files After a Storage Lifecycle Policy Change
questions.prompt: An Autoloader stream ingests hourly JSON files into a Delta table, running on a job cluster that starts and terminates each hour. A few weeks ago the storage team added an account-wide lifecycle rule that deletes any blob older than 30 days, including blobs under the stream's checkpoint location, to save on storage cost. A monthly reconciliation just found that a handful of source files over the last six weeks were never ingested into the table, with no errors, warnings, or failed runs anywhere in the job history. Walk through why Autoloader's checkpoint and file-tracking design makes it vulnerable to exactly this, and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
First I'd rule out the obvious, loud failure mode: malformed or schema-mismatched records. Autoloader's rescue mechanism and bad-records handling leave visible evidence -- a rescued-data column, entries at a configured badRecordsPath, or schema-evolution failures that stop the stream. Since there's zero evidence of any of that and the job history shows clean, successful runs the whole time, that rules out a data-quality skip and points at something structural in how the stream tracks its own progress.

The actual mechanism: a checkpoint location holds more than the standard Structured Streaming offset and commit logs. Autoloader also maintains its own file-tracking state there -- a RocksDB-backed record of which source files have already been seen and enqueued, used by directory-listing mode to avoid reprocessing or losing track of progress. All of that, plus the offset/commit delta log, is written as a long series of small log segments that Spark intends to periodically compact (by default roughly every 10 batches) into a durable snapshot, but which are otherwise expected to persist indefinitely -- they are not disposable application logs.

A blanket 30-day age-based lifecycle rule has no concept of any of that; it deletes blob segments purely by age, regardless of whether Structured Streaming has rolled them into a compacted snapshot yet. Because this job runs on an auto-terminating hourly job cluster, the stream has to fully reconstruct its state from whatever remains in the checkpoint path on every single run. If pieces of that state -- especially the older RocksDB segments or uncompacted offset/commit deltas -- get deleted before a compaction consumed them, recovery can end up with an incomplete picture of what's genuinely still pending versus already processed. In practice that surfaces not as a crash but as the listing high-water mark silently advancing past files that were sitting in the source directory but had not actually been ingested, because the piece of state that would have still flagged them as pending was the piece that got deleted.

To confirm this cheaply: correlate the specific missing files' arrival timestamps against the lifecycle policy's 30-day cutoff and the job's hourly restart cadence, and check the storage account's lifecycle/management policy and its delete activity logs scoped to the checkpoint container or prefix.

The fix has two parts and both matter. First, exclude the checkpoint location (and the Autoloader schema location, if separate) from any lifecycle/retention policy entirely -- those paths need to persist indefinitely and should only ever be managed by Spark or Databricks' own mechanisms. Second, backfill the files that already fell through the gap: simply restarting the stream will not retroactively pick them up, since whatever high-water mark the stream now holds has already moved past them. A one-time scoped batch read using Autoloader with modifiedAfter/modifiedBefore file filters covering the gap window, written into the same Delta table, recovers the missing data. I'd verify by reconciling the full source file inventory against the table afterward, and add an ongoing count-based alert so a future silent gap surfaces immediately rather than at the next manual reconciliation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct whenever Autoloader drops files is to check for the loud, well-known failure mode -- malformed records getting rescued or routed to a bad-records path -- but the fact that this is completely silent, with zero evidence anywhere, tells me it's not that. Malformed data leaves a trail; this didn't.

So I'd go to what actually lives in a checkpoint directory, because people tend to think of it as just 'where Spark remembers its offset,' and that's only half of it. Autoloader keeps its own file-tracking state there too -- a RocksDB-backed record of which source files it's already seen and enqueued -- and that state, along with the standard offset and commit logs, is written as a long series of small log segments that are meant to be periodically compacted, not aged out by a generic cleanup rule.

That's exactly what collides with a 30-day lifecycle policy applied blindly across the whole storage account. It doesn't know those files are special; it just deletes anything old. If this job runs on a cluster that spins up and down every hour, it has to fully reload its state from whatever's left in that checkpoint path on every single run -- so if pieces of that state got swept away before Spark had compacted them into a durable snapshot, recovery can end up with an incomplete picture of what's actually been processed, and in practice that surfaces as files quietly falling through a gap rather than the job crashing outright.

I'd confirm it cheaply -- line up the missing files' timestamps against the lifecycle cutoff and the cluster's restart schedule, and check the storage account's delete activity around those dates. The fix has two parts, and I'd insist on both: exclude the checkpoint (and schema location) from any lifecycle policy going forward, since those paths need to live indefinitely, and then actually backfill the specific files that already fell through the gap -- restarting the stream won't retroactively pick them up, because whatever high-water mark it's working from has already moved past them. A scoped batch read with modifiedAfter/modifiedBefore into the same table handles that backfill cleanly.
questions.example:
# Backfill the gap window without disturbing the live checkpoint
df = (spark.read.format("cloudFiles")
      .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
      .option("modifiedAfter", "2026-08-15T00:00:00Z")
      .option("modifiedBefore", "2026-09-26T00:00:00Z")
      .load("abfss://source@acct.dfs.core.windows.net/events/"))
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("events.landing")

# Exclude the checkpoint path from the account-wide lifecycle rule
az storage account management-policy show --account-name acct \
  --resource-group rg-data | grep -A5 checkpoints
commonMistakes: Assuming any Autoloader gap must be a malformed/bad-records issue, since that's the well-documented, loud failure mode
Not realizing the checkpoint location holds Autoloader's own file-tracking state, not just Spark's standard offset/commit logs
Applying a lifecycle/retention policy account-wide without excluding checkpoint and schema-tracking paths
Restarting the stream and assuming it will automatically catch up on the already-missed files
Fixing the lifecycle policy going forward but never backfilling the files that were already skipped
keyPoints: Autoloader's checkpoint path holds both standard Structured Streaming offset/commit logs and Autoloader's own RocksDB-backed file-tracking state
Checkpoint and state files are not safe to age out under a blanket lifecycle policy; they must be explicitly excluded
An auto-terminating cluster that reloads state on every run makes this failure mode worse
Diagnosis: correlate missing-file timestamps against the lifecycle cutoff and the cluster-restart cadence, plus storage delete logs
Fix requires excluding the checkpoint path AND a manual backfill -- restarting the stream alone will not recover already-missed files

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Rules out malformed/bad-records as the cause with a specific reason
Correctly explains what state actually lives in the checkpoint beyond standard offsets
Explains the mechanism by which lifecycle deletion causes silent skipping rather than a crash
Proposes excluding the checkpoint path from the lifecycle policy
Proposes a concrete backfill approach for the already-missed files
Proposes ongoing verification/monitoring to catch this earlier next time

questions.title: Terraform Apply Fails With 'Resource Already Exists' After a Manual Incident Fix
questions.prompt: During an incident last week, an engineer manually created a storage account and a couple of firewall rules directly in the Azure Portal to restore service quickly, without updating the Terraform code or state for the shared data-platform environment. Nobody has touched the Terraform configuration for those resources since. Today's terraform apply for that environment fails with Azure errors that the storage account and firewall rules already exist. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and safely bring Terraform back in sync, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the actual error carefully first: an Azure 'already exists' or conflict error on an apply, for a resource that terraform plan showed as 'will be created' rather than 'will be updated,' is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change -- the real resource exists in Azure, but Terraform's state has no record of it, so Terraform tries to create it from scratch and Azure's own uniqueness constraints reject the duplicate.

I'd confirm the drift explicitly rather than assume it: run terraform plan and verify the affected resources show as '+ create,' and cross-reference the resource names/IDs from the error against what's actually visible via az resource show or the Portal. In this case that directly confirms the incident-week manual resources are the cause.

Structurally, this happens because Terraform state is only ever updated by Terraform itself -- through apply, import, or refresh. Any resource created directly through the Portal, the CLI, or by an engineer bypassing Terraform is completely invisible to the state file no matter how long it's existed, and a plan has no way to discover it on its own; it only compares the configuration against what's already recorded in state.

The fix is terraform import. For each drifted resource, I'd get its real Azure resource ID (az resource show --name ... --resource-group ... --resource-type ... --query id) and run terraform import <resource_address_in_config> <azure_resource_id> to attach the real object into state under the matching address. This requires a resource block already existing in the .tf configuration for that address -- import only binds state, it doesn't generate configuration, unless using Terraform's newer import block with -generate-config-out, which can scaffold a starting config from the real resource if the .tf code doesn't exist yet.

After importing, I'd immediately run terraform plan again -- this is the step people skip. Import only syncs the state's existence record; it says nothing about whether the .tf configuration's attributes actually match what was configured manually during the incident (for example, a firewall rule's IP range might differ from what's in code). The follow-up plan will show any genuine attribute drift as an '~ update,' which has to be reconciled deliberately: either update the .tf code to match the real, intentional incident configuration, or apply to bring the resource back to the originally-intended configuration, depending on which is actually correct going forward.

Beyond the immediate fix, I'd treat this as a process signal: if manual changes during an incident are sometimes unavoidable, build a habit or runbook step of importing them back into Terraform (or at minimum filing a ticket to do so) right after the incident closes, rather than discovering the drift weeks later at the next unrelated apply.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The error message itself tells me almost everything before I look at anything else -- Azure saying a resource 'already exists' on something Terraform's plan wanted to create, not update, is basically the textbook signature of state drift. Something real exists out there that Terraform's state file has simply never heard of.

I wouldn't just assume that, though -- I'd run plan and actually look at whether it's showing a '+ create' for those resources, and cross-check the names against what's genuinely sitting in the Portal or az resource show. In this case that's trivial to confirm, because we already know exactly what happened: someone created these by hand in the Portal during last week's incident, and nothing about that touched Terraform's code or state.

The mechanical reason this happens is worth being precise about: Terraform's state file only ever gets updated by Terraform itself. It has no way to notice, on its own, that a human created something matching its configuration out-of-band -- it just compares its config against whatever it already has on record, and if there's no record, its only option is to try to create it, which collides with the real one that's already there.

So the fix is terraform import -- get the real Azure resource ID, point it at the matching resource address in the .tf config, and import binds the two together in state. The part I'd be careful not to skip is what comes right after: import only fixes the fact that Terraform now knows the resource exists. It says nothing about whether the configuration in code actually matches what got configured by hand during the incident.
