So the very next thing is another plan, and whatever shows up as an update this time -- maybe a firewall rule's IP range doesn't match -- is a deliberate decision to make: update the code to reflect the real, intentional incident fix, or apply to bring it back to what was originally intended. Either is fine, but it has to be a decision, not an accident. And longer-term, I'd push for a habit of importing incident-time manual changes back into Terraform right away, rather than discovering this kind of drift at the next unrelated apply weeks later.
questions.example:
# Get the real Azure resource ID
az storage account show --name stdataplat01 --resource-group rg-data-platform --query id -o tsv

# Bind it into state at the matching config address
terraform import azurerm_storage_account.data_platform \
  /subscriptions/xxxx/resourceGroups/rg-data-platform/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stdataplat01

# ALWAYS re-plan after import to catch attribute-level drift
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Assuming the Terraform code itself is broken since 'nothing in it changed'
Deleting the manually-created Azure resources to let Terraform recreate them cleanly, discarding the incident fix
Running terraform import without first confirming via plan which specific resources/attributes are actually drifted
Treating import as a complete fix and not re-running plan afterward to catch attribute-level drift
Importing into the wrong resource address, not matching an existing/correct resource block, causing a different drift
keyPoints: 'Already exists' on a planned create, not an update, is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change
Terraform state only changes via Terraform itself; manually-created resources are invisible to it until explicitly imported
terraform import attaches an existing real resource to a state address but requires a matching config block (or the import block with -generate-config-out)
Import only fixes existence tracking -- a follow-up plan is required to catch and reconcile attribute-level drift
Process takeaway: import out-of-band incident changes back into Terraform promptly, not weeks later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses 'already exists on a create' as state drift from an out-of-band manual change
Explains why Terraform state doesn't auto-discover manually created resources
Walks through terraform import correctly (resource ID lookup, address, requires config)
Emphasizes re-running plan after import to catch attribute drift
Notes a process improvement for future incidents

questions.title: A Stuck Terraform State Lock Is Blocking Every Deployment After a CI Crash
questions.prompt: A CI pipeline running terraform apply against a remote state backend lost network connectivity partway through and the job was killed before it could finish. Every terraform apply, and even terraform plan, run against that environment since has failed immediately with a state lock error, and the team is blocked from deploying anything to that environment. Walk through how you'd safely diagnose and resolve this, in the order you'd actually do it, including what you'd check before touching the lock.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the lock error output carefully first. Most backends that support locking (Azure Storage via a blob lease, S3 with a DynamoDB lock table, Terraform Cloud) surface identifying details directly in the error -- a Lock ID, who or what acquired it, and a timestamp. That information is the starting point, not something to skip past to get straight to unlocking.

Before touching anything, I'd rule out that this is a real, currently-in-progress apply rather than a stale lock left behind by the crashed job. I'd check the CI system's own run history or dashboard for that environment to confirm no other pipeline run is actively executing right now, and if there's any ambiguity I'd check with the team or on-call directly. The entire point of the lock is to prevent two concurrent applies from reading and writing the shared state file at the same time, which can corrupt it -- one apply's changes getting silently overwritten by the other's stale read is the real danger here, not a hypothetical one, so removing a lock that's protecting a genuinely active apply is the actual risk I'm managing against.

Once I've confirmed no other apply is running, I'd check whether the underlying state storage itself was left in a bad condition by the crash, not just locked -- for an Azure Storage backend, checking the blob's lease status directly (az storage blob show), and checking whether blob soft-delete or versioning is enabled so I could inspect or recover a prior good version of the state file if needed. For other backends I'd check the equivalent, such as a DynamoDB lock table item for S3, or the run status in Terraform Cloud.

To resolve the stale lock itself, I'd run terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> using the Lock ID from the error message. This only removes the lock record; it doesn't touch or validate the actual state file contents.

Immediately afterward I'd verify state integrity before trusting it: run terraform plan and read it carefully. If the crashed apply got partway through actually changing real infrastructure before losing connectivity, the state file may not fully reflect that, and the plan might show unexpected diffs for resources that were mid-change. I'd compare anything surprising against what's actually deployed (az resource show or the Portal) before applying further, and if the state looks meaningfully inconsistent with reality, I'd consider reconciling it or, in the worst case, pulling a previous good state version from backend versioning rather than trusting a possibly-partial write.

Once plan looks sane, I'd proceed with a normal apply. As a process follow-up, I'd flag whether the CI pipeline needs better handling for interrupted runs -- a cleanup step, or relying on the backend's native lease/lock timeout where supported -- so an infrastructure blip doesn't require a manual force-unlock every time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I touch the lock at all, I want to understand what it's actually there to prevent, because that framing changes how carefully I approach this. The lock exists so two applies can't read and write the same state file at the same time -- if that happened, one apply's changes could silently get clobbered by the other's stale read, which is a much worse problem than being temporarily blocked. So my first move isn't force-unlock, it's making sure I'm not about to remove a lock that's protecting something that's genuinely still running.

I'd check the CI system's own history for that environment to confirm nothing is actively executing, and if there's any doubt, I'd just ask the team directly rather than guess. Once I'm confident the lock is stale -- left behind by the job that got killed mid-run when it lost connectivity -- I'd look at the lock error itself, which for most backends gives me a Lock ID and some context about who/what acquired it, and I'd also check the underlying storage directly, like the blob's lease status if this is an Azure Storage backend, to see if there's anything else inconsistent beyond just the lock.

Then force-unlock with that specific Lock ID. But I don't treat that as the finish line -- force-unlock only removes the lock record, it doesn't tell me anything about whether the state file itself is trustworthy after a crash that happened mid-apply. So the very next thing is a plan, read carefully: if the crashed run had actually started changing real infrastructure before it lost connectivity, the state might not fully reflect that, and I'd expect to see it in unexpected diffs. If anything looks off, I'd rather pull a known-good prior version of the state from the backend's versioning than apply on top of something I don't trust. Only once plan looks sane do I let anyone apply again, and I'd flag the CI pipeline's handling of interrupted runs as a real follow-up so this doesn't become a recurring manual fire drill.
questions.example:
# Error typically includes the Lock ID and holder info:
# Error: Error acquiring the state lock
# Lock Info:
#   ID:        7f3a1c2e-...
#   Operation: OperationTypeApply
#   Who:       ci-runner-42
#   Created:   2026-10-02 09:14:03 UTC

# Confirm no apply is genuinely still running (CI history), then:
az storage blob show --container-name tfstate --name prod.terraform.tfstate --account-name tfstateacct

terraform force-unlock 7f3a1c2e-...

# Verify state integrity before trusting it
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Running terraform force-unlock immediately without first confirming no apply is genuinely still in progress
Treating the lock itself as the problem rather than asking what it's protecting against
Assuming the state file is definitely fine once the lock is removed, without reviewing plan output for signs of a partial write
Not checking whether the crashed apply actually changed real infrastructure before the connection dropped
Manually deleting the lock blob/file instead of using the proper force-unlock command, risking an inconsistent backend locking state
keyPoints: The lock exists to prevent two concurrent applies from corrupting shared state via simultaneous read-modify-write, not as an arbitrary safeguard
Always confirm no apply is genuinely still running before force-unlocking
terraform force-unlock removes the lock record only; it doesn't validate or repair the state file itself
Review plan output carefully afterward for signs the crashed apply partially changed infrastructure
Backend versioning/soft-delete, where available, is the safety net if the state file itself looks inconsistent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains what the lock actually protects against
Confirms no concurrent apply is running before acting
Correctly uses terraform force-unlock with the Lock ID
Verifies state/plan integrity after unlocking rather than assuming it's fine
Notes a process improvement or backend-recovery safety net

questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes deadlock (1205) from ordinary blocking
Describes SQL Server's automatic deadlock detection and victim rollback
Names a real diagnostic method for capturing the deadlock graph
Identifies inconsistent access order as the root cause
Proposes a concrete redesign (consistent order, shorter transactions, retry logic)
Clear, structured troubleshooting narrative

questions.title: A Nightly Staging Query's Runtime Quietly Tripled
questions.prompt: A nightly ETL step that filters Sales.SalesOrderHeader by a date range used to finish in under a minute. After a recent, unrelated application release, it now takes over 20 minutes most nights, even though nobody touched the query text itself. Walk through your full diagnostic process, in the order you'd actually do it, to find the real cause and prove your fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd work outward from the query itself before looking anywhere else, because the fact that nobody touched this query's text doesn't mean nothing that affects it changed.

First, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run it, looking specifically for whether an operation that used to be an Index Seek is now a Scan -- that's the single most common visible signature of a regressed query. I'd also compare estimated vs. actual row counts on each operator; a big gap there points at stale statistics giving the optimizer bad cardinality estimates, which can push it toward a much worse plan even though the query text is identical.

Second, I'd capture SET STATISTICS TIME and SET STATISTICS IO output and compare it mentally against what I'd expect for this table's size. If CPU time and elapsed time are close, it's genuinely doing more logical work; if elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, something else -- blocking, waits, disk I/O contention -- is adding wait time on top of comparable actual work, and I'd pivot to sys.dm_exec_requests / sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks to see what wait type is dominating.

Third, I'd specifically check whether the query's WHERE clause is still SARGable the way it was before. The "unrelated application release" detail is a flag: if the application layer changed how it passes the date parameter -- say, switching from a DATETIME parameter to a string that now gets implicitly converted, or wrapping the column in a function somewhere upstream that got introduced in the release -- that alone can silently turn a seek into a scan without anyone touching this specific query's text.

Fourth, if this runs as a parameterized query or inside a stored procedure, I'd consider parameter sniffing: if the release changed what date ranges get passed first after a recompile, SQL Server may have cached a plan optimized for a very different-sized result set than what's typically requested now. I'd check sys.dm_exec_query_stats for that procedure's cached plan and compare it against a fresh OPTION (RECOMPILE) run.

Fifth, I'd check whether an index this query relied on was changed, disabled, or had its fill factor/maintenance schedule altered as part of the release, and whether statistics were updated recently -- a large data load with no corresponding stats update is a very common, very quiet cause of exactly this symptom.

Finally, I'd correlate the actual onset against the release timeline and any index maintenance job history, form a specific hypothesis from whichever of the above turned up concrete evidence, apply the fix (rebuild/update statistics, restore a missing index, fix an implicit conversion, add OPTION (RECOMPILE) or a plan guide for parameter sniffing), and then prove it with a direct before/after comparison of logical reads via SET STATISTICS IO -- that number is the most reliable proof a fix genuinely reduced work, independent of how busy the server happened to be at the moment I measured it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't jump straight to 'rebuild the index' or 'update stats' -- I'd want to actually see what changed first. So step one for me is always the actual execution plan, Ctrl+M, run the query, and look specifically for a scan where I'd expect a seek, plus a big gap between estimated and actual row counts, because that gap is basically SQL Server telling you its statistics are lying to it.

Step two, I'd pull SET STATISTICS TIME and IO and look at whether CPU time and elapsed time line up. If they're close, the engine's genuinely doing more work. If elapsed time is way bigger than CPU time, I know to go look at waits and blocking instead of the query logic itself.

The detail that really jumps out at me in this scenario is 'an unrelated application release' right before this started. That's exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks SARGability without anyone touching the SQL -- maybe the app now sends the date as a string instead of a proper date, and now there's an implicit conversion happening on every row. I'd check that specifically.

If this lives inside a stored procedure, parameter sniffing is next on my list -- the first execution after a recompile caches a plan shaped for whatever parameter came in that first time, and if the typical date range changed after the release, that cached plan might be wrong for almost every call since. And I'd double check whether an index got dropped, disabled, or just went stale from a big data load with no corresponding stats update around the same time as the release.

Whatever I land on, I don't call it fixed until I've got a before-and-after comparison of logical reads from STATISTICS IO -- that number doesn't lie the way timing can when the server's under different load each time I test.
commonMistakes: Assuming the query must be unchanged and therefore can't be the cause
Jumping to 'rebuild all the indexes' without first checking the actual plan for a scan-vs-seek regression
Ignoring that an unrelated application change can break SARGability through implicit conversion
Not checking for parameter sniffing on parameterized/stored-procedure queries
Declaring victory based on a single wall-clock timing instead of logical reads before/after
keyPoints: Start with the actual execution plan: look for scan-vs-seek regressions and estimated/actual row count gaps
SET STATISTICS TIME/IO separates CPU-bound work from waiting/blocking
An unrelated release can break SARGability via implicit conversion or a changed parameter type
Parameter sniffing is a real suspect for parameterized/stored-procedure queries after a recompile
Check for dropped/disabled indexes and stale statistics correlated with the release timeline
Prove the fix with a before/after logical-reads comparison, not just a timing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts diagnosis with the actual execution plan
Uses STATISTICS TIME/IO to separate CPU vs. wait-driven slowness
Considers SARGability/implicit conversion broken by the unrelated release
Considers parameter sniffing as a plausible cause
Checks indexing/statistics changes correlated with the release
Proves the fix with evidence (logical reads before/after)

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'nobody changed the code' rules out a regression, missing that growing data volume is itself the real cause
Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with STATISTICS TIME/IO or direct timing, not assumption
Cursor cost scales with fixed per-row overhead that compounds as row counts grow month over month
Check the cursor's own driving query for separate degradation (stale stats, scan vs. seek)
Rewrite as one set-based UPDATE ... FROM statement
Validate the rewrite produces identical results before replacing the original in production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a concrete way to confirm the cursor is the bottleneck
Explains why cursor cost compounds as data grows
Correctly rewrites the loop as a set-based UPDATE
Addresses validation before production rollout

questions.title: Blocking Caused by a Missing Index, Not a Bug in the Code
questions.prompt: Every weekday around 10 AM, the order-entry application starts timing out for a few minutes. SQL Server's Activity Monitor shows dozens of INSERT statements from the app blocked behind a single SELECT from a management report that joins Orders to OrderLines. The report query and the INSERT statements haven't changed in months. sys.dm_tran_locks shows the report query holding a table-level (not row-level) lock on OrderLines. Diagnose why a plain SELECT is blocking INSERTs this badly, and fix it.
questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, ol.ProductId, ol.Quantity
FROM Orders o
JOIN OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderId = o.OrderId
WHERE o.SalesRepId = @RepId;
questions.modelAnswer:
A SELECT without an explicit hint doesn't normally take a table lock, so the first question is how that scan turned into one. With no supporting index on OrderLines for whatever predicate or join path the optimizer chose, the engine has to touch a large number of rows via a scan, taking a shared lock on each one it visits. SQL Server has a finite lock memory budget, and when the number of individual locks held by one statement crosses an internal threshold, it automatically escalates from many fine-grained row/page locks to a single table-level lock to reduce lock management overhead. That table-level shared lock is compatible with other readers but blocks writers outright, which is exactly why INSERTs into OrderLines pile up behind it even though the report is 'just reading.'

The fix starts with the execution plan: confirm there's a scan (not a seek) on OrderLines and identify which column the join or filter actually needs. If OrderLines has no index on OrderId (or on whatever column anchors the join to Orders), add a nonclustered index on that column, with included columns for ProductId and Quantity if this query is frequent enough to want a fully covering index. A seek against that index touches far fewer rows, likely staying well under the escalation threshold. If the table is simply very large and even a seek'ed range returns many rows, enabling Read Committed Snapshot Isolation removes the shared-lock-vs-insert conflict entirely for this pattern, since readers would work off row versions rather than blocking locks - though that's an instance-wide (or database-wide) behavior change that needs sign-off, not a drive-by fix. I'd pair the index fix with monitoring for LOCK_ESCALATION events going forward so this class of problem surfaces before users notice it again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by not trusting 'nothing changed in the code' as proof nothing changed - data volume grows even when queries don't, and a join that used to be cheap can quietly cross the row-count threshold where the optimizer stops seeking and starts scanning. So first I pull the actual execution plan for that report query and check OrderLines for a scan versus a seek. If it's scanning, that tells me there's no supporting index for the join, and all those row locks it's picking up along the way are what's triggering SQL Server's automatic lock escalation to a table lock - which is the real reason a read is blocking writes so hard. My fix is almost always to add the missing index first, because a seek that only touches the rows it needs rarely escalates at all. If I add the index and it's still escalating because the table's genuinely huge and the result set is wide, then I'd bring RCSI into the conversation as a bigger architectural change, but I wouldn't reach for that first since it changes isolation behavior for everyone, not just this one report.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderLines_OrderId ON dbo.OrderLines (OrderId) INCLUDE (ProductId, Quantity);
-- Verify with: SET STATISTICS IO ON; and re-check the plan for an Index Seek instead of a Clustered Index Scan on OrderLines.
commonMistakes: Assuming a SELECT can't cause serious blocking, so looking everywhere except the report query itself
Jumping straight to NOLOCK hints or snapshot isolation without first checking whether a missing index is the real root cause
Not checking sys.dm_tran_locks or the execution plan to confirm an escalation actually happened versus assuming it from symptoms alone
Adding an index without included columns, fixing the seek but still causing extra key lookups under load
Treating the fix as done without monitoring for future LOCK_ESCALATION events as data grows
keyPoints: Lock escalation automatically converts many row/page locks into one table lock once a statement exceeds the lock count threshold
A missing index forcing a scan is the most common trigger for escalation on an otherwise 'simple' read
Confirm with the execution plan (scan vs seek) and sys.dm_tran_locks before proposing a fix
A targeted covering index is usually the right first fix; RCSI is a bigger, instance-level decision
Index design should include the columns actually returned, not just the join key, to avoid extra lookups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the scan-to-lock-escalation mechanism
Identifies missing index as the likely root cause and how to confirm it
Proposes a correct, appropriately scoped index fix
Mentions RCSI as a secondary option with its tradeoffs, not a first resort
Clarity and structure of the answer

lessonLink.label: Clustered vs. Nonclustered Indexes: Choosing Wisely

questions.title: Converging Batch POS and Streaming Clickstream in a Medallion Architecture
questions.prompt: You're designing a full medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture on Databricks for a retail analytics platform that ingests nightly batch POS exports (sales transactions, returns) and a continuous streaming clickstream feed (web/app browsing events) off the same storefront. Walk through what belongs at each layer and why, and be specific about where the batch and streaming sources actually converge into a single picture of the customer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Bronze stays raw and source-specific, and the two feeds get their own parallel bronze tables rather than being forced together early. The POS exports land via Auto Loader or a scheduled COPY INTO job as an append-only bronze_pos_transactions table, preserving the file's native grain and schema plus ingestion metadata (source file name, load timestamp). The clickstream lands via a Structured Streaming job reading from Event Hub/Kafka into bronze_clickstream_events, also append-only, also schema-preserved, with the stream's offset/watermark tracked through checkpointing. Nothing is deduplicated, cleaned, or joined yet -- bronze's only job is to be a faithful, replayable copy of what arrived, because the grain of a sales transaction and the grain of a page-view event are fundamentally different things and forcing them into one shape this early loses information you can't get back.

Silver is where each source gets cleaned and conformed independently, but still kept separate. Silver POS resolves returns/voids against their original transactions, standardizes currency/timezone, and enforces quality constraints (no null transaction IDs, valid store IDs). Silver clickstream deduplicates retried events, filters bot traffic, and sessionizes raw page-views into sessions using a watermark-based groupBy on session gaps. Both are still at their own grain -- transaction grain and session/event grain -- because merging them here would mean picking one grain and throwing away the other's detail.

The real convergence point is gold, where both are conformed against shared dimensions (customer, product, date, store) into an analytics-ready model -- a customer_360 or product_performance gold table that joins purchase facts from silver POS with browsing-behavior facts from silver clickstream via the shared customer or session-to-purchase linkage. That's the layer built for cross-source analysis, so it's the right place to pay the join cost once rather than scattering ad-hoc joins across every downstream query. The one exception worth naming: if there's a genuine near-real-time requirement -- say, personalizing the site based on a customer's browsing behavior from the last five minutes plus their purchase history -- that specific need justifies an earlier, narrower stream-static join in silver (enriching the live clickstream against a static snapshot of customer/purchase data) rather than waiting for a batch gold refresh, but that's a deliberate exception for a specific use case, not the general convergence strategy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the team to resist the urge to join these two sources early just because they both describe the same customer. Bronze is two separate tables, full stop -- bronze_pos_transactions from the nightly batch drop, bronze_clickstream_events from the streaming job -- each one just a faithful raw copy of what came in, no cleaning, no joining, because they're different grains and trying to force them together before you've even cleaned either one just creates a mess you have to undo later.

Silver is still two tables, but now each one is actually usable on its own -- POS silver has returns resolved and quality rules enforced, clickstream silver is deduped and sessionized. They stay separate at this layer because a transaction and a session are genuinely different things, and collapsing them too early throws away detail you'll want downstream.

Where they actually come together is gold, through shared dimensions like customer and date -- that's where you build the customer_360 or product performance view that actually answers cross-source questions, and it's the one place I'd want to pay that join cost, not fifty different places. The one thing I'd flag as an exception: if there's a real need for near-real-time personalization using live browsing behavior, that's worth a targeted stream-static join in silver just for that use case -- but that's a carve-out for a specific requirement, not how I'd design the general pipeline.
commonMistakes: Joining raw bronze streaming and batch data directly, before either side has been cleaned or deduplicated
Treating medallion as one table per layer instead of parallel per-source bronze/silver tables that converge downstream
Collapsing transaction grain and event grain together too early and losing information neither side can recover
Forgetting to handle late-arriving batch data relative to clickstream silver that's already processed and sessionized
Defaulting every near-real-time requirement into gold instead of recognizing when a targeted earlier stream-static join is justified
keyPoints: Bronze is raw and source-specific -- one table per source, no joining
Silver cleans and conforms each source independently while preserving its own grain
Gold is the real convergence point, joined through shared dimensions
A genuine near-real-time use case can justify an earlier, narrow stream-static join in silver
Medallion is parallel pipelines merging downstream, not a single linear chain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct bronze design per source (raw, separate, append-only)
Correct silver design per source including cleaning/dedup at the right grain
Correctly identifies gold as the convergence point with sound reasoning
Addresses the near-real-time exception and when an earlier join is justified
Clarity and structure

questions.title: A Combined CI/CD Pipeline for Databricks Code and Terraform Infrastructure
questions.prompt: Design a combined CI/CD pipeline that deploys both Databricks notebook/pipeline changes and the underlying Terraform-managed infrastructure for a data platform together. Walk through ordering -- infra before code or the other way around -- environment promotion, and rollback for each layer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Infra generally has to be in place before the code that depends on it runs -- a job can't use a Unity Catalog schema, a cluster policy, or a secret scope that Terraform hasn't provisioned yet. But that doesn't mean they belong in one lockstep pipeline; it means infra deploys through its own pipeline, on its own cadence (infra changes far less often than notebooks/jobs do), with its own gating -- plan review, policy checks via something like Checkov or tflint, and a required approval for anything touching prod. The code pipeline, packaging notebooks/jobs/pipelines as versioned Databricks Asset Bundles, runs separately and more frequently, and only needs to wait on the infra pipeline when a specific code change actually depends on an infra change that hasn't landed yet.

Both pipelines promote through the same dev -> test/staging -> prod sequence, each with environment-specific configuration -- infra via tfvars per environment, code via DAB's own per-environment target configuration -- and each gated by automated validation appropriate to that layer: infra gets plan review and policy-as-code checks before apply, code gets unit and integration tests run against the dev or staging workspace before promotion. Prod promotion for both layers requires an explicit manual approval, but they're still two separate approvals for two separate changes, not one combined gate that forces every code deploy to also re-approve infra.

Rollback also has to stay decoupled, because conflating the two makes a simple code bug into an infra incident. A bad notebook or job change rolls back by redeploying the previous version of the Databricks Asset Bundle -- since it's a versioned, git-tagged artifact, that's a fast, low-risk redeploy that doesn't touch infrastructure at all. A bad infra change rolls back by reverting to a previous Terraform state/module version and re-applying -- never by manually editing resources in the portal, which breaks the state's accuracy going forward. Keeping these two rollback paths independent is exactly why the pipelines shouldn't be merged into one: the far more common failure mode is a code bug, and you want that fixable in minutes without touching infra at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My rule of thumb: infra needs to exist before the code that depends on it runs, but that's a dependency, not a reason to merge the pipelines. Infra gets its own pipeline that runs less often, with stricter gating -- plan review, policy checks, a real approval for prod -- because infra mistakes are expensive and slow to notice. Code -- notebooks, jobs, pipelines packaged as Databricks Asset Bundles -- gets its own pipeline that runs more often, with its own tests, and it only waits on the infra pipeline when a specific change genuinely needs something infra hasn't provisioned yet.

Both go through the same dev -> staging -> prod promotion sequence, each with their own environment-specific config and their own tests appropriate to what they are, and prod for either one needs an actual approval -- but two separate approvals, not one that drags code changes into re-approving infra every time.

Where I'd really push to keep them separate is rollback. If a notebook breaks something, I want to redeploy the previous version of that bundle in minutes and be done -- no infra involved. If an infra change breaks something, that's a Terraform state revert and a careful re-apply, never a manual portal edit that leaves the state lying about reality. Code bugs are the far more common failure, and the whole point of keeping these pipelines decoupled is that fixing one doesn't require touching the other.
commonMistakes: Coupling infra and code into one monolithic pipeline so every code change risks triggering unnecessary infra changes
Giving infra changes the same light-touch approval as routine code deploys instead of stricter gating
Manually applying Terraform for prod instead of running it through a gated pipeline
Having no versioned rollback story for jobs/notebooks, relying on manual redeploy from memory
Not testing infra changes (plan review, policy-as-code) with the same rigor code changes get before promotion
keyPoints: Infra generally deploys ahead of dependent code, but as a separate, less frequent, more strictly gated pipeline
Both layers promote through the same dev -> test -> prod sequence with their own environment-specific configuration
Databricks Asset Bundles version and parameterize code deployments analogous to how Terraform modules version infra
Rollback means redeploying a prior versioned artifact or state, never manual edits
Decoupled pipelines mean a code rollback never requires touching infra, and vice versa

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ordering/dependency reasoning between infra and code pipelines
Correct promotion and environment-gating design for both layers
Mentions Databricks Asset Bundles or an equivalent versioned code deployment mechanism
Correct, decoupled rollback strategy for infra versus code
Clarity

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the materialization mechanism and unique clustered index requirement
Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario
Correctly reverses the recommendation for the high-write scenario with reasoning
Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Moving a Portal-Clicking Team to Terraform/Bicep Over Skeptical Senior Pushback
questions.prompt: Your team has always provisioned Azure resources by clicking through the portal, and you want to move the team to Terraform/Bicep for a new data platform build. Two senior teammates are skeptical, citing 'it's slower than just clicking the thing I need' and past frustration with a previous team's over-engineered Terraform setup. How do you negotiate this adoption?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the skepticism as legitimate signal rather than resistance to be overcome by mandate. The candidate should start by separating the two objections, since they need different responses: 'portal is faster for a one-off' is often true and should be acknowledged honestly rather than argued away, while the past bad experience with over-engineered Terraform is a real scar that a new rollout needs to explicitly design against -- by keeping the initial module set small, flat, and genuinely necessary rather than building abstraction layers nobody asked for.

The candidate should propose an approach that lets the skeptics experience the value rather than being told about it: start with a new, lower-stakes piece of the platform build, let the team keep clicking for genuinely one-off exploratory resources for now, and bring the skeptics into writing the first modules rather than handing them a framework decided in isolation. The real argument for adoption -- consistent, reviewable, repeatable environments; drift detection; faster disaster recovery -- should be made concretely against this specific platform build's needs, not as an abstract best-practice argument, and the candidate should be honest that there's a real short-term velocity cost that pays off over the project's lifetime, not instantly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win an argument -- I'd go in treating their pushback as two separate, legitimate points that need different answers. 'Clicking is faster for the thing I need right now' is just true a lot of the time, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 'the last Terraform setup I used was over-engineered and painful' is the one I actually need to address head-on, by being explicit that whatever we build this time starts small and flat -- no module-of-modules, no abstraction for things we don't have yet.

Practically, I'd rather let them feel the benefit than argue them into it. I'd pick a lower-stakes piece of the new platform build to go first, keep it genuinely simple, and actually have the two of them help write those first modules instead of handing them something I designed alone and asking them to adopt it. And I'd be straight with them that yes, this is going to be a bit slower than clicking for the first few weeks -- the payoff is in repeatable environments and not having to remember what we clicked six months from now when we need to rebuild something, and that's a real tradeoff, not a free win I'm selling them.
commonMistakes: Treating the skepticism as pure resistance to change instead of partially valid feedback
Arguing that Terraform is strictly faster, which isn't true for small one-off changes and damages credibility
Ignoring or dismissing the team's past bad experience with an over-engineered IaC setup instead of designing against it
Mandating the switch top-down without letting the skeptics co-author the first real modules
Overselling adoption as a free win instead of being honest about the short-term velocity cost
keyPoints: Separates the 'portal is faster' objection from the 'past over-engineering' objection and addresses each specifically
Explicitly designs the new rollout to be small and simple, directly countering the past bad experience
Lets skeptics experience the value on a real, lower-stakes piece of work rather than mandating from above
Involves the skeptical senior teammates in authoring the first modules
Is honest about the real short-term velocity tradeoff rather than overselling adoption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates and responds to the two distinct objections
Proposes a concrete plan to avoid repeating the past over-engineering experience
Involves the skeptical teammates directly rather than mandating adoption top-down
Makes a concrete, project-specific case for adoption rather than an abstract best-practices argument
Is honest about real tradeoffs instead of overselling the change

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on a Terraform Apply That Took Down a Shared Event Hub
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` run by a teammate, approved in a rushed review, took down a shared production Event Hub namespace for 40 minutes before anyone noticed. You're leading the blameless postmortem. How do you run it so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless does not mean avoiding naming what happened -- the postmortem should state plainly that a specific Terraform change, approved in a rushed review, triggered the outage, while keeping the framing on the system that allowed it rather than on the individuals as people. The candidate should reframe the central question from 'who broke the Event Hub' to 'what let a plan with this blast radius get approved in a rushed review, and why did it take 40 minutes to notice a shared production namespace was down.' That reframing is what produces durable fixes instead of two people -- the author and the reviewer -- feeling punished while the same gap exists for the next risky change.

The candidate should explicitly involve both the author and the reviewer in walking through their reasoning: what the plan output looked like, what time pressure existed, why the blast radius of the change (a shared resource used by other teams) wasn't flagged in review. The postmortem should close with concrete, owned, dated action items distinct from the individuals' behavior -- for example, requiring plan output to explicitly call out changes to shared/cross-team resources, a mandatory second reviewer or cooling-off period for changes touching shared infrastructure, and alerting on the Event Hub namespace's health so a future outage is caught in minutes, not 40.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we're vague about what happened -- I'll say directly that a specific apply, approved in a review that got rushed, is what took the namespace down. But I keep steering the room toward the system question: what let a change with this big a blast radius get approved quickly, and why did it take 40 minutes before anyone noticed a shared production resource was gone, rather than who personally messed up.

I'd ask both the person who wrote the change and the person who reviewed it to actually walk through their side -- what the plan output showed, what the time pressure looked like, whether anything flagged that this touched a resource other teams depend on. And I'm not going to let the meeting end as just a good conversation -- I want it to end with specific fixes: plan output that calls out changes to shared resources explicitly, maybe a required second reviewer or a short cooling-off window for anything touching shared infra, and health alerting on that namespace so next time we catch it in minutes instead of 40.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'blameless' with being vague about what actually happened or who was involved
Focusing on the individual author's or reviewer's judgment instead of the systemic review gap
Not inviting both the author and the reviewer to explain their actual context and reasoning
Treating the 40-minute detection delay as a footnote instead of an equally important separate finding
Ending with a narrative discussion but no concrete, owned, dated action items
keyPoints: States plainly what happened and who was involved without making it about individual blame
Reframes toward the systemic gap: why a high-blast-radius change cleared a rushed review
Involves both the author and reviewer constructively to surface real context
Treats the 40-minute detection delay as its own distinct, important finding
Closes with concrete, owned, dated action items covering both the review gap and detection gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes blameless from avoiding naming the actual cause and people involved
Reframes the discussion toward the systemic review gap rather than individual fault
Involves both author and reviewer constructively to surface context, not blame
Identifies the detection delay as a separate, equally important finding
Produces concrete, owned, dated action items addressing both gaps

questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.
questions.example: Split: (1) Validate CLV calculation logic with Product, (2) Confirm/connect data sources, (3) Build semantic model & measures, (4) Build dashboard visualization — each separately estimated.
commonMistakes: Accepting a vague, oversized story as a single sprint item without decomposing it
Silently re-estimating the story unilaterally instead of involving the team
Publicly undermining the junior analyst's original estimate instead of framing it as a normal grooming gap
Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery
keyPoints: Decomposes a vague, oversized backlog item into independently valuable, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation and data-source unknowns during grooming, not mid-sprint
Reframes the original estimate's gap constructively rather than as a mistake by the junior analyst
Facilitates collaborative team re-estimation rather than overriding unilaterally
Models proactive unknown-surfacing as a senior responsibility within the Scrum process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and decomposes the oversized/ambiguous story into discrete, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation logic and data source unknowns proactively during grooming
Handles the junior analyst's original estimate constructively and respectfully
Uses collaborative, team-based re-estimation rather than unilateral override
Demonstrates understanding of how senior ownership operates within the Scrum process

questions.title: AWS Glue Worker Types, DPU Sizing, and When Auto-Scaling Hides a Real Problem
questions.prompt: Explain how AWS Glue's worker types (Standard, G.1X, G.2X, and G.025X) differ in terms of vCPU, memory, and local disk allocated per worker, and how the number of workers you choose relates to the number of Spark executors available to your job. Then explain when Glue's job computation auto-scaling (available on G.1X/G.2X with Glue 3.0+) genuinely helps a workload, and describe a concrete scenario where enabling auto-scaling just masks a real performance problem instead of fixing it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each Glue worker type maps to a fixed hardware profile. Standard workers provide 4 vCPUs, 16 GB of memory, and 50 GB of local disk per worker, and are configured to run 2 Spark executors per worker. G.1X workers provide 4 vCPUs, 16 GB of memory, and 64 GB of disk, but run only 1 executor per worker with the full memory allocation dedicated to it, which is why G.1X is the default recommendation for most ETL jobs — more memory headroom per executor than Standard. G.2X doubles everything: 8 vCPUs, 32 GB memory, 128 GB disk, still 1 executor per worker, intended for memory-intensive transforms, large joins/aggregations that need to cache data, or ML transforms. G.025X is a quarter-DPU profile (2 vCPUs, 4 GB memory) meant specifically for low-volume streaming ETL jobs where you don't want to pay for a full worker's capacity.

The relationship between NumberOfWorkers and usable Spark executors is not 1:1. Glue reserves one worker's capacity to run the Spark driver. So for G.1X/G.2X (1 executor per worker), total executors available for actual task processing is NumberOfWorkers minus 1. For Standard (2 executors per worker), it's roughly (2 x NumberOfWorkers) minus 1. This matters directly for parallelism: if your source data has far fewer partitions than available executor cores, adding workers buys you nothing because there's no work to distribute to the extra executors.

Auto-scaling (--enable-auto-scaling, or the 'Automatically scale the number of workers' option in Glue Studio) lets the job start with a minimum worker count and grow toward MaxCapacity mid-run based on observed Spark metrics like pending tasks and executor utilization at each stage boundary. It genuinely helps when a job's parallelism need is genuinely uneven across stages — for example, a wide shuffle-heavy aggregation stage that benefits from many executors, followed by a narrow final write stage that needs far fewer. It also helps for bookmark-driven incremental jobs where the data volume is unpredictable run to run.

Where it becomes a mask rather than a fix is data skew. Say a join key like customer_id has one value responsible for 70% of rows. Spark partitions tasks by key, so one task ends up with a massively oversized partition and runs for 35 minutes while every other task finishes in under a minute. Auto-scaling will add workers to speed up the many small tasks, and the job 'succeeds' faster on paper with a higher DPU-hour bill, but the single skewed task's wall-clock time is unaffected — Spark cannot split one task's partition across multiple executors. The job's total runtime stays dominated by that one task. The actual fix is addressing the skew directly: salting the join key, using Spark 3's adaptive query execution skew-join optimization, or repartitioning before the join — not adding DPUs.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I think about Glue worker sizing in two separate questions that people tend to collapse into one: 'how much compute do I need' and 'what shape of compute do I need.' The shape question is the worker type. Standard gives you two lighter-weight executors per node, which is fine for simple read-transform-write jobs. G.1X gives you one beefier executor per node — more memory per unit of work — and that's my default unless I have a specific reason to deviate. G.2X I reach for only when I've actually seen OOM errors or spill-to-disk warnings in the Spark UI on a job doing big joins or caching; it's twice the cost per worker so I don't default to it. G.025X is the oddball — basically for a tiny Kinesis-triggered streaming job that would be wasteful on even a quarter of a full G.1X worker.

The thing people get wrong on the worker-count side is assuming NumberOfWorkers equals your executor count. It doesn't — Glue eats one worker for the driver. So if I set NumberOfWorkers to 10 on G.1X, I've got 9 executors doing real work, not 10. I always do that subtraction before I reason about expected parallelism versus my number of input partitions.

On auto-scaling — I'll be honest, the first time I used it I thought it was a free lunch. Turn it on, let Glue figure out the right worker count, done. Then I had a job that kept 'succeeding' on time but with a DPU bill that kept creeping up month over month, and when I actually opened the Spark UI and looked at the stage timeline, I saw the real story: one task per run was taking 20-plus minutes while hundreds of others finished in seconds. That's classic skew — one key dominating the partition. Auto-scaling was dutifully throwing more executors at the other, fast-finishing tasks, which did nothing for the one slow task, and all it bought me was a bigger bill with the same wall-clock runtime. I ended up fixing it by salting the hot key and repartitioning before the join, and the auto-scaling setting became almost irrelevant after that because the work was actually balanced. That's the lesson I'd give anyone: auto-scaling is great for genuinely uneven, unpredictable workloads, but if you haven't looked at your job's stage timeline and confirmed the slowness is breadth-of-work and not a single skewed task, you're probably paying to mask a problem rather than solve it.
commonMistakes: Assuming NumberOfWorkers directly equals Spark executor count without accounting for the worker reserved for the driver
Scaling up worker count or DPUs to fix a job that is actually suffering from data skew rather than insufficient parallelism
Defaulting to G.2X for every job 'to be safe,' overpaying for workloads that aren't actually memory-bound
Enabling auto-scaling as a substitute for proper incremental/bookmark design, letting unnecessarily large scans get 'scaled through' every run
Never setting or reviewing MaxCapacity, so auto-scaling or concurrent job runs blow past expected cost budgets
keyPoints: Standard = 4 vCPU/16GB/50GB disk, 2 executors per worker; G.1X = 4 vCPU/16GB/64GB disk, 1 executor; G.2X = 8 vCPU/32GB/128GB disk, 1 executor; G.025X = 2 vCPU/4GB, quarter-DPU for low-volume streaming
One worker is always reserved to run the Spark driver, so usable executor count is less than NumberOfWorkers
Auto-scaling (Glue 3.0+, G.1X/G.2X) adjusts worker count mid-run between a minimum and MaxCapacity based on Spark stage metrics
More DPUs cannot fix data skew — a single oversized partition's task still caps the job's wall-clock runtime regardless of total executors
Worker type should match the workload profile: CPU/shuffle-heavy benefits from more G.1X workers; memory-heavy joins/caching need G.2X; low-volume streaming fits G.025X

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes worker type hardware specs and executor allocation per type
Explains relation between worker count, reserved driver worker, and Spark executors
Correctly explains auto-scaling's mechanism and triggers
Provides a concrete, technically valid skew scenario where auto-scaling masks the real problem
Identifies the correct remediation (repartition/salt key/AQE) rather than just adding workers

questions.title: Redshift Distribution Styles and How a Bad DISTKEY Causes Shuffle During Joins
questions.prompt: Explain exactly how Redshift's four distribution styles — KEY, ALL, EVEN, and AUTO — place rows across a cluster's node slices. Then explain, in terms of what the query engine actually does at execution time, how a poorly chosen DISTKEY on a large fact table causes a broadcast or redistribute step during a join, and why that hurts performance.
questions.modelAnswer:
KEY distribution hashes every row's value in the designated distribution key column and sends rows with the same hash to the same slice, consistently, across all nodes. The goal is collocation: if two tables that are frequently joined on that same column both use KEY distribution on it, matching rows for any given key value end up on the identical slice on the identical node for both tables, so the join can be computed entirely locally within that slice with zero network movement.

ALL distribution copies the complete table onto every node (not just one slice per node — the full table on each node). This is intended for small, relatively static dimension tables: since the whole table is present everywhere, any join against it never requires moving data over the network, regardless of what column it's joined on.

EVEN distribution assigns rows to slices in simple round-robin fashion, ignoring any column's value entirely. It's used when there's no dominant join key, or for tables that are scanned more than joined, since it guarantees balanced data volume across slices for scan-heavy workloads.

AUTO lets Redshift choose and can change the style as the table grows — typically starting a small table as ALL and converting it to EVEN (or recommending KEY) as row count increases, done as an online background operation.

At execution time, the query optimizer needs matching join-key rows co-located on the same slice to avoid data movement. When a query joins two tables whose distribution style/key doesn't guarantee that alignment — for example, a multi-billion-row fact table distributed by a column that isn't the join column, joined to a dimension table on a different column — Redshift must physically move data before the join can execute. If one side is small enough, the optimizer broadcasts it: sends a full copy of that table (or the relevant portion) to every node, visible in EXPLAIN output as a DS_BCAST_INNER step. If neither side is small, Redshift redistributes: it re-hashes rows from one or both tables across the network so that matching keys land on the same slice, visible as DS_DIST_INNER or DS_DIST_BOTH. Both are network-bound operations that block compute until the data arrives, and for the broadcast case specifically, the smaller table's entire content must flow across the interconnect to every node for every query execution, repeating the cost every single time the query runs rather than being a one-time setup cost.

A concrete bad-DISTKEY scenario: distributing a large orders fact table by a low-cardinality column such as order_status (a handful of distinct values) instead of customer_id. This causes two separate problems at once — severe data skew, because most rows cluster onto only a few slices corresponding to the common statuses, overloading those slices' storage and scan workload; and a forced redistribution on nearly every analytical query, because BI queries typically join on customer_id or product_id, neither of which aligns with the chosen distribution key.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I'm reviewing a Redshift schema, the first thing I check is whether the DISTKEY on the big fact tables actually matches how those tables get joined in practice — not what looks like a 'natural' key. I've seen teams pick the primary key or the first column in the table as DISTKEY out of habit, and that's almost never right for a fact table, because the primary key usually isn't the column you're joining on at query time.

The way I'd explain the mechanics out loud: picture the cluster as a grid of little buckets, one set of buckets per node. KEY distribution runs every row's distribution-key value through a hash function and that hash decides which bucket the row lands in — deterministically, so the same value always lands in the same bucket.
