If I distribute my fact table and my dimension table by the same column, their matching rows end up in the same bucket on the same node, so when I run the join, each node just joins its own local buckets against each other — no data has to travel over the network at all. That's the ideal case, and in EXPLAIN you'll see it as DS_DIST_NONE, basically 'nothing moved.'

Now if I get that wrong — say my fact table is huge and distributed by order_status, which has like five values — two things go wrong simultaneously. First, I've basically dumped 90% of my rows onto whichever handful of buckets correspond to the common statuses, so those nodes are doing way more scan work than the others — that's skew. Second, and this is the part people miss, every single analytical query joining that fact table to a customer or product dimension now has to redistribute data across the network at query time, every time, because the rows aren't sitting where the join needs them. If the dimension table is small, Redshift will just broadcast a full copy of it to every node — fine, cheap-ish. But if it's a big-to-big join, you get a full redistribute, which means re-hashing and shuffling potentially billions of rows across the cluster's network before the join logic even runs. That's exactly the kind of thing I'd go hunting for in SVL_QUERY_SUMMARY or the EXPLAIN plan — if I see DS_BCAST_INNER or DS_DIST_BOTH showing up on a query that runs constantly, that's my signal the distribution key doesn't match the real join pattern, and I'd go fix the DISTKEY rather than trying to tune the query itself.
commonMistakes: Using a low-cardinality column as DISTKEY, causing skewed slices with uneven data volume
Choosing DISTKEY based on a query's filter columns rather than its join columns
Defaulting every table to EVEN distribution 'for safety,' losing collocation benefits on frequently-joined tables
Never checking EXPLAIN or SVL_QUERY_SUMMARY for DS_BCAST/DS_DIST steps after a schema or query pattern change
Using ALL distribution on a large, frequently-updated table, causing expensive full-table replication on every load
keyPoints: KEY: hash-distributes rows by column value; matching values land on the same slice, enabling collocated joins
ALL: replicates the full table onto every node; eliminates shuffle for small, relatively static dimension tables
EVEN: round-robin placement with no key affinity; suited to scan-heavy tables or tables with no dominant join key
AUTO: Redshift selects and can evolve the style (e.g. ALL for small tables, EVEN as they grow) automatically in the background
EXPLAIN plans reveal the real cost: DS_DIST_NONE means collocated (good), DS_BCAST_INNER means broadcast, DS_DIST_INNER/DS_DIST_BOTH mean a redistribute shuffle occurred

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains all four distribution styles and their row-placement mechanics
Explains the collocated join concept and slice-level local computation
Correctly explains broadcast vs. redistribute steps and when each occurs
Gives a concrete, technically accurate bad-DISTKEY scenario and its performance impact
References EXPLAIN plan / query summary verification (DS_BCAST/DS_DIST) or skew diagnostics

questions.title: Kinesis Data Streams Shard Limits and Why Resharding Isn't Instantaneous
questions.prompt: Explain the throughput limits of a single Kinesis Data Streams shard (writes and reads), and how records are mapped to shards via partition key hashing. Then explain what actually happens during a shard split or merge operation on the underlying hash key ranges, and why a resharding operation takes time and doesn't immediately fix a hot-shard problem.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each Kinesis shard has fixed throughput ceilings: 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second for writes, whichever limit is hit first, and 2 MB per second or 5 GetRecords transactions per second for reads (that read limit is shared across all consumers polling the shard via the classic GetRecords API; enhanced fan-out consumers each get a dedicated 2 MB/second pipe per shard instead of sharing it).

Every record written carries a partition key, which Kinesis runs through an MD5 hash to produce a 128-bit integer. The full range of possible hash values (0 to 2^128 minus 1) is divided into contiguous, non-overlapping sub-ranges, and each shard owns exactly one sub-range. A record's partition key hash determines, deterministically, which shard's range it falls into — the same partition key value will always hash to the same shard, regardless of how many shards exist in the stream.

A split operation takes one existing shard's hash key range and divides it into two new child shards, each owning a sub-range of the parent's original range (you can let UpdateShardCount choose the split point, or use SplitShard to specify an exact new starting hash key). The parent shard immediately transitions to a CLOSED state — it stops accepting new writes — but it is not deleted; it remains readable until all of its already-written records either get consumed or age out past the stream's retention period. The two new child shards begin accepting writes for their respective sub-ranges right away. A merge operation is the reverse: two adjacent shards' ranges are combined into a single new child shard that inherits the full combined range, while both parent shards close.

Resharding is not instantaneous for several concrete reasons. The control-plane API call itself takes measurable time (seconds to low minutes) to propagate the updated shard map through the service. The parent shards don't disappear — they stay in a CLOSED, readable state, and any consumer must keep tracking them (via the ParentShardId relationship in DescribeStream/ListShards) until their data is fully drained, meaning old and new shards coexist for a window of time. Client-side consumers using the Kinesis Client Library have to detect the updated shard map, finish processing the closed parent shards, and only then establish new leases on the child shards — this lease migration itself takes additional time governed by KCL's lease-renewal and shard-discovery polling intervals.

Most importantly, resharding does not fix a hot-shard problem caused by a single, consistently repeated partition key value. Because the hash of a fixed partition key is deterministic, that key will always map into whatever shard currently owns the sub-range containing its hash — splitting shards around it just isolates that same hot range into a smaller, still-hot shard; it does not spread that key's write volume across multiple shards. The only real fix for a hot key is changing the partition key strategy itself (e.g., adding a random or round-robin suffix to spread a dominant key's traffic across multiple shards).
questions.professionalAnswer:
I usually walk through this with a concrete incident I've seen before: a stream starts throttling, someone's first instinct is 'let's just add more shards,' they run UpdateShardCount, and the throttling doesn't go away. That confuses people because on paper they just doubled their capacity. The reason is the hashing. Every partition key gets MD5-hashed into this huge number space, and that number space is sliced up into contiguous ranges, one range per shard. A given partition key always hashes to the same number, so it always lands in whichever shard currently owns that slice of the range — shard count doesn't change that, it just changes where the boundaries are drawn.

So if the real problem is that, say, 80% of your write volume is coming from one device ID or one tenant ID used as the partition key, that key is going to dump all its traffic onto one shard no matter how many total shards you have, because splitting shards just redraws boundaries — it doesn't take that one specific key's traffic and spread it across multiple destinations. The actual fix there is almost always on the producer side: change what you're hashing on, maybe add a random suffix to the hot key so its traffic gets spread across several shards instead of funneling into one.

On the mechanics of resharding itself — I'd explain that a split takes a shard's range and cuts it into two child shards, each getting half the range (or wherever you tell it to cut, if you use SplitShard directly). The old shard doesn't just vanish; it goes CLOSED, which means no new writes land there, but anything already written to it is still sitting there and has to be read out before it expires. That's the part that trips people up operationally — if you're running KCL-based consumers, they have to notice the new shard map, finish draining the closed parent, and then go set up brand new leases on the children, and all of that takes real wall-clock time. I always budget for a resharding operation taking a few minutes minimum before things actually settle, and I never treat it as an instant lever. And the hard limits underneath all of this — 1MB/s or 1000 records/s in, 2MB/s or 5 reads/s out per shard unless you're on enhanced fan-out — those are the numbers I use to actually size shard count up front, rather than reacting to throttling after the fact.
commonMistakes: Assuming adding more shards automatically fixes any throughput problem regardless of key distribution
Ignoring the shared 2 MB/s and 5-transactions/s read limit per shard when multiple consumers poll the same shard, causing ProvisionedThroughputExceededException
Treating a resharding operation as instantaneous and expecting zero transition time for consumers
Forgetting that CLOSED parent shards must still be drained by consumers, so code that only looks at 'current' shards can silently miss data
Using a low-cardinality or near-constant partition key, producing a permanently hot shard that resharding cannot resolve
keyPoints: Per-shard limits: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s writes; 2 MB/s or 5 GetRecords calls/s reads (shared), with enhanced fan-out giving each consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s
Partition keys are MD5-hashed into a 128-bit space; each shard owns a contiguous sub-range of that space
Split creates two child shards from sub-ranges of a parent; merge combines two adjacent shards; parent shards go CLOSED but remain readable until drained
Resharding has real latency: the control-plane update itself plus consumer-side shard-map discovery and lease migration (KCL)
Resharding cannot fix a hot shard caused by one deterministic, dominant partition key — the fix is changing the partition key strategy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states per-shard write and read throughput limits
Correctly explains partition key hashing and hash-range-to-shard mapping
Correctly explains split/merge mechanics and the parent shard's CLOSED lifecycle
Explains why resharding itself takes time (control plane plus consumer lease migration)
Explains why resharding does not fix a deterministic hot key

questions.title: Lambda Cold Start Mechanics, and Reserved vs. Provisioned Concurrency
questions.prompt: Walk through exactly what happens during a Lambda cold start — from the moment an invocation arrives for which no warm execution environment exists, to the function handler actually running. Then explain the real difference between reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency, including what each one does and does not guarantee, and describe a scenario in a data pipeline where you'd need each.
questions.modelAnswer:
A cold start begins when an invocation arrives and no existing warm execution environment is available to serve it. Lambda provisions a brand-new execution environment, which is a Firecracker microVM: it mounts the function's deployment package and any attached layers, then starts the configured runtime (for example, the Node.js or Python interpreter process, or the JVM for Java). This is followed by the Init phase, which executes everything in your code that sits outside the handler function — top-level imports, SDK client construction, static/global variable initialization, and, where Lambda Extensions are attached, their own initialization as well. Only once Init completes does the Invoke phase begin, which is when your actual handler function runs against the specific event payload. The total latency a caller experiences on a cold invocation is the sum of environment provisioning, runtime startup, and this Init-phase code — which is exactly why best practice is to put SDK client creation and other one-time setup outside the handler: it still costs you the full Init time on the first invocation of a fresh environment, but every subsequent warm invocation against that same environment skips Init entirely and jumps straight into Invoke.

After an invocation finishes, Lambda may keep that execution environment around for a period of time so it can be reused for a later invocation without repeating Init — this reuse is not contractually guaranteed or documented as a fixed duration, but it's the mechanism behind why some invocations are fast ('warm') and others pay the full cold-start cost.

Reserved concurrency, set via PutFunctionConcurrency, does two things simultaneously for one function: it sets a hard ceiling on how many concurrent executions that function can ever have (any invocation beyond it is throttled), and it carves that amount of concurrency out of the shared account-and-region concurrency pool so other functions cannot consume it and starve this one. Critically, reserved concurrency does not pre-initialize anything — it is purely a concurrency limit and guarantee. A cold start still happens every time Lambda needs to spin up a new environment to meet demand within that limit.

Provisioned concurrency, set via PutProvisionedConcurrencyConfig on a published function version or an alias pointing to one, actually pre-runs the Init phase for a specified number of execution environments ahead of time and keeps them warm and idle, ready to serve. Invocations routed to one of these pre-initialized environments skip Init entirely, which is what actually eliminates cold-start latency — at the cost of paying for that reserved capacity continuously, whether it's invoked or not. Provisioned concurrency can be scaled up or down on a schedule or via a target-tracking metric using Application Auto Scaling.

In a data pipeline, reserved concurrency fits a Lambda triggered per S3 object during a sudden backfill, where you need a hard cap so the function doesn't exceed a downstream RDS connection limit or a rate-limited third-party API — effectively a throttle. Provisioned concurrency fits a latency-sensitive synchronous Lambda — for example, one behind API Gateway doing real-time feature lookups for a dashboard — where an SLA can't tolerate even occasional multi-hundred-millisecond-to-second cold starts, especially for heavier-Init runtimes like Java or .NET.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by separating two things that get conflated constantly: concurrency control and latency control. Reserved concurrency is a concurrency control — it's a knob that says 'this function may never run more than N copies at once, and I'm guaranteeing it gets at least that much room out of the shared pool.' That's it. It doesn't pre-warm anything. If Lambda needs a new environment to hit that cap, it still cold-starts it exactly like it would without reserved concurrency set at all.

Provisioned concurrency is a latency control. It's Lambda actually going and running your Init code ahead of time — creating the SDK clients, running your top-level imports, whatever's outside the handler — for some number of environments, and then just sitting there holding them warm, waiting. When a request comes in and gets routed to one of those pre-warmed environments, it skips straight to your handler code. That's the only thing that genuinely removes cold-start latency; reserved concurrency never does that on its own.

The cold start sequence itself, if I'm walking someone through it: request comes in, no warm environment exists, so Lambda spins up a new microVM, mounts your code and layers, boots the runtime, and then runs everything in your file that's not inside the handler — that's the Init phase. Only after that finishes does it actually call your handler with the event. That's why I always tell people, if you're creating a boto3 client or a database connection pool, do it at module scope, not inside the handler — on a cold start you pay for it once per environment either way, but at least on every warm invocation after that you're not redoing it.

For where I'd actually use each — say I've got an S3-triggered Lambda that kicks off per object, and someone's about to backfill five million files. I'm setting reserved concurrency there, not because I care about speed, but because I need a hard ceiling so I don't blow out my downstream Redshift or RDS connection limit. That's purely a safety valve. On the other hand, if I've got a Lambda sitting behind an API that a dashboard calls synchronously and users are sensitive to latency, that's where I'd pay for provisioned concurrency — probably scheduled via Application Auto Scaling to ramp up before business hours and back down overnight, because I don't want to pay for pre-warmed capacity I don't need at 3am.
commonMistakes: Believing reserved concurrency pre-warms a function the way provisioned concurrency does
Accidentally setting reserved concurrency to 0 (fully blocking the function) when intending just to cap it at a non-zero value
Putting SDK or database client initialization inside the handler, paying init cost on every invocation instead of once per environment
Assuming provisioned concurrency eliminates all throttling risk rather than just cold-start latency for the provisioned portion
Forgetting that all functions in an account/region share one concurrency pool, so an unrelated spiky function can throttle others unless reserved concurrency carves out protection
keyPoints: Cold start = environment provisioning, runtime startup, then the Init phase (code outside the handler) before the Invoke phase runs
Warm environments skip Init and go straight to Invoke, which is why global-scope SDK client setup matters
Reserved concurrency sets a hard cap and guarantees a slice of account concurrency for one function, but never pre-warms anything
Provisioned concurrency pre-runs Init on a fixed number of environments ahead of time, directly eliminating cold start for invocations it serves
Provisioned concurrency targets a published version/alias (not $LATEST) and can be auto-scaled on a schedule or target-tracking metric

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately describes the cold start sequence (environment provisioning, runtime start, Init vs. Invoke phase)
Correctly explains reserved concurrency's cap-plus-guarantee semantics
Correctly explains provisioned concurrency's pre-warming mechanism
Correctly distinguishes that reserved concurrency does not eliminate cold starts
Gives a concrete, valid data-pipeline scenario for each setting

questions.title: How AWS DMS Actually Reads Change Data, and What a Validation Task Checks
questions.prompt: Explain how an AWS DMS replication task performs change data capture — specifically, what mechanism DMS actually reads from on the source (e.g., SQL Server CDC/transaction log, or MySQL binlog) to detect changes, and how the task transitions from full load to ongoing CDC without losing or duplicating changes that occurred during the full load. Then explain what DMS data validation actually checks, and what it does NOT guarantee.
questions.modelAnswer:
DMS CDC is always log-based, never trigger-based or polling-based, but the exact mechanism differs by source engine. For MySQL, Aurora MySQL, and MariaDB, DMS reads the binary log directly (this requires binlog_format=ROW on the source). For SQL Server, DMS relies on SQL Server's own transaction log mechanisms — typically by leveraging SQL Server's native CDC feature (enabled via sp_cdc_enable_db/table-level CDC) or reading the active transaction log, and requires the database to be in Full or Bulk-Logged recovery model with sufficient log retention so DMS doesn't lose log records before it consumes them. For Oracle, DMS reads redo logs, generally via Oracle LogMiner (or its own binary reader for higher-throughput scenarios), requiring supplemental logging to be enabled. For PostgreSQL, DMS uses logical replication: it creates a replication slot and reads the write-ahead log (WAL) through a logical decoding plugin such as pgoutput or test_decoding. In every case, a DMS replication instance connects to the source, parses the native log/CDC structure, translates captured row-level INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations into DMS's internal representation, and applies them to the target in the original commit order.

The full-load-to-CDC transition is designed specifically to avoid both lost and duplicated changes. Before starting the bulk full load, DMS first records the current log position on the source — a binlog file-and-offset for MySQL, an LSN for SQL Server or PostgreSQL, an SCN for Oracle — and uses that exact point as the CDC starting point going forward. It then performs the full load (typically a parallelized bulk extraction per table, with no ordering guarantee across different tables), while any source changes occurring from that recorded start position onward are captured and cached rather than discarded. Once a given table's full load finishes, DMS applies that table's cached changes — in original log order — to bring it fully current. Because the starting point is an exact log position rather than a wall-clock timestamp, there is no gap during which changes could be silently missed, and no overlap that would cause the same change to be applied twice.

DMS data validation, when enabled, re-reads both source and target rows for each migrated table after full load and/or CDC apply, matches rows primarily by primary key, and compares column-by-column to detect mismatches or missing/extra rows, surfacing failures that can be queried via the console or the describe-table-statistics API. What it validates is data content fidelity: that values were correctly transferred and converted between source and target data types.

What it does NOT guarantee: validation does not check business-logic correctness, does not validate schema or DDL changes made mid-migration (DMS does not replicate DDL by default), does not enforce or verify cross-table referential integrity, and does not continuously monitor ongoing replication lag — a table validated as correct at one point in time can still be behind as of right now. Validation itself also adds read load to both source and target, which is why it's frequently run selectively rather than continuously.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I like to explain this with the mental model of 'DMS is a log reader wearing different hats depending on the source engine, never a polling tool.' If someone asks how it actually sees changes, the answer is always some flavor of 'it's reading the transaction log, not querying the tables.' For MySQL it's literally tailing the binlog, which is why binlog_format has to be ROW — statement-based binlogs don't give DMS enough information to replay row-level changes faithfully. For SQL Server, it's either riding on SQL Server's own CDC tables or reading the transaction log directly, and you need the database in full or bulk-logged recovery with the log retained long enough, or DMS can fall behind and lose its place. Postgres is logical replication slots off the WAL. Oracle is LogMiner off the redo logs. Different plumbing, same principle: read the log, don't poll the data.

The part I actually find most interesting, and the part that tends to come up in real incidents, is the full-load-to-CDC handoff. I remember once reviewing a migration where someone assumed DMS just 'starts CDC after full load finishes' using wall-clock time as the cutover point, and got worried about a gap where changes could be lost during the bulk copy. That's not actually how it works — DMS grabs the exact log position, the LSN or binlog offset or SCN, right before the full load starts, and that becomes the CDC anchor. Anything that happens on the source from that exact point forward gets captured and buffered, even while the bulk copy is still running. Once a table finishes its full load, DMS just plays back whatever was buffered for that table since the anchor point, in log order, and now it's caught up. Using an exact log position instead of a timestamp is what rules out both losing changes and double-applying them.

On validation — I always tell people it's checking one specific thing really well: did the bytes that went in on the source match the bytes that landed on the target, row for row, keyed by primary key. It's not checking whether your schema evolved correctly mid-migration, it's not checking foreign key integrity across tables, and it's absolutely not telling you how far behind CDC currently is — that's a separate lag metric you'd watch through CloudWatch. I treat 'validation passed' as 'the data that was compared at that moment was correct,' not as a blanket certification of the whole migration being healthy forever after.
commonMistakes: Assuming DMS CDC polls source tables on a schedule rather than reading the native transaction log/binlog/WAL
Believing full load and CDC changes apply without any recorded log-position anchor, risking lost or duplicated changes
Assuming a running task implies validated, correct data without explicitly enabling DMS validation
Believing DMS validation guarantees schema (DDL) parity between source and target
Overlooking source-side prerequisites (binlog_format=ROW, SQL Server CDC enablement, Oracle supplemental logging, Postgres wal_level=logical) before CDC can function at all
keyPoints: DMS CDC is log-based per source engine: MySQL binlog, SQL Server transaction log/native CDC, Oracle redo via LogMiner, PostgreSQL WAL via logical replication slot
DMS records an exact starting log position (LSN/SCN/binlog offset) before full load begins, preventing lost changes during the bulk-load window
Changes captured during full load are buffered and applied per table, in log order, immediately after that table's full load completes
Validation performs primary-key-matched, column-by-column comparison between source and target rows and flags mismatches
Validation does not cover DDL replication correctness, cross-table referential integrity, or ongoing real-time replication lag after the comparison point

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the log-based CDC mechanism per source engine
Correctly explains the recorded start log position before full load and why it prevents lost changes
Correctly explains buffered-change application per table after full load completes
Correctly explains what validation actually compares
Correctly identifies what validation does NOT guarantee

questions.title: S3 Storage Class Mechanics: Retrieval Tradeoffs, Minimum Duration Charges, and Lifecycle Transitions
questions.prompt: Compare S3 Standard, Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, and the three Glacier tiers (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, Deep Archive) in terms of retrieval latency, retrieval cost, and minimum storage duration charges. Then explain what actually happens, mechanically, when an S3 Lifecycle rule transitions an object between storage classes, and why transitioning many small objects can end up costing more than it saves.
questions.modelAnswer:
S3 Standard offers millisecond retrieval with no retrieval fee and no minimum storage duration, at the highest per-GB storage price, aimed at frequently accessed data replicated across at least three AZs. Standard-IA also gives millisecond retrieval, but adds a per-GB retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum storage duration charge — deleting or transitioning an object before 30 days still bills as if it stayed the full 30 days — and effectively bills smaller objects as if they were a minimum size, making it a poor fit for large volumes of small objects. Intelligent-Tiering also retrieves at millisecond latency at all times, but instead of retrieval fees it charges a small per-object monitoring and automation fee; it automatically moves each object between a Frequent Access tier, an Infrequent Access tier (after 30 days with no access), an Archive Instant Access tier (after 90 days), and, if opted into, Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers (after 90-180+ days) — with no minimum duration charge on the base tiers, though the optional archive tiers carry their own minimums once enabled. Glacier Instant Retrieval keeps millisecond latency and costs less to store than Standard-IA, but costs more to retrieve, and carries a 90-day minimum storage duration — suited to data accessed roughly quarterly that still needs instant access when it is touched. Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly simply 'Glacier') does not provide instant access at all: retrieval requires an explicit restore request, with options of Expedited (1-5 minutes, limited availability and higher cost), Standard (3-5 hours), or Bulk (5-12 hours); it has a 90-day minimum storage duration, and until a restore completes, the object cannot be read directly even though it still appears in the bucket's listing. Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest of all, restoring via Standard (about 12 hours) or Bulk (about 48 hours) retrieval, with a 180-day minimum storage duration, meant for compliance or long-term archival data rarely if ever accessed.

Mechanically, a Lifecycle rule is evaluated on a daily batch cycle rather than firing the instant an object crosses its configured age threshold — so there's a built-in evaluation lag, not an exact-second transition. When a transition is due, S3 changes the object's underlying storage backend and metadata while the object's key (and, for versioned buckets, its specific version) stays exactly the same from the application's point of view. This transition itself is a billed event — a per-object Lifecycle Transition request charge, priced in the PUT-request tier — in addition to any early-deletion-before-minimum-duration charges incurred if the object is later deleted or further transitioned before its current class's minimum duration elapses. In a versioned bucket, this applies independently to noncurrent versions too, so old versions can accumulate their own transition charges.

Transitioning large counts of small objects can cost more than it saves because the Lifecycle Transition request fee is flat per object regardless of size, and Glacier-class tiers additionally bill a fixed amount of metadata/index overhead per object (on the order of tens of kilobytes) on top of the object's actual data. For millions of small objects — a common shape for poorly batched logging or IoT data — the combination of per-object transition request fees and per-object storage overhead can exceed whatever per-GB savings the cheaper storage class would otherwise provide, especially once the real object size is smaller than the fixed overhead itself.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I usually frame this around one question I ask whenever someone proposes a lifecycle policy: 'how big are the individual objects, and how often will they actually be touched?' Those two answers decide almost everything else.

On the access-latency side, I think of it in three buckets. Standard, Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, and Glacier Instant Retrieval are all 'instant' in the sense that a GetObject just works immediately — the differences between them are purely about who pays what and when. Standard has no retrieval fee and no minimum commitment, so it's the default for anything actively used. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant both trade a lower storage rate for a retrieval fee and a minimum-duration commitment — 30 days for IA, 90 for Glacier Instant — so they only make sense if you're confident the data won't be deleted or moved again inside that window, otherwise you eat the full minimum charge anyway. Intelligent-Tiering is the one I reach for when I genuinely don't know the access pattern in advance — it watches actual usage and moves objects between tiers for you, charging a small per-object monitoring fee instead of betting on a fixed tier.

Then there's the real archive tiers — Glacier Flexible and Deep Archive — where I have to be very explicit with people that 'it's in the bucket' does not mean 'you can read it right now.' You have to issue a restore request and wait, anywhere from a few hours to two full days for Deep Archive's bulk tier, before the object becomes directly readable again. I've seen people build an architecture assuming they could grab an archived object on demand for a compliance request and panic when they realize there's a built-in multi-hour wait.

The part that actually surprises people the most, though, is the small-object trap. Say you've got a logging pipeline dumping a few-KB object per event, millions of them. Someone decides 'let's lifecycle these to Glacier to save money,' not realizing that every single transition is its own billed request, and Glacier tiers tack on a fixed chunk of metadata overhead per object regardless of how tiny the object is. If your object is 2KB and the fixed overhead is tens of KB, you're now paying more in overhead than the data itself would have cost to just leave in Standard. My rule of thumb: never lifecycle a sea of tiny objects directly — batch or compact them into larger files first, then apply the lifecycle policy to the aggregated objects. And I always remind people that lifecycle rules run on a daily evaluation cycle, not instantly at the exact age threshold, so don't design anything that depends on a transition happening at a precise moment.
commonMistakes: Assuming Glacier Flexible Retrieval objects are instantly readable without first issuing a restore request
Ignoring minimum storage duration charges when designing lifecycle rules with a short overall object lifetime
Applying Glacier or Deep Archive lifecycle rules directly to large volumes of small objects instead of aggregating them first
Treating Intelligent-Tiering as always cheaper without accounting for its per-object monitoring fee at very high object counts
Expecting a lifecycle transition to execute at the exact moment an object crosses its configured age threshold
keyPoints: Retrieval latency: Standard, Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering, and Glacier Instant Retrieval are all millisecond; Glacier Flexible needs a restore request (minutes to hours); Deep Archive restores in hours
Minimum storage duration: Standard-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant 90 days, Glacier Flexible 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days — early deletion or transition bills the remainder
Intelligent-Tiering auto-moves objects based on observed access recency, charging a monitoring fee instead of retrieval fees
Lifecycle rules evaluate on a roughly daily cycle, and each transition is itself a billed per-object request
Small objects are disproportionately expensive to transition: fixed per-request fees plus Glacier/Deep Archive metadata overhead can outweigh per-GB savings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately compares retrieval latency and cost structure across all listed storage classes
Accurately states the minimum storage duration for each applicable class
Correctly explains lifecycle transition execution mechanics (daily evaluation cycle, per-request billing)
Explains the small-object cost problem with correct reasoning (fixed fees plus metadata overhead)
Response is technically precise with no fabricated classes, numbers, or behaviors

questions.title: Glue PySpark Job: Partitioned Parquet Read/Write with Job Bookmarks
questions.prompt: Write a PySpark AWS Glue ETL job script that reads partitioned Parquet data from an S3 path, applies a transformation (such as deriving a new column), and writes the result back to S3 partitioned by a date column, with Glue job bookmarks enabled so that re-running the job only processes newly arrived data. Then explain what DPU count and worker type you'd choose for this workload and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
The script needs three things working together for bookmarking to actually function: a unique transformation_ctx string on the source read call, a unique transformation_ctx string on the sink write call, and the job-level bookmark setting itself enabled outside the script (via the --job-bookmark-option job-bookmark-enable job parameter, set in the Glue console, CLI, or Terraform/CloudFormation job definition — it cannot be turned on from inside the script code). The transformation_ctx values are what Glue actually uses as the state key to remember which S3 objects/partitions have already been processed, so that a re-run only picks up files that weren't seen last time.

The read uses glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_options against the S3 source path with groupFiles set to combine small files for efficient reading, and a transformation_ctx of 'source_dyf'. After converting to a Spark DataFrame for the transformation logic (deriving order_total_usd and a load_date column from the existing timestamp), the result is converted back into a DynamicFrame and written with glueContext.write_dynamic_frame.from_options, specifying partitionKeys=['load_date'] so the output is written as Hive-style partitioned Parquet (load_date=YYYY-MM-DD folders), with its own transformation_ctx of 'output_dyf'. The job.init() and job.commit() calls bracket the whole script — job.commit() is what actually persists the new bookmark state, and it must execute unconditionally after a successful run, since skipping it (for example inside an early-return branch) means the next run won't know this run's files were already processed.

For DPU/worker type: this is a read-transform-write job with light shuffle — the only real shuffle-like operation is the repartition implied by partitionBy on write, and the transformation itself (arithmetic on existing columns, a date derivation) is CPU-light and doesn't require caching or large join buffers. That workload profile fits G.1X workers well: each gets a full, dedicated Spark executor with 16 GB of memory, which is comfortable headroom for this kind of transform without paying G.2X's doubled price for memory capacity this job doesn't need. A reasonable starting point is around 10 G.1X workers with job computation auto-scaling enabled (MinimumCapacity low, MaxCapacity capped at a sane ceiling) so the job can grow if a particular run's incoming data volume spikes, without permanently provisioning for the worst case. G.2X would only become justified if the transformation grew to include large multi-table joins, wide aggregations needing to cache intermediate results, or if profiling in the Spark UI showed spill-to-disk or out-of-memory errors on G.1X.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I write one of these jobs, the thing I'm most careful about is the transformation_ctx strings, because that's the detail that silently breaks bookmarking if you get it wrong. I always give the source read and the sink write their own distinct transformation_ctx value, and I never reuse the same string across two different source or sink calls in the same job — if I did, Glue would conflate their bookmark state and either skip data it shouldn't or reprocess data it already handled. And I always remind people that passing transformation_ctx in the code isn't enough by itself — the job also has to have job-bookmark-enable actually turned on as a job parameter, outside the script. I've debugged more than one 'bookmarks aren't working' ticket that turned out to be exactly that — code looked right, but the job-level setting was never flipped on.

For the actual script, I read the partitioned Parquet with create_dynamic_frame.from_options pointed at the S3 path, convert to a DataFrame because it's just easier to do column-level transformations in native Spark SQL functions than in the DynamicFrame API, derive my new columns, convert back to a DynamicFrame, and write it out with partitionKeys set to my date column so I get proper Hive-style partitioning on the way out. And job.commit() has to run at the very end, every time, unconditionally — that's the line that actually saves the new bookmark state, so if I ever have a code path that returns early on success, I make sure commit still gets called before that happens.

On sizing — I'd ask first what this transformation is actually doing. Here, it's pretty light: deriving a couple of columns, no joins, no aggregations, no caching. That tells me I don't need G.2X's extra memory headroom; I'd go with G.1X, which gives each worker a full dedicated executor with 16 GB, and that's plenty for this kind of job. I'd start around 8 to 10 workers and turn on auto-scaling with a reasonable MaxCapacity ceiling, so if one particular day's data volume is unusually large the job can grow into it, but I'm not paying for that peak capacity on every single run. If I ever saw spill-to-disk warnings or actual OOM errors in the Spark UI once this job's logic grew more complex, that's my signal to bump up to G.2X rather than just throwing more G.1X workers at it.
questions.example:
import sys
from awsglue.utils import getResolvedOptions
from pyspark.context import SparkContext
from awsglue.context import GlueContext
from awsglue.job import Job
from awsglue.dynamicframe import DynamicFrame
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, to_date

args = getResolvedOptions(sys.argv, ['JOB_NAME', 'source_path', 'target_path'])

sc = SparkContext()
glueContext = GlueContext(sc)
spark = glueContext.spark_session
job = Job(glueContext)
job.init(args['JOB_NAME'], args)

# Read partitioned Parquet from S3. transformation_ctx is required and must be
# unique -- Glue uses it as the bookmark state key for this source.
source_dyf = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_options(
    connection_type="s3",
    connection_options={
        "paths": [args['source_path']],
        "recurse": True,
        "groupFiles": "inPartition"
    },
    format="parquet",
    transformation_ctx="source_dyf"
)

df = source_dyf.toDF()

# Transformation: derive a load_date column used as the write partition key
transformed_df = (
    df
    .withColumn("order_total_usd", col("quantity") * col("unit_price"))
    .withColumn("load_date", to_date(col("order_timestamp")))
)

output_dyf = DynamicFrame.fromDF(transformed_df, glueContext, "output_dyf")

# Write back to S3 partitioned by load_date. Its own transformation_ctx
# lets Glue track this sink's bookmark state independently of the source.
glueContext.write_dynamic_frame.from_options(
    frame=output_dyf,
    connection_type="s3",
    connection_options={
        "path": args['target_path'],
        "partitionKeys": ["load_date"]
    },
    format="parquet",
    transformation_ctx="output_dyf"
)

# Persists the new bookmark state -- must run unconditionally on success.
job.commit()

# Job parameter required at the job level (not in script) for bookmarks:
# --job-bookmark-option job-bookmark-enable
commonMistakes: Forgetting transformation_ctx entirely, which silently disables bookmarking for that source/sink even with the job-level bookmark option enabled
Reusing the same transformation_ctx string across multiple distinct sources or sinks, corrupting bookmark state tracking
Enabling bookmarks in the script but changing the source's underlying file paths or partition scheme, which resets or breaks bookmark tracking
Calling job.commit() conditionally or inside a branch that can be skipped on some successful runs, so new bookmark state is never persisted
Defaulting to G.2X or an oversized worker count for a workload that is actually light and I/O-bound, overpaying without any performance benefit
keyPoints: transformation_ctx on both the source and sink calls is what Glue's bookmark state actually tracks per job
Job bookmarks must also be enabled at the job configuration level (--job-bookmark-option job-bookmark-enable), not only via transformation_ctx in code
job.init() and job.commit() bracket the script, and job.commit() must run unconditionally on success to persist the new bookmark state
partitionKeys on the sink write produces Hive-style partitioned output (load_date=YYYY-MM-DD folders)
Worker type should match the workload's actual resource profile: shuffle-light read/transform/write fits G.1X; memory-heavy joins or caching justify G.2X

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of transformation_ctx on both source and sink to support bookmarking
Correct job.init/job.commit bracketing and getResolvedOptions usage
Correct partitionBy/partitionKeys write logic keyed on the date column
Valid transformation logic producing a derived column
Correct, well-reasoned DPU/worker type recommendation tied to the workload's characteristics

questions.title: Redshift Fact Table DDL with DISTKEY/SORTKEY, and Separating ETL from BI Queries in WLM
questions.prompt: Write Redshift DDL for a large fact table, order_line_items, with columns for order_id, line_item_id, customer_id, product_id, order_date, quantity, and line_total, choosing an appropriate DISTKEY and a compound SORTKEY for a workload that frequently joins to a customers dimension and filters/aggregates by date range. Then describe a WLM (workload management) configuration that keeps long-running ETL load queries from starving interactive BI dashboard queries.
questions.modelAnswer:
The DISTKEY choice should follow the dominant join pattern, not the table's own primary key. Since this fact table is frequently joined to a customers dimension on customer_id, distributing order_line_items by customer_id means that as long as the customers dimension table is either also distributed by customer_id or small enough to use DISTSTYLE ALL, matching rows for any given customer land on the same slice for both tables, letting the join execute locally without a network redistribute or broadcast step. Using order_id or line_item_id instead would be a mistake here, since neither is the actual join column BI queries use.

The compound SORTKEY on (order_date, customer_id) is chosen because the stated workload filters and aggregates heavily by date range. A compound sortkey physically orders data on disk by the first column, then the second within ties, and Redshift maintains zone maps (min/max value per 1MB block) for sorted columns — when a query filters on order_date, Redshift can skip entire blocks whose min/max range falls outside the requested date range, dramatically reducing I/O for range-restricted scans. Putting order_date first maximizes that block-skipping benefit for the stated access pattern; customer_id as the second sortkey column provides additional pruning benefit for queries that further filter by both date range and customer within that range.

It's worth noting PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL constraints in Redshift are accepted syntactically and used by the query planner as hints for optimization, but are not actually enforced at the storage layer the way they are in a transactional database — Redshift will not reject a duplicate primary key value or a NULL in a NOT NULL column inserted via COPY or INSERT.

For WLM, the goal is to prevent a long-running nightly ETL load or transformation from monopolizing cluster concurrency slots that interactive BI dashboard queries need. With manual WLM, this means defining at least two separate queues: an ETL queue, assigned via a query_group label (SET query_group TO 'etl_load' before running load/transform SQL, or via a dedicated service/IAM-mapped user group), configured with lower concurrency (for example 2-3 slots) but a larger memory allocation per slot appropriate for heavy COPY and transform statements, plus a Query Monitoring Rule that can abort or log any query exceeding an expected runtime threshold to catch runaway loads. A separate BI queue, mapped to the BI service account or user group, gets higher concurrency (for example 10-15 slots) with less memory per slot, sized for typically small, fast dashboard queries. This way a long ETL statement occupying its own queue's slots cannot block BI queries from getting a slot in their own queue. Enabling Short Query Acceleration on top of this lets Redshift additionally fast-track genuinely small ad hoc queries ahead of a queue that's backed up, regardless of which queue they'd otherwise wait in. On newer Redshift (RA3 clusters or Redshift Serverless), Automatic WLM with query priority can achieve a similar effect by assigning the BI workload HIGHEST priority and the ETL workload LOW or NORMAL priority, letting the scheduler preempt resources toward the higher-priority queries automatically.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always start the distkey conversation by asking 'what's the join column that shows up in the most expensive, most frequent queries' — not 'what's the primary key.' Here it's clearly customer_id, because that's how this fact table gets joined to the customers dimension constantly. So I'd distribute order_line_items by customer_id, and as long as the customers table is either distributed the same way or small enough that I've just made it DISTSTYLE ALL, those joins should collocate on each slice without any network shuffle — that's the whole point.

For the sort key, since the real workload here is heavy on date-range filtering, I put order_date first in the compound sort key. Redshift keeps a zone map — basically a min/max value — for every 1MB block on a sorted column, so if I'm filtering WHERE order_date BETWEEN X AND Y, it can skip blocks that fall entirely outside that range without even reading them. customer_id goes second, because once you've already pruned down to the right date range, it gives a bit more pruning on top for queries that also filter by customer within that window. I'd avoid putting customer_id first, because that would prioritize pruning by customer over pruning by date, and the stated workload cares more about date-range scans.

One thing I always mention, because it trips people up coming from a transactional background: don't rely on PRIMARY KEY or NOT NULL in Redshift to actually enforce anything. Redshift accepts that syntax and the optimizer can use it as a hint, but it won't stop a duplicate key or a null value from landing in the table via COPY. If dedup matters, that has to be handled in the ETL logic itself.

On WLM, the story I'd tell is pretty simple: nightly ETL loads and interactive BI dashboards should never be fighting over the same queue. I'd set up a dedicated ETL queue — lower concurrency, since load jobs tend to be big and sequential rather than many-at-once, but with enough memory per slot that a COPY or big transform doesn't spill to disk — and tag my load scripts with SET query_group so they land there. Then a separate BI queue with higher concurrency and smaller memory per slot, since dashboard queries tend to be small and numerous rather than huge and rare. That separation alone means a 40-minute nightly load sitting in its own queue can't block a 2-second dashboard query from getting a slot in its queue. And if I'm on newer Redshift, I'd honestly just lean on Automatic WLM with query priority instead of hand-tuning manual queues — set BI to HIGHEST priority, ETL to LOW, and let the scheduler handle the rest, plus turn on Short Query Acceleration so small ad hoc queries never get stuck behind something heavy regardless of which queue they're nominally in.
questions.example:
CREATE TABLE order_line_items (
    order_id        BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    line_item_id    BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    customer_id     BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    product_id      BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    order_date      DATE          NOT NULL,
    quantity        INTEGER       NOT NULL,
    line_total      DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_item_id)
)
DISTSTYLE KEY
DISTKEY (customer_id)
COMPOUND SORTKEY (order_date, customer_id);

-- WLM: route ETL load/transform sessions to a dedicated low-concurrency,
-- higher-memory queue so they never compete with BI dashboard sessions
-- for the same slots.
SET query_group TO 'etl_load';
-- (ETL load/transform statements run here)
RESET query_group;

SET query_group TO 'bi_dashboards';
-- (interactive BI dashboard queries run here, in a higher-concurrency,
--  lower-memory-per-slot queue configured separately in the cluster's WLM)
RESET query_group;
commonMistakes: Using order_id or line_item_id (not the join column) as DISTKEY when queries actually join on customer_id
Choosing DISTSTYLE ALL for a large, frequently-loaded fact table, causing expensive full replication on every load
Putting a low-selectivity column first in the compound sortkey, reducing its block-skipping benefit for date-range queries
Running BI dashboards and ETL loads through the same default WLM queue with no query_group separation, causing dashboard timeouts during nightly loads
Relying on Redshift's PRIMARY KEY or NOT NULL constraints for uniqueness/dedup guarantees, which Redshift does not actually enforce
keyPoints: DISTKEY should match the dominant large-table join key (customer_id) so matching rows co-locate with the dimension table for collocated joins
Compound SORTKEY on (order_date, customer_id) enables zone-map block skipping for date-range filters, with customer_id as secondary pruning
Redshift accepts but does not enforce PRIMARY KEY/NOT NULL uniqueness constraints
Separate WLM queues (or query priority in Automatic WLM) isolate long-running ETL/COPY statements from interactive BI concurrency
Short Query Acceleration lets small ad hoc dashboard queries jump ahead even when a batch-heavy queue is backed up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DDL syntax with appropriate column types
Correct DISTKEY choice with justification tied to the join pattern
Correct compound SORTKEY choice with justification tied to the filter pattern
Valid, concrete WLM configuration separating ETL from BI (queues/query groups/priority)
Mentions Redshift's non-enforcement of PK/NOT NULL or another accurate caveat

questions.title: Step Functions State Machine: Glue Job then Lambda, with Retry, Catch, and Fallback Notification
questions.prompt: Write an AWS Step Functions state machine definition in Amazon States Language (ASL) JSON for a pipeline that starts an AWS Glue job, waits for it to complete, then invokes a Lambda function to validate the output. Include Retry blocks for transient service errors and a Catch block that routes any unhandled failure to a fallback notification step (e.g., publishing to an SNS topic) instead of letting the execution just fail silently.
questions.modelAnswer:
The cleanest way to run the Glue job and wait for completion in one state is the arn:aws:states:::glue:startJobRun.sync service integration. The .sync suffix tells Step Functions to start the job and then poll Glue's GetJobRun on your behalf until the run reaches a terminal state, rather than requiring you to build your own Wait/GetJobRun polling loop — the state machine execution simply pauses at that state until the job finishes, succeeds, or fails.

The Retry block on that state matches specific error names via ErrorEquals (for example Glue.ConcurrentRunsExceededException for a transient capacity conflict, or States.Timeout) and backs off exponentially: IntervalSeconds is the initial wait, BackoffRate multiplies that interval on each subsequent attempt, and MaxAttempts caps how many times it will retry before giving up and falling through to any Catch block. Retry is evaluated first for any error that occurs — only after retries are exhausted (or for error types not listed in any Retry block) does control fall through to Catch.

The Catch block uses ErrorEquals: ['States.ALL'] as a catch-all, intentionally placed after the more specific Retry rules have had their chance to handle known transient errors — it exists to make sure no failure mode, including ones not explicitly anticipated, falls through the state machine ungracefully. ResultPath on the Catch is important: by default, a Catch's result would overwrite the entire state input with just the error information, discarding whatever data earlier states produced; setting ResultPath to something like $.errorInfo instead merges the captured error details into the existing state data, preserving context for the notification step.

The Lambda validation step uses the arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke integration, with its own Retry for Lambda.ServiceException and Lambda.TooManyRequestsException (both genuinely transient), and its own Catch routing to the same fallback notification state.

The fallback state publishes to SNS via arn:aws:states:::sns:publish, passing the captured error information as the message body. Critically, after notifying, the state machine must still transition to a Fail state rather than ending on the notification state itself — otherwise the execution's status in the Step Functions console and in CloudWatch metrics would show as Succeeded, even though the underlying pipeline actually failed, which would make monitoring and alerting on real failures impossible. A Succeed state is used for the actual happy path, giving a clear, correct distinction between genuine success and a notified-but-still-failed execution.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point out is that I would never hand-roll a polling loop to wait for a Glue job to finish — Step Functions has a native way to do that with the .sync suffix on the Glue integration, startJobRun.sync. You call it like a normal Task state, and under the hood Step Functions just keeps checking the job status for you and only moves on once it's actually done. That saves you from writing your own Wait-then-GetJobRun loop, which is what people did before these .sync integrations existed and honestly still see in older state machines.

On error handling, I think about Retry and Catch as two completely different jobs that happen to live next to each other in the same state definition. Retry is for 'I know this specific error is usually transient, give it another shot before giving up' — so I'd list something like Glue.ConcurrentRunsExceededException there, with an exponential backoff, because that's a classic 'try again in a bit' situation, not a real failure. Catch is the safety net underneath that — States.ALL as the ErrorEquals value there means 'anything that wasn't already handled by a Retry, or that exhausted its retries, lands here.' One subtlety I always double check: Retry gets first crack at any error, and only once it's exhausted does Catch even see it, so ordering and scoping those correctly matters.

When I catch an error, I'm careful about ResultPath — if you don't set it, the Catch's output completely replaces whatever data was flowing through the state machine with just the error object, and then my notification step has lost all the original context about what job run or what input it was processing. Setting ResultPath to something like $.errorInfo keeps the original data and just appends the error details alongside it.

And the thing I'd flag as the easiest mistake to make here: after you publish to SNS to notify someone, you cannot just let that be the last state. If the notification state is terminal, Step Functions marks the whole execution as Succeeded in the console and in CloudWatch, because from its perspective, every state ran and nothing errored out. That's exactly backwards from what you want — you want failures to show up as failures in your monitoring. So after the SNS publish, I always transition into an explicit Fail state, so the execution status honestly reflects that the pipeline didn't actually complete successfully, even though we did our job of alerting someone about it.
commonMistakes: Manually polling Glue job status with a hand-built Wait/GetJobRun loop instead of using the startJobRun.sync integration
Placing a catch-all States.ALL Catch in a way that intercepts errors before more specific Retry rules get a chance to run
Omitting BackoffRate or MaxAttempts on Retry blocks, causing either no backoff (hammering a throttled service) or effectively unbounded retries
Letting the fallback notification state be the execution's terminal state, so the console/CloudWatch shows the execution as Succeeded despite the real failure
Hardcoding ARNs and job names directly in the definition without parameterizing per environment, making the state machine non-portable across dev/staging/prod
keyPoints: glue:startJobRun.sync is a native run-and-wait service integration; Step Functions polls Glue on your behalf, no manual polling needed
Retry blocks match specific ErrorEquals values and back off exponentially (IntervalSeconds times BackoffRate per attempt) up to MaxAttempts before falling through
Catch with States.ALL is a catch-all evaluated only after more specific Retry rules have exhausted their attempts
ResultPath on a Catch preserves the original state input alongside the captured error info for downstream steps
A Fail state must follow the fallback notification, otherwise the execution shows as Succeeded despite the underlying failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct overall state machine structure and valid ASL JSON syntax
Correct use of glue:startJobRun.sync and lambda:invoke service integrations
Correct, realistic Retry block (ErrorEquals, IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, BackoffRate)
Correct Catch block routing to a fallback notification state with appropriate ResultPath
Correct distinction between Succeed and Fail terminal states so failure is visible in execution status

questions.title: Least-Privilege IAM Policy for a Glue Job Execution Role
questions.prompt: Write an IAM policy JSON for an AWS Glue job's execution role that may only: (1) read objects from a specific S3 prefix (raw data), (2) write objects to a different specific S3 prefix (processed data), and (3) read/write the Glue Data Catalog — without granting broader S3 access or wildcard permissions across all Glue resources.
questions.modelAnswer:
This policy needs to separate bucket-level actions from object-level actions, because IAM treats them differently with different ARN shapes. s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action — it operates on the bucket itself (to list keys), so it must be granted against the bucket's own ARN (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name), not an object ARN. To keep the listing scoped to only the intended prefix rather than letting the job see the entire bucket's key listing, I add a Condition using StringLike on the s3:prefix request key, restricted to raw/orders/*. By contrast, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, and s3:DeleteObject are object-level actions, which require object ARNs using the /* suffix pattern (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/raw/orders/* for read, and a completely separate arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/processed/orders/* for write) — using two distinct prefixes in two distinct statements is what actually prevents the job from being able to read its own output or overwrite its own source data.

For the Glue Data Catalog, permissions need to be granted at each ARN level the called APIs actually touch: a catalog-level ARN (arn:aws:glue:region:account:catalog), a database-level ARN for the specific database, and a table-level ARN scoped to that database's tables — GetTable, CreateTable, and similar actions reference this hierarchy, and Glue requires the appropriate level of ARN be included in the policy's Resource list for the call to succeed, even though logically it feels like one action. I grant only the specific actions actually needed (GetDatabase/GetDatabases, GetTable/GetTables, GetPartition/GetPartitions for reads, and CreateTable/UpdateTable/BatchCreatePartition/BatchUpdatePartition for writes) rather than a glue:* wildcard, which would grant far more — including the ability to delete tables or modify unrelated databases in the same account.

Finally, I include a narrowly-scoped CloudWatch Logs permission (CreateLogGroup, CreateLogStream, PutLogEvents) restricted to the /aws-glue/* log group path, because a Glue job execution role also needs this to actually produce visible job run logs — without it, the job may still run but leaves no debuggable output, which is its own operational problem even though it isn't a security one. Nowhere in the policy does Resource appear as a bare '*', and no action is granted via a service-wide wildcard like s3:* or glue:*.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I'm writing an execution role for something like this, I start by listing out literally every API call the job will make, then work backward to the minimum permissions that cover exactly those calls — not what's convenient to copy from an example. For S3, the first thing I separate in my head is 'is this a bucket-level action or an object-level action,' because that decides what the ARN in the policy has to look like. ListBucket is bucket-level — you're asking 'what keys exist under this prefix,' so the ARN target is the bucket itself, and I'd scope it down further with an s3:prefix condition so the job can't even list keys outside the raw/orders prefix it's supposed to touch. GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject are object-level, so those ARNs need the /* suffix, and critically, I give read access to one prefix and write access to a completely different prefix. I've seen setups where someone gives a job read-write to the same prefix 'to keep it simple,' and that's exactly how you end up with an ETL job that can accidentally overwrite its own raw input data.

For the Glue Catalog side, the thing that trips people up is that catalog permissions are hierarchical — there's a catalog-level ARN, a database-level ARN, and a table-level ARN, and depending on which API you're calling, you may need more than one of those levels present in the policy simultaneously. I always double-check the actual AWS docs for each action's required resource type rather than guessing, because getting this wrong just produces a confusing AccessDenied error at runtime that doesn't obviously point back to a missing ARN level.

And I'd never reach for glue:* as a shortcut, even though it's tempting when you're not sure exactly which actions a job needs — that wildcard would also let the role do things like delete tables in a totally unrelated database in the same catalog, which is way outside what this specific job should ever be able to do. The last thing I always remember, because it's easy to forget until a job 'works' but produces zero visible logs, is the CloudWatch Logs permissions scoped to the Glue log group path — without CreateLogGroup, CreateLogStream, and PutLogEvents, the job runs, maybe even succeeds, but you get nothing to debug it with if something does go wrong later.
commonMistakes: Granting s3:* or Resource: '*' on S3 'just to make it work' during testing and never tightening it afterward
Omitting the bucket-level ListBucket permission entirely, causing access-denied errors on list/prefix operations even though GetObject is allowed
Using the same prefix or ARN for both read and write access, allowing the job to accidentally overwrite its own raw source data
Omitting the CloudWatch Logs permissions, causing the Glue job to run but produce no visible logs for debugging
Granting glue:* instead of the specific Get/Create/Update actions actually needed, unnecessarily broadening the role's blast radius
keyPoints: s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action requiring the bucket ARN, and should be scoped with an s3:prefix condition to match only the intended prefix
GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject are object-level actions requiring the /* object ARN pattern under each specific prefix
Glue Data Catalog permissions need ARNs at the catalog, database, and table levels, since actions like GetTable and CreateTable reference that hierarchy
A separate CloudWatch Logs statement scoped to the Glue log group path is required for job run logs to actually be written
No wildcard 's3:*', 'glue:*', or 'Resource: *' appears anywhere in the policy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct separation of bucket-level vs. object-level S3 actions and ARNs
Correctly scoped read-only access to the raw prefix and write access to the processed prefix with no overlap
Correct, appropriately scoped Glue Data Catalog permissions (not a glue:* wildcard)
Includes necessary supporting permissions (e.g., CloudWatch Logs) for the job to actually run
No wildcard Resource or Action usage anywhere in the policy
