questions.title: CloudFormation: Kinesis Data Stream in On-Demand vs. Provisioned Capacity Mode
questions.prompt: Write a CloudFormation YAML snippet that provisions an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, and show how the resource definition differs between on-demand capacity mode and provisioned capacity mode with an explicit shard count. Then explain the real operational tradeoffs between the two modes and when you'd choose each for a data engineering workload.
questions.modelAnswer:
The property that actually switches capacity modes in CloudFormation is StreamModeDetails.StreamMode on the AWS::Kinesis::Stream resource, set to either ON_DEMAND or PROVISIONED. In ON_DEMAND mode, the ShardCount property is omitted (or ignored if present) — Kinesis manages shard count internally and automatically, scaling the stream's capacity up to handle observed throughput, defaulting to limits around 200 MB/second write and 400 MB/second read that it can grow further if sustained demand continues, adjusting within minutes based on the traffic observed over roughly the trailing 30 days of peak usage. Billing in this mode is per-stream-hour plus a per-GB data charge, rather than per-shard-hour.

In PROVISIONED mode, ShardCount becomes a required property — you declare the exact number of shards up front, and Kinesis will not change that count on its own; any resharding (via UpdateShardCount, SplitShard, MergeShards, or a custom automation such as the community Kinesis Scaling Utility built on CloudWatch alarms) has to be triggered explicitly. Billing is a flat per-shard-hour rate regardless of whether each shard's throughput is fully utilized.

The real operational tradeoff is this: on-demand removes the burden of capacity planning and continuous monitoring of per-shard IncomingBytes/IncomingRecords metrics, and is the safer default for a new, unpredictable, or spiky workload where you genuinely don't know what peak throughput will look like — but it costs more per unit of throughput at sustained, high, predictable volume, and its auto-scaling is reactive to a trailing window of observed traffic, meaning a sudden, unprecedented spike far beyond any recently observed peak can still momentarily throttle before the service scales up to match it. Provisioned mode is more cost-efficient at steady, well-characterized volume — for example, a known fleet of IoT devices with a stable aggregate throughput — but it puts the operational burden of capacity planning and active resharding back on you; under-provisioning directly causes ProvisionedThroughputExceededException on writes or reads, and you either have to build your own scaling automation or accept manual intervention when traffic grows.

For a data engineering workload, I'd default to on-demand for anything new, anything with unknown or highly variable traffic, or anything where the operational cost of someone monitoring shard metrics and manually resharding isn't justified by the data volume. I'd choose provisioned specifically when the throughput is well understood, stable, and large enough that the per-shard-hour rate comes out meaningfully cheaper than on-demand's per-stream-hour-plus-per-GB rate — and when the team is prepared to actually own ongoing capacity monitoring and resharding as traffic evolves.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain this by first pointing at the one property that actually flips the switch: StreamModeDetails, with StreamMode set to either ON_DEMAND or PROVISIONED. That's the whole difference in the CloudFormation template structurally — in on-demand mode you just don't specify ShardCount at all, because Kinesis is managing that behind the scenes; in provisioned mode, ShardCount becomes something you have to explicitly decide and declare.

What that actually means operationally is the interesting part. With on-demand, I'm handing Kinesis the job of watching my traffic and scaling shard count up or down to match it — it looks at roughly the last 30 days of observed peak throughput and adjusts. That's great because I'm not the one staring at IncomingBytes metrics in CloudWatch deciding when to reshard, but it's not magic — if traffic suddenly spikes to something way beyond anything it's seen recently, there can be a brief window where I still get throttled before it catches up. So I wouldn't call on-demand 'infinite instant elasticity,' I'd call it 'reactive elasticity with a lookback window.'

With provisioned, I'm the one deciding the shard count up front, and Kinesis will not change it for me — if I set 8 shards, it stays 8 shards until I run an UpdateShardCount or a split/merge myself, or build something on top with CloudWatch alarms to automate that. The upside is cost — per-shard-hour pricing at a known, steady volume tends to come out cheaper than on-demand's per-stream-hour-plus-data pricing. The downside is that I'm now on the hook for capacity planning, and if I get the shard count wrong on the low side, I'm the one getting ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, not Kinesis quietly scaling around it.

So my actual decision rule, when someone asks me which to pick for a new pipeline: if I don't yet know the traffic pattern, or it's genuinely spiky and unpredictable, I default to on-demand every time — the cost premium is worth not babysitting shard counts. If I've got a stable, well-understood, high-volume stream — something like a known device fleet pushing a consistent aggregate rate — and the team actually has the discipline to monitor and reshard as it grows, that's when provisioned's per-shard-hour economics start to make more sense.
questions.example:
Resources:
  OrdersStreamOnDemand:
    Type: AWS::Kinesis::Stream
    Properties:
      Name: orders-stream-on-demand
      StreamModeDetails:
        StreamMode: ON_DEMAND
      RetentionPeriodHours: 24

  OrdersStreamProvisioned:
    Type: AWS::Kinesis::Stream
    Properties:
      Name: orders-stream-provisioned
      StreamModeDetails:
        StreamMode: PROVISIONED
      ShardCount: 8
      RetentionPeriodHours: 24
commonMistakes: Specifying both ShardCount and StreamMode: ON_DEMAND together, not realizing ShardCount is ignored/invalid in on-demand mode
Assuming on-demand mode carries zero throttling risk even for a sudden, unprecedented traffic spike
Leaving a provisioned stream statically sized after traffic has grown, causing chronic throttling instead of resharding or switching to on-demand
Using on-demand for a very large, stable, 24/7 high-throughput stream where provisioned pricing would be meaningfully cheaper
Forgetting other properties that matter regardless of capacity mode, such as RetentionPeriodHours or StreamEncryption
keyPoints: StreamModeDetails.StreamMode (ON_DEMAND or PROVISIONED) is the CloudFormation property that controls capacity mode
ON_DEMAND mode omits ShardCount; Kinesis auto-scales based on observed trailing throughput, billed by stream-hour plus data volume
PROVISIONED mode requires an explicit ShardCount; scaling needs manual UpdateShardCount or custom automation, billed per-shard-hour
On-demand suits unpredictable, new, or spiky workloads; provisioned suits stable, well-characterized high-volume workloads where per-shard-hour pricing is cheaper
On-demand's elasticity is reactive to recent observed traffic, not instantaneous for a never-before-seen spike

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, valid CloudFormation syntax for both stream definitions
Correctly uses StreamModeDetails.StreamMode to distinguish on-demand from provisioned
Correctly omits or includes ShardCount appropriately per mode
Accurately explains the scaling and billing mechanics of each mode
Gives a correct, concrete recommendation of when to choose each mode

questions.title: Configuring Lambda Reserved and Provisioned Concurrency via AWS CLI/boto3
questions.prompt: Write an AWS CLI (or boto3) snippet that sets reserved concurrency on a Lambda function to cap its maximum concurrent executions, and separately configures provisioned concurrency on a published version/alias of that function. Then explain the operational difference between the two settings and what happens if you set provisioned concurrency higher than reserved concurrency.
questions.modelAnswer:
Reserved concurrency is set at the function level, unqualified — it applies across $LATEST and all versions/aliases of that function collectively, since it's a cap drawn from the shared account-and-region concurrency pool, configured via put-function-concurrency / PutFunctionConcurrency with a single ReservedConcurrentExecutions value. Provisioned concurrency, by contrast, must be set against a specific published version or an alias pointing to one — put-provisioned-concurrency-config / PutProvisionedConcurrencyConfig requires a Qualifier that is not $LATEST, because provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments tied to immutable, specific code; $LATEST can change at any time, so AWS disallows attaching provisioned concurrency directly to it. In practice this means you first call publish-version to snapshot the current code as an immutable version, optionally create or update an alias pointing at that version, and only then configure provisioned concurrency against that version or alias.

If you attempt to set provisioned concurrency higher than the function's reserved concurrency, the API call fails with a validation error, because provisioned concurrency must fit within whatever ceiling reserved concurrency has established — you cannot pre-warm more environments than the function is even allowed to run concurrently across all its versions and aliases combined. In other words, reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency aren't independent settings; reserved concurrency defines the outer boundary that provisioned concurrency must live inside.

Operationally, the two serve different purposes entirely. Reserved concurrency is a safety and fairness control: it throttles the function once concurrency exceeds the configured ceiling, and simultaneously guarantees that ceiling's worth of capacity is reserved away from the shared pool so other functions in the account can't starve it. It does not pre-initialize anything — a cold start still happens whenever Lambda needs to spin up a new environment within that limit. Provisioned concurrency is a latency and cost control: it keeps a fixed number of execution environments pre-initialized and warm at all times, which is what actually removes cold-start latency for invocations routed to them, at the cost of paying for that capacity continuously whether or not it's actively being invoked. Provisioned concurrency amounts can be adjusted dynamically via Application Auto Scaling, either on a fixed schedule (for predictable traffic patterns like business hours) or via target-tracking based on utilization metrics.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame the difference for someone is: reserved concurrency lives on the function itself and acts like a ceiling that applies no matter which version or alias gets invoked, while provisioned concurrency has to be pointed at one specific, immutable version or an alias that resolves to one — never $LATEST. That restriction on $LATEST actually makes sense once you think about why provisioned concurrency exists: it's pre-running your Init code ahead of time and keeping environments warm, and that only makes sense against code that's frozen in place. $LATEST can be edited at any moment, so AWS just doesn't let you attach provisioned concurrency to it — you have to publish-version first to lock in a snapshot, then maybe point an alias at it, and configure provisioned concurrency against that.

On the interaction between the two settings — if I try to set provisioned concurrency to some number that's bigger than the function's reserved concurrency limit, that call just gets rejected outright. It makes intuitive sense once you say it out loud: I can't pre-warm 20 environments if I've told the function it's only ever allowed to run 10 concurrent executions total. Reserved concurrency is the hard outer boundary, and provisioned concurrency has to live inside it.

Where I see people get confused operationally is treating these as two flavors of the same thing — 'concurrency settings' — when they're solving different problems. Reserved concurrency is there to protect the account's shared concurrency pool and to put a ceiling on a function so it can't accidentally overwhelm a downstream dependency, like a database connection limit. It doesn't make anything faster. Provisioned concurrency is purely about latency — it's the thing that actually removes the cold-start tax for whatever slice of traffic lands on the pre-warmed environments. If I've got a latency-sensitive API behind this function, I want provisioned concurrency scheduled to ramp up before I expect a traffic wave and back down afterward through Application Auto Scaling, because I'm paying for that warm capacity around the clock otherwise. But if my real concern is 'don't let this function take down my RDS instance during a backfill,' that's reserved concurrency's job, and provisioned concurrency wouldn't even be the right tool for that problem.
questions.example:
# AWS CLI

# Cap the function at 20 concurrent executions total (reserved concurrency,
# applies across $LATEST and all versions/aliases)
aws lambda put-function-concurrency \
  --function-name order-validation-fn \
  --reserved-concurrent-executions 20

# Publish an immutable version so provisioned concurrency has a fixed
# code target (provisioned concurrency cannot target $LATEST)
aws lambda publish-version \
  --function-name order-validation-fn

# Point a "live" alias at that published version
aws lambda create-alias \
  --function-name order-validation-fn \
  --name live \
  --function-version 3

# Pre-warm 10 execution environments for the "live" alias
aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config \
  --function-name order-validation-fn \
  --qualifier live \
  --provisioned-concurrent-executions 10


# boto3 equivalent
import boto3

client = boto3.client("lambda")

client.put_function_concurrency(
    FunctionName="order-validation-fn",
    ReservedConcurrentExecutions=20
)

version = client.publish_version(FunctionName="order-validation-fn")["Version"]

client.create_alias(
    FunctionName="order-validation-fn",
    Name="live",
    FunctionVersion=version
)

client.put_provisioned_concurrency_config(
    FunctionName="order-validation-fn",
    Qualifier="live",
    ProvisionedConcurrentExecutions=10
)
commonMistakes: Trying to set provisioned concurrency directly on $LATEST instead of a published version or an alias pointing to one
Setting provisioned concurrency higher than the function's reserved concurrency and being surprised when the API call fails
Treating reserved and provisioned concurrency as interchangeable ways to 'avoid throttling,' when only provisioned concurrency avoids cold starts
Forgetting that reserved concurrency also removes that capacity from the shared account-wide pool, potentially starving other functions if set too high
Leaving provisioned concurrency permanently sized for peak traffic, paying for idle warm capacity during off-peak hours
keyPoints: Reserved concurrency (put-function-concurrency) applies to the whole function, capping and guaranteeing total concurrent executions from the account pool
Provisioned concurrency (put-provisioned-concurrency-config) must target a published version or an alias pointing to one, never $LATEST
Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes and keeps warm a fixed number of execution environments, billed continuously regardless of invocation
Setting provisioned concurrency above the function's reserved concurrency limit is rejected by the API
Application Auto Scaling can adjust provisioned concurrency on a schedule or target-tracking metric; reserved concurrency stays static until explicitly changed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CLI/boto3 syntax for put-function-concurrency
Correct CLI/boto3 syntax for publishing a version/alias and configuring provisioned concurrency
Correctly explains that provisioned concurrency requires a version/alias, not $LATEST
Correctly explains the constraint between reserved and provisioned concurrency values
Accurately distinguishes the operational purpose of each (throttle/guarantee vs. pre-warm/cost)

questions.title: Athena External Table with Partition Projection Instead of a Glue Crawler
questions.prompt: Write Athena DDL to create an external table over S3 data partitioned by year, month, day, and hour, using partition projection instead of relying on a Glue crawler or explicit ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION statements. Then explain why partition projection is preferable to crawler-maintained partitions for a high-cardinality, predictable partition scheme like this one.
questions.modelAnswer:
Partition projection works by computing the full set of valid partition values, and the exact S3 location for each, algorithmically from TBLPROPERTIES at query planning time — it never looks those values up from partition metadata stored in the Glue Data Catalog. The projection.enabled property turns this mode on for the table; without it, the other projection.* properties are simply ignored. Each partition column then gets its own type, range, and (for zero-padded values) digits properties — for example projection.month.type = integer, projection.month.range = 1,12, projection.month.digits = 2 — which together tell Athena the full universe of valid values for that column and how to format them into the S3 path. The storage.location.template property supplies the actual path pattern, with placeholders like ${year}, ${month}, ${day}, and ${hour} substituted in according to those rules, letting Athena construct the exact S3 prefix for any combination of partition values that satisfies a query's filters.

With a crawler-based or manually-managed approach, every new partition that appears in S3 — in this case, every new hour — requires a corresponding entry to exist in the Glue Data Catalog before Athena can query it. That entry gets created either by waiting for the next scheduled crawler run (introducing latency and cost, and risking staleness between when data actually lands and when the crawler next discovers it) or by issuing an explicit ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION or MSCK REPAIR TABLE call. At the cardinality implied by year times month times day times hour over a few years of data — tens of thousands of distinct partition entries — the catalog itself becomes large, which slows down both crawler runs and the partition-listing step Athena performs during query planning, since it has to enumerate and filter potentially tens of thousands of stored partition records to figure out which ones are relevant to a given query.

With partition projection, none of that catalog storage or lookup happens at all. Athena computes, purely in memory during query planning, which partition values are relevant to the query's WHERE clause predicates, derives their S3 paths directly from the template, and reads from exactly those locations. New data becomes queryable the instant it lands in S3 at the expected path, with no crawler run and no ADD PARTITION call ever required, and query planning tends to be faster because Athena isn't fetching and filtering a large stored partition list from the catalog.

The tradeoff, and the reason this isn't universally the right choice, is that partition projection requires the partition values to follow a fully predictable, enumerable pattern — sequential integers or dates within a defined range, or an explicit enumerated list of values. It's not suitable for partition columns with arbitrary, sparse, or unpredictable values, such as a column keyed by customer ID, where no closed-form range or formula could describe the valid set of values.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain partition projection by contrasting it directly with what a crawler does. A crawler's whole job is to go look at what's actually sitting in S3, figure out the partition structure, and write entries into the Glue Catalog so Athena knows those partitions exist. That means there's always a lag between data landing and the crawler noticing it, and at some point you've got potentially tens of thousands of stored partition entries for something like year/month/day/hour over a couple of years, which starts to slow down both the crawler itself and Athena's own query planning, since it has to sift through all those stored entries.

Partition projection skips the whole 'go discover and store partition metadata' step entirely. Instead, I tell Athena, right in the table's properties, exactly what the valid range of values looks like for each partition column — year is an integer between, say, 2023 and 2030, month is 1 through 12, zero-padded to two digits, and so on — plus a template for how those values get stitched into an S3 path. Athena then computes which partitions are relevant to a query purely mathematically, at query time, and goes straight to those S3 locations. There's no catalog entry to look up and nothing to keep in sync.

The practical win is that the moment new data lands in S3 at the expected path — say a new hour's worth of clickstream data — it's immediately queryable. No crawler run, no ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION, no waiting. And for a scheme like year/month/day/hour, which is about as predictable and enumerable as partition schemes get, that's exactly the use case projection is designed for.

The caveat I always give people, though: this only works because the partition values here are fully predictable — integers in known ranges following a known formula. If someone's partition column were something arbitrary, like an account ID with no predictable pattern, I couldn't express that as a projection range, and I'd be back to crawler-maintained or manually-added partitions. So it's not 'always use projection' — it's 'use projection when the partition scheme is genuinely enumerable, and this date/hour scheme is a textbook case for it.'
questions.example:
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE clickstream_events (
    event_id      STRING,
    user_id        STRING,
    event_type     STRING,
    event_payload  STRING
)
PARTITIONED BY (
    year   STRING,
    month  STRING,
    day    STRING,
    hour   STRING
)
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION 's3://ltv-clickstream-data/events/'
TBLPROPERTIES (
    'projection.enabled' = 'true',

    'projection.year.type' = 'integer',
    'projection.year.range' = '2023,2030',

    'projection.month.type' = 'integer',
    'projection.month.range' = '1,12',
    'projection.month.digits' = '2',

    'projection.day.type' = 'integer',
    'projection.day.range' = '1,31',
    'projection.day.digits' = '2',

    'projection.hour.type' = 'integer',
    'projection.hour.range' = '0,23',
    'projection.hour.digits' = '2',

    'storage.location.template' = 's3://ltv-clickstream-data/events/year=${year}/month=${month}/day=${day}/hour=${hour}'
);
commonMistakes: Forgetting 'projection.enabled' = 'true', which silently makes all the other projection properties no-ops
Mismatched digits or range settings versus the actual zero-padded S3 folder naming, causing queries to silently return no data
Still running a Glue crawler on a projection-enabled table 'just in case,' wasting cost since catalog-stored partitions aren't used for query planning anyway
Using partition projection on a column with unpredictable, non-enumerable values, such as arbitrary customer IDs, where no clean range or formula applies
Not updating the projection range (e.g., the year range) as time moves forward, causing newer data outside the configured range to become silently unqueryable
keyPoints: projection.enabled set to true, plus per-column projection.<name>.type/range/digits properties, replace catalog-stored partition metadata entirely
storage.location.template tells Athena how to construct the exact S3 path for any combination of partition values
New partitions become queryable immediately on data arrival, with no crawler run or ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION needed
At high partition cardinality, crawler/catalog-based partition lookup becomes slow and costly; projection computes partitions in memory at query time instead
Partition projection requires a predictable, enumerable partition scheme (sequential date/time or integer ranges, or explicit enum lists), not arbitrary or sparse values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, valid Athena DDL syntax with PARTITIONED BY and STORED AS
Correct and complete projection TBLPROPERTIES (enabled plus type/range/digits per column)
Correct storage.location.template matching the stated partition scheme
Accurately explains why projection avoids catalog/crawler lookup overhead at high cardinality
Correctly identifies when projection is and isn't appropriate (predictable vs. arbitrary partition values)

questions.title: A Nightly Glue Job Quietly Grew From 20 Minutes to 6+ Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly AWS Glue ETL job that used to cost roughly $15 per run and finish in about 20 minutes has, over the last two months, crept up to running 6+ hours and costing hundreds of dollars per run. Nobody noticed until Finance flagged the AWS bill. Walk through how you'd diagnose the root cause and fix it, and then how you'd make sure this never goes unnoticed for two months again.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the job's run history from the Glue console or CloudWatch (glue.driver.aggregate.elapsedTime, numCompletedTasks, and DPU-hour billing metrics) going back the full two months to find exactly when the regression started, not just that it happened. A sudden step-change points to a code or config change; a gradual slope points to data growth outpacing a fixed configuration. Second, I'd check whether job bookmarks are actually working. If job.commit() isn't reliably reached, or the transformation_ctx changed, the job silently falls back to full reprocessing every run - this is one of the most common causes of a job that used to be fast suddenly scanning the entire dataset every night, and it gets worse every day as the source table grows. I'd confirm by comparing the input record/byte count logged per run against the known size of 'just yesterday's data.' Third, I'd check the DPU/worker configuration - was NumberOfWorkers or MaxCapacity hardcoded months ago for a dataset a fraction of today's size, with no auto scaling (Glue Auto Scaling, available on Glue 3.0+) enabled? Fourth, I'd look at the Spark UI or job metrics for task duration skew - one or two tasks taking far longer than the rest usually means a skewed join key or an uneven partition causing most workers to sit idle while one straggler runs for hours. Fifth, I'd check the S3 input side for partition or small-file explosion - if an upstream process started writing many more, smaller files or new partitions, Glue's listing and planning overhead alone can balloon runtime. The fix depends on which of these is the actual cause: re-enable or repair bookmarks (verify job.commit() always executes, keep transformation_ctx stable), right-size workers and turn on auto scaling, repartition/coalesce or redesign the join key to fix skew, or compact small files upstream. To prevent this from hiding for two months again, I'd set a CloudWatch alarm directly on job duration and/or DPU-hours per run (not just a monthly AWS Budget alarm, which is too coarse and too late), wired to SNS, plus a job timeout so a runaway job fails loudly instead of quietly finishing six hours late. I'd also tag the job for cost allocation so it shows up in a weekly cost-by-job dashboard rather than only an end-of-month bill review.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly the first question I'd ask the team is 'what actually changed two months ago?' - but since nobody caught it in real time, I can't rely on institutional memory, so I'd go straight to the CloudWatch metrics for that job and plot elapsed time over the last 60-90 days to find the inflection point. That tells me whether I'm looking for a one-time change or a slow creep tied to data volume. In my experience, the single most common culprit for 'a Glue job that used to be fast is now scanning everything' is a broken bookmark - something as subtle as someone changing the transformation_ctx string when they added a new source, or an exception path that skips job.commit(). So that's genuinely the first thing I check, before I even think about DPUs. If bookmarks check out, I'd open the Spark UI for a recent run and look at the task duration distribution - if I see one task running for five hours while three hundred others finished in two minutes, that's data skew, not a sizing problem, and throwing more DPUs at it would just waste more money without fixing anything. If the tasks are evenly distributed but there are just way more of them, then it's probably legitimate data growth that the worker count never kept up with, and that's a straightforward right-sizing or auto-scaling fix. I'd fix whichever of those it turns out to be, then re-run and confirm the fix against the cost and duration metrics before calling it done. But the part I'd actually spend the most time on in an interview is the prevention side, because the real failure here wasn't technical, it was that nobody was watching. A fifteen-dollar job quietly becoming a three-hundred-dollar job for two straight months without anyone noticing means there was no alerting at the job level at all - the team was relying on a human reading an invoice once a month. I'd put a CloudWatch alarm directly on that job's duration and DPU-hour consumption, set a hard job timeout so it fails instead of limping along for six hours, and make sure whoever owns that pipeline gets paged the first night it drifts, not two months later.
commonMistakes: Assuming more DPUs always means faster and cheaper without checking for data skew first
Not verifying job bookmarks actually advanced, which hides a full-reprocess regression behind a seemingly normal job status
Only looking at wall-clock runtime without correlating it against two months of data volume growth
Relying on an end-of-month AWS bill review instead of job-level CloudWatch alarms for cost anomalies
Not checking the Spark UI task duration distribution before scaling worker count up
keyPoints: Pull CloudWatch job metrics across the full two months to find exactly when the regression started
Verify job bookmarks are actually advancing and job.commit() is reached every run
Check for data skew via Spark UI task duration distribution before adding workers
Right-size DPUs/workers and consider Glue Auto Scaling instead of a fixed allocation
Add CloudWatch alarms on job duration/DPU-hours and a job timeout, not just a monthly budget alarm

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Diagnoses via CloudWatch job metrics history correlated with the regression timeline
Checks whether job bookmarks are actually functioning as a root cause candidate
Identifies data skew or DPU/worker misconfiguration as candidates
Proposes a concrete fix (right-sizing, bookmark fix, repartitioning)
Proposes proactive monitoring/alerting to prevent recurrence

questions.title: BI Dashboards Timing Out on a Redshift Cluster That Looks Only Moderately Loaded
questions.prompt: A Redshift cluster serves both nightly ETL loads and daytime BI dashboard queries. Dashboards have started timing out during business hours, but cluster CPU utilization only looks moderately loaded in the console. Walk through how you'd diagnose this using Redshift's workload management internals, and what you'd actually change to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: CPU utilization is the wrong metric to start with here, because a query can be perfectly healthy in terms of resource usage and still time out if it's sitting in a queue waiting for a WLM slot. The first thing I'd check is queue wait time versus execution time, using SVL_QUERY_QUEUE_INFO or STV_WLM_QUERY_STATE, to see whether the dashboard queries are actually running slowly or are mostly just waiting their turn behind other queries. In my experience, nine times out of ten this scenario is a single shared WLM queue - often just the default queue - handling both the nightly ETL load and the daytime BI traffic, with a low concurrency slot count (say 5), so a handful of long-running or poorly-written ad hoc analyst queries, or an ETL job that overran into business hours, are occupying all the available slots and everything else queues behind them. Second, I'd check whether the nightly ETL is actually finishing on schedule - if it's bleeding into business hours, that alone could be the entire cause, independent of WLM config. Third, I'd look at whether Concurrency Scaling is enabled; if it isn't, Redshift has no way to add transient burst capacity for read queries during the business-hours spike. The fix is to stop treating this as one workload: create separate WLM queues with their own concurrency slot counts and priorities - one for ETL with lower priority, one for BI dashboards with dedicated slots and higher priority - either via manual WLM or query priority groups in automatic WLM. I'd add Query Monitoring Rules to cap or demote runaway queries (e.g., kill anything over a row-count or runtime threshold in the BI queue) so one bad dashboard query can't starve the others. If the business truly needs guaranteed isolation, I'd consider Redshift Serverless workgroups or a separate consumer via data sharing so BI and ETL don't compete for the same compute at all, and if ETL is simply running too long, I'd fix that pipeline directly rather than papering over it with more WLM slots. Concurrency Scaling should also be enabled so unexpected BI bursts get extra capacity automatically instead of queuing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap in this question is the phrase 'CPU looks only moderately loaded,' because that's exactly the kind of detail that sends people down the wrong path - they go look at compute graphs when the real problem is almost always queuing, not raw horsepower. So I'd skip the CPU graph entirely and go straight to the WLM query queue views to split out queue wait time from actual execution time for the slow dashboard queries. If I see queries sitting in queue for most of their total time, that confirms it's a concurrency/slot problem, not a processing problem. Then I'd ask the obvious operational question: is everything - the nightly load and the daytime dashboards - sharing one queue? Almost always, yes, and almost always that queue has a small fixed number of concurrency slots, so the moment a few long-running analyst queries or a late-running ETL job grab those slots, every dashboard behind them just waits. I'd also specifically check whether the ETL job is spilling into business hours, because if it is, that's honestly the simplest root cause and the simplest fix - get it to finish before the business day starts. Assuming WLM contention is confirmed, my fix is to give BI its own queue with dedicated concurrency and a sensible priority, separate from ETL, and put Query Monitoring Rules on that queue so a single misbehaving dashboard query gets killed or demoted instead of eating all the capacity. If I were advising a team on where to go next, depending on how much isolation they actually need, I'd talk about Concurrency Scaling to absorb bursts automatically, or in a more mature setup, actually splitting the workloads onto separate compute entirely - a Serverless workgroup or a data share to a second consumer - so BI stops competing with ETL for the same cluster at all. The key insight I'd want to get across in an interview is that 'the cluster isn't busy' and 'queries are slow' are not contradictory once you understand that WLM queuing happens independently of raw CPU usage.
commonMistakes: Reading CPU utilization as the whole story and ignoring WLM queue wait time
Running nightly ETL and daytime BI dashboards in the same default WLM queue with shared concurrency slots
Not using Query Monitoring Rules to cap or demote runaway queries
Overlooking that the nightly ETL job may simply be overrunning into business hours
Not considering Concurrency Scaling or workload isolation (a separate workgroup or data share) for BI traffic
keyPoints: Distinguish queue wait time from execution time using WLM query queue views, not CPU graphs
Identify shared/default queue contention between ETL and BI as the likely root cause
Separate WLM queues by workload with appropriate priority and concurrency slots
Consider Concurrency Scaling or a separate Serverless workgroup/data share for true isolation
Use Query Monitoring Rules and check whether ETL is overrunning into business hours

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Diagnoses via WLM queue wait-time metrics rather than CPU utilization alone
Identifies shared/single-queue contention as the root cause
Proposes WLM queue separation with appropriate priority/concurrency tuning
Considers Concurrency Scaling or workload isolation for BI bursts
Notes Query Monitoring Rules or a scheduling fix to prevent ETL overlap

questions.title: Kinesis Consumer Lag Keeps Climbing With No Errors and No Rate Change
questions.prompt: A Kinesis Data Streams consumer application is falling further and further behind in real time - GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds keeps climbing - even though no errors are being thrown and the stream's incoming data rate hasn't changed. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Rising IteratorAgeMilliseconds with a stable incoming rate and no errors tells me the stream itself probably isn't the problem - something downstream of ingestion is either a bottleneck or unevenly loaded. First, I'd pull per-shard CloudWatch metrics (IncomingBytes, IncomingRecords, and crucially, per-shard read/write throughput) rather than stream-level aggregates, because an aggregate rate can look unchanged while one shard is actually hot due to a skewed partition key - for example, one high-volume customer ID or device ID hashing disproportionately to a single shard. A hot shard will show as consistently near its 1,000 records/sec or 1 MB/sec write limit while siblings are quiet, and it's the classic cause of IteratorAge creeping on that shard's consumers specifically. Second, I'd check the consumer side directly - is the application's per-record or per-batch processing time increasing, independent of Kinesis? A downstream dependency like a database write, an API call, or a Lambda invocation that's gotten slower (throttling, connection pool exhaustion) would show up exactly like this: no Kinesis errors, no rate change, just growing lag because the consumer can't keep pace. Third, I'd check whether this consumer uses standard GetRecords consumption or Enhanced Fan-Out, and whether multiple applications share the stream - standard consumers share a fixed 2 MB/sec and 5 transactions/sec read throughput per shard across all consumers reading it, so adding even one more consumer application to a stream can quietly starve an existing one of read throughput without any error being thrown. Fourth, I'd check whether the shard count itself is simply too low for the consumer's achievable throughput even without skew. The fix depends on which of these it is: if it's a hot shard from partition key skew, I'd redesign the partition key to a higher-cardinality field and reshard (split the hot shard or use UpdateShardCount) to spread load evenly; if it's a shared-throughput problem from multiple consumers, I'd register the application for Enhanced Fan-Out so it gets its own dedicated 2 MB/sec per shard; if it's a downstream processing bottleneck, I'd fix or scale that dependency and tune KCL/consumer batch size and worker count independently of Kinesis.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I like about this question is that the two details they gave - no errors, no rate change - are actually the clues, not red herrings. No errors rules out throttling exceptions being thrown back at the producer or consumer, and no rate change rules out 'the business just sent more data than usual.' So in my head that immediately narrows it down to either a hot shard or a consumer-side slowdown, and I'd check both in parallel rather than guessing. For the hot shard theory, I go to per-shard metrics, not the stream aggregate - I've been burned before by looking at stream-level IncomingRecords and thinking everything's fine, when really one shard was pinned at its throughput ceiling because of a skewed partition key, like all traffic from one big customer landing on the same shard. If I see that pattern, I know immediately what's wrong and the fix is a partition key redesign plus resharding, not throwing more consumers at the problem. On the consumer side, I'd check whether the actual per-record processing time has grown - maybe there's a downstream call, like a database write or an external API, that's gotten slower without throwing hard errors, just getting gradually sluggish. That would explain lag growing with nothing visibly broken. One thing I always ask in this scenario that people sometimes forget: is this the only application reading this stream? Because standard consumers share a fixed per-shard read throughput - two megabytes a second and five read transactions a second - across every consumer attached to that shard, so if someone recently added a second consumer app to the same stream, that alone would explain lag creeping up with zero errors on either side. If that's it, the fix is usually to move the important consumer onto Enhanced Fan-Out so it gets its own dedicated throughput instead of competing. I'd walk through all three paths with actual metrics before committing to a fix, because resharding for a problem that's really a downstream bottleneck just wastes effort and still leaves the lag growing.
commonMistakes: Treating 'no errors thrown' as proof nothing is wrong instead of checking lag metrics directly
Looking only at stream-level aggregate metrics instead of per-shard metrics that reveal a hot shard
Confusing simply adding more consumers with fixing a shared standard-consumer throughput limit
Not considering Enhanced Fan-Out when multiple consumers share a shard's standard read throughput
Overlooking a downstream processing bottleneck as the real cause rather than the stream itself
keyPoints: Rising IteratorAgeMilliseconds with a stable incoming rate points to a consumer-side or shard-level bottleneck
Check per-shard CloudWatch metrics for skew caused by a hot partition key
Standard consumers share a fixed 2MB/s and 5 TPS read throughput per shard; Enhanced Fan-Out gives each consumer its own
Resharding or partition key redesign addresses shard-level skew; scaling consumer compute addresses processing bottlenecks
Check whether another consumer application was recently added to the same stream

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets rising IteratorAge as a lag/bottleneck signal, not a throughput increase
Diagnoses a hot shard via per-shard CloudWatch metrics and partition key skew
Diagnoses a consumer-side bottleneck or shared read-throughput limit as an alternate cause
Proposes resharding and/or partition key redesign
Proposes Enhanced Fan-Out or consumer scaling as a fix

questions.title: A Step Functions Pipeline Is Silently Retrying the Same Failed Step for Days
questions.prompt: A Step Functions state machine orchestrating a multi-step ETL (Glue job, then Lambda validation, then Redshift load) is silently re-running the same failed step many times per day without ever failing the whole execution or alerting anyone, burning compute cost the whole time. Walk through diagnosing the Retry/Catch configuration causing this and how you'd redesign it properly.
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom - repeated re-runs with no visible failure or alert - points squarely at the Retry block on whatever state is failing, most likely the Glue job step given the cost impact described. I'd pull the Amazon States Language definition for that state and look at three things specifically: the ErrorEquals list, the MaxAttempts value, and whether there's a Catch clause at all. A very common misconfiguration is using ErrorEquals: ['States.ALL'] in the Retry block - that's meant for truly transient errors, but it also catches permanent errors (like a Glue job failing on bad data every single time), so the state machine keeps retrying something that will never succeed, burning a full Glue job run on every attempt. If MaxAttempts is set high, or the IntervalSeconds/BackoffRate combination allows many attempts over a day, that explains 'many times per day' directly. Next I'd check the execution history in the Step Functions console for a recent day's executions - I'd expect to see an execution that never reaches a terminal Fail state, either because it's still retrying when I look, or because it eventually succeeds by chance (e.g., transient resource contention clears up) and the overall execution reports as 'succeeded,' which is exactly why nobody got alerted - a CloudWatch alarm on ExecutionsFailed would never fire if the execution technically succeeds after enough retries. The fix has three parts. First, narrow the Retry's ErrorEquals to genuinely transient error types only (specific Glue exceptions, throttling, service exceptions) and set a sane bounded MaxAttempts (2-3) with an appropriate BackoffRate so a real transient issue gets a few chances but a permanent one fails fast. Second, add an explicit Catch clause after the Retry exhausts its attempts, routing to a Fail state or, better, to a notification state that publishes to SNS/EventBridge with the error details before failing the execution - so a genuine failure is visible immediately rather than silently absorbed. Third, add a CloudWatch alarm on the state machine's ExecutionsFailed and ExecutionsTimedOut metrics, and consider a state-level or execution-level TimeoutSeconds so a stuck step can't silently consume resources indefinitely even within its retry budget.
questions.professionalAnswer: This one's a classic 'it's not broken, it's just quietly expensive' bug, and the giveaway for me is 'never actually fails the whole execution.' That tells me there's a Retry block doing exactly what it was configured to do - retry - just configured way too permissively. So the very first thing I'd pull up is the ASL definition for the Glue step, because that's almost certainly where the cost is coming from, and I'd look specifically at what's in ErrorEquals. I've seen this exact bug before where someone used States.ALL to be safe, thinking 'this will catch anything that goes wrong and retry it,' without realizing that also means a permanent, deterministic failure - bad data, a bug in the Glue script, whatever - gets retried just as aggressively as a genuine transient blip like a throttling error. If MaxAttempts is generous on top of that, you get exactly this symptom: the same expensive Glue job running over and over, for the exact same doomed reason, multiple times a day. The other half of why nobody noticed is just as important to call out in an interview - if the execution eventually succeeds after enough retries, or if there's simply no Catch block routing a true exhaustion to a Fail state, then any alarm on ExecutionsFailed is never going to trip, because as far as Step Functions is concerned, nothing failed. So the fix isn't just 'tighten the retry policy,' it's really two separate fixes. One, make the Retry policy honest - only retry error types that are actually transient, with a small bounded number of attempts and real backoff, so a permanent failure stops burning money after two or three tries instead of running all day. Two, make failure visible - add a Catch after the Retry exhausts, send it to a notification step or straight to Fail, and put a CloudWatch alarm on ExecutionsFailed so a human finds out the same day, not whenever Finance happens to notice the bill.
commonMistakes: Using ErrorEquals: ['States.ALL'] in a Retry block without distinguishing transient from permanent errors
Setting MaxAttempts too high or BackoffRate/interval too aggressive, burning cost on a doomed retry
Omitting a Catch clause entirely so failures loop via Retry instead of ever surfacing
Not alarming on ExecutionsFailed/ExecutionsTimedOut for the state machine
Assuming 'the execution didn't fail' means everything is fine instead of inspecting execution history for repeated retries
keyPoints: Inspect the Retry configuration (ErrorEquals, MaxAttempts, BackoffRate) on the specific failing state
Narrow ErrorEquals to genuinely transient error types and bound MaxAttempts
Add a Catch clause routing exhausted retries to a Fail or notification state
Add a CloudWatch alarm on ExecutionsFailed/ExecutionsTimedOut for the state machine
Add a state or execution-level TimeoutSeconds to bound worst-case cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses an overly broad or unbounded Retry as the root cause
Identifies the missing Catch routing persistent failures to a failure/notification state
Proposes a specific Retry fix (bounded MaxAttempts, narrow ErrorEquals, BackoffRate)
Proposes a CloudWatch alarm on ExecutionsFailed/ExecutionsTimedOut for alerting
Notes an execution/state timeout to bound worst-case cost

questions.title: A DMS CDC Task That Ran Fine For Months Starts Falling Hours Behind
questions.prompt: A DMS change data capture replication task that has run reliably for months suddenly shows growing CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget metrics, and the target Redshift data is now falling hours behind the source database - but the task itself never fails or shows an error state. Walk through diagnosing this and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd do is separate CDCLatencySource from CDCLatencyTarget, because they measure completely different stages and point to different root causes - treating them as one 'DMS is slow' metric wastes time. CDCLatencySource measures how far behind DMS is in reading and capturing changes from the source transaction log; CDCLatencyTarget measures how far behind DMS is in applying already-captured changes to the target. If source latency is the one climbing, I'd look at the source database first: is there a long-running, uncommitted transaction holding the log reader back - DMS's log-based CDC generally can't advance past an open transaction, so one forgotten long transaction on the source can single-handedly stall capture for hours even though nothing 'fails.' I'd also check source transaction log retention and growth, and whether the source is under unusually heavy write load (a bulk batch job, a migration, an index rebuild) generating far more log volume than DMS can keep up with reading. If target latency is the one climbing instead, the bottleneck is on the apply side - I'd check the DMS replication instance's own CloudWatch metrics (CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, SwapUsage, NetworkTransmitThroughput) for resource exhaustion, and separately check whether batch apply is enabled and tuned appropriately versus transactional apply, since transactional (statement-by-statement) apply to Redshift is dramatically slower for high change volumes. I'd also check Redshift itself - is the WLM queue DMS applies into contending with other workloads, or is COPY/apply throughput simply saturated because changes are landing faster than Redshift can ingest them. Network throughput between the replication instance and both source and target is worth checking too, since a degraded network path produces exactly this symptom without an outright task failure. The fix follows from whichever branch is confirmed: resolve or kill the long-running source transaction and work with the DBA team to prevent recurrence, scale up the DMS replication instance class if it's resource-constrained, enable or retune batch apply settings, or relieve Redshift-side contention (separate WLM queue, more capacity) so apply can keep pace. Throughout, I'd make sure source log retention is generous enough to not lose data while root-causing, since log-based CDC depends on those logs still being available.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd zero in on immediately is that there are two separate latency metrics mentioned, source and target, because most people treat 'DMS is behind' as one undifferentiated problem, and that's the wrong instinct. I'd pull up both metrics side by side first, because which one is actually growing tells me which half of the pipeline to investigate - there's no point tuning Redshift if the real problem is DMS can't even read fast enough from the source. If it's source latency climbing, my first suspicion, from having seen this before, is a long-running open transaction on the source - something somebody kicked off, maybe a big batch update or a reporting query that opened a transaction and never closed it, and log-based CDC just can't move past that point until it commits. That's a genuinely sneaky failure mode because the DMS task itself looks completely healthy the whole time; it's just stuck waiting. I'd go check the source database directly for open transactions before I touch anything on the AWS side. If it turns out to be target latency instead, I'd pivot to the replication instance's own health - CPU, memory, swap - because an undersized instance that was fine for months can start falling over the moment change volume creeps up even slightly, and I'd also ask whether batch apply is actually turned on, because applying changes to Redshift one statement at a time instead of in batches is painfully slow once change volume gets non-trivial. And I wouldn't rule out Redshift itself being the bottleneck - if the WLM queue DMS writes into is also handling a bunch of other traffic, the apply step queues just like any other query would. The reason I'd walk through both branches explicitly in an interview rather than just picking one is that the fix is completely different depending on which side is actually slow, and jumping straight to 'scale up the replication instance' when the real issue is a stuck source transaction wouldn't fix anything - it would just make a more expensive instance sit there waiting on the same lock.
commonMistakes: Treating CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget as one undifferentiated 'DMS is slow' metric
Not checking the source database for a long-running open transaction blocking log advancement
Assuming task status of 'running' means there is no problem, ignoring latency metrics entirely
Not checking the DMS replication instance's own CPU/memory/swap for resource exhaustion
Not checking the Redshift-side WLM/COPY throughput as the apply-side bottleneck
keyPoints: CDCLatencySource measures capture-from-source lag; CDCLatencyTarget measures apply-to-target lag; diagnose them separately
A long-running or open source transaction can stall CDC log reading without failing the task
Check DMS replication instance CloudWatch metrics for resource exhaustion
Check Redshift-side WLM contention or COPY/apply throughput for a target-side bottleneck
Verify source transaction log retention is sufficient while root-causing to avoid data loss

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the source-latency vs target-latency diagnostic paths
Identifies a long-running source transaction as a plausible cause
Checks DMS replication instance resource metrics
Checks the Redshift-side apply/WLM bottleneck
Proposes a concrete fix per branch plus safeguards like log retention

questions.title: Lambda Functions Throttle During a Spike Even Though the Account Limit Wasn't Hit
questions.prompt: Multiple Lambda functions feeding a data pipeline start throwing TooManyRequestsException during a traffic spike, even though the team's initial check shows the account-level concurrency limit wasn't hit. Walk through diagnosing this and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The team's check of the account-level limit is the right instinct but the wrong granularity, because Lambda concurrency throttling can happen well below the account ceiling for a few specific reasons. First, I'd explain and check the unreserved concurrency pool: the account's total concurrency limit is a shared pool, but any function with Reserved Concurrency configured carves its allocation out of that shared pool permanently, whether or not it's currently using it. So if some other, possibly unrelated, function in the account has a large Reserved Concurrency setting, it can shrink the pool available to everyone else enough that a traffic spike on the pipeline's functions gets throttled, even though the account-wide number still has headroom on paper. Second, I'd check whether the throttled functions themselves have Reserved Concurrency set too low - that acts as a hard per-function ceiling regardless of what's available at the account level, so a function reserved for say 10 concurrent executions will throttle at the 11th invocation even if the account has thousands of unreserved slots free. Third, I'd check burst concurrency behavior specifically - Lambda doesn't scale concurrency instantly; it has an initial burst capacity (varies by region, historically in the 500-3000 range) and then scales by an additional increment per minute after that, so a sudden, sharp spike can exceed the scaling rate even when the steady-state limit is far from reached. I'd pull per-function CloudWatch Throttles and ConcurrentExecutions metrics (not just account-wide UnreservedConcurrentExecutions) to see exactly which functions are hitting their ceiling and when, which tells me whether this is a reserved-concurrency misallocation, a burst-rate issue, or genuinely an account limit problem the initial check missed. The fix depends on the finding: reallocate or right-size Reserved Concurrency across functions so no single function starves the shared pool unnecessarily, request a Service Quotas increase for account-level concurrency if genuinely needed, add Provisioned Concurrency for functions with predictable spike patterns, and in general decouple the pipeline's producers from Lambda with an SQS buffer so invocation rate is smoothed rather than hitting Lambda as a raw instantaneous spike, with retry/DLQ handling for anything that still throttles.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd push back on gently in this scenario is the team's framing - 'the account limit wasn't hit' is true but it's checking the wrong thing, and that's actually a really common mistake, so I'd walk through why. Account concurrency in Lambda isn't one flat number everyone draws from freely; any function with Reserved Concurrency configured takes that allocation out of the shared pool permanently, used or not. So I'd ask, almost immediately, whether any function in this account - even one totally unrelated to this pipeline - has a chunky reserved concurrency setting, because that alone can explain throttling well below the account ceiling. Separately, I'd check whether the pipeline's own functions have reserved concurrency set, because that's a hard per-function cap regardless of how much room the account has elsewhere - a function capped at ten concurrent executions throttles at eleven no matter what. And there's a third angle people often miss entirely: Lambda doesn't scale concurrency instantly during a spike, it has a burst allowance and then ramps up gradually, so even a function with plenty of theoretical concurrency available can throttle for a few minutes if the spike arrives faster than Lambda's scaling rate. So rather than guessing, I'd go straight to per-function CloudWatch Throttles metrics, not the account-wide number, because that tells me exactly which function throttled and roughly when relative to the spike, which narrows it down fast. Depending on what I find, the fix is either reallocating reserved concurrency more sensibly across functions, bumping up the account quota if it's genuinely needed, adding Provisioned Concurrency to smooth out a predictable burst pattern, or - and this is the fix I'd actually recommend for a data pipeline specifically - putting an SQS queue in front of the functions so Lambda is pulling at its own pace instead of getting hit with the full force of the spike directly, with a DLQ to catch anything that still fails.
commonMistakes: Checking only the account-level concurrency limit without checking each function's Reserved Concurrency setting
Not realizing Reserved Concurrency on one function shrinks the shared unreserved pool available to all others
Ignoring the burst (scale-up rate) concurrency limit versus the steady-state account limit
Not reviewing per-function CloudWatch Throttles metrics to pinpoint which function is actually starved
Not implementing backpressure (SQS buffering, retries with a DLQ) upstream of Lambda to absorb spikes
keyPoints: Account concurrency is a shared pool minus any Reserved Concurrency carve-outs on other functions
A function can throttle below account headroom if its own Reserved Concurrency is too low or a burst exceeds the scaling rate
Check per-function CloudWatch Throttles and ConcurrentExecutions, not just the account-wide metric
Request a Service Quotas increase and/or reallocate Reserved Concurrency appropriately
Decouple with SQS buffering and Provisioned Concurrency for predictable spike patterns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the shared unreserved concurrency pool and Reserved Concurrency interaction correctly
Identifies the burst limit vs steady-state limit distinction
Diagnoses via per-function CloudWatch Throttles/ConcurrentExecutions metrics
Proposes a concrete fix (reserved concurrency reallocation, quota increase, provisioned concurrency)
Proposes decoupling/backpressure (SQS, retry/DLQ) for resilience

questions.title: Glue Job Bookmark Reprocesses the Entire Dataset After a Schema Change
questions.prompt: After adding a new column to the source files, a Glue ETL job with job bookmarks enabled starts reprocessing the entire dataset from scratch on every run, instead of picking up only new data. Walk through the real, specific causes of this failure mode and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd confirm the basics - that Job bookmark is actually set to 'Enable' and not 'Disable' or 'Pause' in the job configuration, since that's the cheapest thing to rule out. Assuming it's enabled, bookmark state is only persisted when job.commit() executes successfully at the very end of the script run, after job.init() was called at the start. If the schema-change deployment introduced a code path where the script errors out, exits early, or the new column causes a downstream exception before reaching job.commit(), the bookmark for that run never gets written, and the next run has nothing to resume from, so it reprocesses everything. I'd check the actual job run logs for the deployment date for any exception, even one that didn't technically fail the job status. Second, and more specific to a code change like this, Glue tracks bookmark state keyed by the transformation_ctx string passed into create_dynamic_frame.from_catalog or from_options. If whoever added the new column also touched that call and changed the transformation_ctx value - even slightly, or regenerated it dynamically rather than using a fixed literal - Glue treats it as a brand-new, never-before-seen context with no prior bookmark history, and starts from scratch. This is the single most common cause of exactly this symptom after a code deployment, and I'd check the diff on that deployment specifically for any change to the transformation_ctx argument. Third, I'd check whether anyone ran aws glue reset-job-bookmark during the deployment - sometimes this is done intentionally to force a one-time full reprocess to backfill the new column for historical data, and if so, this might actually be expected for that one run, but should not persist into subsequent runs. Fourth, I'd check the job's max concurrency setting - running the same bookmarked job with concurrency greater than 1 is not safe, since concurrent runs can race on reading and writing bookmark state, leaving it in an inconsistent state. The fix is to make job.commit() unconditionally reached (wrap the core logic so the script always reaches commit unless it needs to intentionally fail), restore the transformation_ctx to the stable value it had before, avoid dynamically generating it, keep concurrency at 1 for this job, and after deploying the fix, explicitly verify on the next run that the input record count matches only new data, not the full table, to confirm bookmarks resumed correctly.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'we added a column and now it reprocesses everything,' my mind goes straight to one specific thing before anything else: did the transformation_ctx string change? That's because Glue's bookmark state isn't tied to the table or the job name the way people assume - it's tied to that exact context string on the from_catalog or from_options call, and it's genuinely common for someone touching the extraction code to add a new column, maybe refactor the read call a little, and inadvertently change that string, even without meaning to. From Glue's perspective that's not 'the same source with a new column,' it's an entirely new source it's never tracked before, so of course it starts from zero. I'd ask to see the diff from that deployment specifically looking for any change near the DynamicFrame creation call. If that comes back clean, my second suspect is job.commit() not being reached - bookmarks only persist on a clean commit at the end of the run, so if the new column introduced some downstream type error or null-handling bug that's throwing an exception partway through, even if the overall job status doesn't obviously scream 'failed,' the bookmark for that run just never gets saved, and next time there's nothing to resume from. I'd go check the actual run logs around that date for anything unusual, not just the job status flag. There's also a simpler, almost boring explanation I always ask about directly: did someone intentionally call reset-job-bookmark to force a one-time full reprocess so the new column gets backfilled into historical rows? If so, that's expected for one run, and the real question becomes whether it's still happening on subsequent runs, which would point back to one of the other causes. Whatever the actual cause turns out to be, my fix always ends the same way - after I patch it, I don't just trust that it's fixed, I check the next run's input record count and confirm it's processing only new data, not the whole table again, because that's the only real proof the bookmark is actually working.
commonMistakes: Forgetting job.commit() at the end of the script, or an unhandled exception preventing it from being reached
Dynamically generating the transformation_ctx string so Glue never recognizes the prior bookmark state
Running the job with max concurrency greater than 1 and assuming bookmarks are concurrency-safe
Not realizing a manual reset-job-bookmark call during a hotfix deploy forces a full reprocess on the next run
Assuming bookmarks are generically 'broken' instead of checking the specific commit/context/concurrency mechanics
keyPoints: Bookmark state is only persisted when job.commit() executes successfully at the end of a run
The transformation_ctx string must remain stable across runs and deployments for a given source
A manual reset-job-bookmark call explicitly wipes state and forces full reprocessing on the next run
Max concurrency greater than 1 is not safe for job-bookmark-enabled sources
After an expected one-time full reprocess, verify the next run's input size to confirm incremental behavior resumed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Confirms bookmarks are enabled and explains the job.commit() persistence mechanism correctly
Diagnoses transformation_ctx instability as a specific root cause
Checks for a manual bookmark reset or max concurrency greater than 1 as contributing causes
Proposes a concrete fix ensuring commit() is always reached and transformation_ctx is stable
Proposes a verification step confirming incremental behavior post-fix

questions.title: Choosing Glue+Redshift vs. Glue+Athena as the Serving Layer
questions.prompt: Design the end-to-end flow for a batch analytics pipeline that lands raw data in S3, and justify choosing Glue+Redshift versus Glue+Athena as the serving layer. Cover query patterns, concurrency, and cost at scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline starts the same way regardless of which serving layer gets chosen: raw data lands in S3 in its native format, a Glue Crawler (or an explicit Glue ETL job writing with catalog updates) registers it in the Glue Data Catalog, and a Glue ETL job transforms and cleans it into a curated S3 layer, typically partitioned Parquet. The Glue Catalog is the shared metadata layer either serving layer will query against, so that part of the design doesn't change - the decision is purely about where queries ultimately run. I'd choose Redshift when the query pattern is frequent, repeated, and concurrency-heavy: dashboards that many analysts hit throughout the day, sub-second or low-second latency expectations, and complex joins across several large tables that benefit from sort keys and distribution keys. Redshift's cost model is essentially fixed - you pay for cluster/RA3 node-hours (or Serverless RPU-seconds) regardless of how many queries run against it, so the marginal cost of an additional dashboard query is close to zero, which is exactly the right economics for high-frequency repeated access. Concurrency is handled through WLM queues with a bounded, predictable number of slots, giving consistent performance under load. I'd choose Athena when the query pattern is ad hoc, exploratory, or infrequent - data scientists running one-off analyses, infrequent historical lookups, or a large archive that's rarely touched. Athena's cost model is pay-per-TB-scanned with zero infrastructure to manage, which is ideal when usage is sporadic, but becomes expensive and unpredictable if the same large tables get queried constantly, especially if the underlying data isn't partitioned and stored in a columnar format like Parquet - unoptimized Athena usage at high query volume can easily cost more than a provisioned Redshift cluster would have. Athena also has per-account query concurrency limits and variable per-query latency (each query effectively 'cold starts'), making it a poor fit for latency-sensitive, high-concurrency BI dashboards at scale. In practice, many real architectures use both: hot, frequently-queried, recent data gets loaded into Redshift, while cold, historical, or rarely-accessed data stays in S3 and is queried via Athena or, bridging the two, Redshift Spectrum, which lets Redshift SQL directly query that same S3/Catalog data without a separate load step. The recommendation framework comes down to query frequency and concurrency driving the Redshift decision, and sporadic, cost-sensitive, exploratory access driving the Athena decision.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by pointing out that this decision doesn't actually change the first half of the pipeline at all - raw to S3, crawled into the Glue Catalog, transformed by Glue ETL into curated Parquet - that part is identical either way, so the real design conversation only starts once the data is clean and sitting in S3 ready to be queried. The way I actually think about the choice in practice is: who's hitting this data, how often, and how fast do they need an answer? If I'm picturing a BI dashboard that forty people refresh throughout the day, running the same handful of aggregation queries over and over, Redshift is the obvious call, because once you're paying for that cluster, running the query an extra thousand times a day costs basically nothing more - the economics reward repeated access. Athena flips that completely; you're paying per terabyte scanned every single time, so if I put a high-traffic dashboard on top of Athena without thinking about it, I could easily end up paying more in scan costs than a provisioned cluster would've cost outright, especially if the data isn't partitioned and compressed well. On the flip side, if I'm picturing a data scientist who runs one exploratory query against a five-year-old archive maybe twice a month, standing up Redshift capacity - or even loading that data into Redshift at all - for that access pattern is just wasted spend; Athena against that same S3 data, serverless, pay only when it's actually queried, is clearly the right call there. The concurrency piece matters too and I'd bring it up without being asked - Redshift gives you predictable, bounded concurrency through WLM queues, so a dashboard under load behaves consistently, whereas Athena has account-level concurrency limits and each query has its own latency profile, so it's just not built for a hundred people hammering the same dashboard simultaneously. In a real system I've usually ended up recommending both at once - recent, hot data loaded into Redshift for the dashboards, older cold data left in S3 and reached either directly through Athena or through Redshift Spectrum so analysts can still query it from the same SQL interface without anyone having to load it anywhere.
commonMistakes: Treating Athena as a drop-in Redshift replacement without accounting for concurrency and latency differences
Not partitioning or compressing S3 data into Parquet before relying on Athena, causing high scan costs
Loading everything into Redshift 'just in case' and paying for unused cluster capacity
Ignoring Redshift Spectrum as a hybrid middle ground between the two options
Not considering query pattern (ad hoc vs repeated dashboard) when choosing the serving layer
keyPoints: The Glue Catalog is the shared metadata layer regardless of which serving option is chosen
Redshift: consistent low latency, higher concurrency ceiling via WLM, fixed/committed cost regardless of query volume
Athena: serverless, pay-per-scan, ideal for sporadic or exploratory access, needs partitioning and columnar format for cost control
Redshift Spectrum bridges both, letting Redshift SQL query cold S3 data without a separate load
Recommendation hinges on query frequency, concurrency needs, latency SLA, and cost predictability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the end-to-end flow using the Glue Catalog as a shared metadata layer
Compares query pattern and concurrency tradeoffs accurately
Compares cost model accurately (committed cost vs per-scan cost)
Mentions how partitioning/format choice affects Athena cost
Gives a clear, justified recommendation framework
