questions.modelAnswer: Devices publish events onto a Kinesis Data Streams stream, which serves as the durable ingestion point feeding two independent consumers. The first, a Firehose consumer, buffers and delivers the complete, untransformed raw event stream to S3 (converted to Parquet, partitioned by arrival or event time) with no aggregation applied at all. The second, a Kinesis Data Analytics (Managed Service for Apache Flink) application, performs windowed aggregation - tumbling or sliding windows over device metrics - and writes the aggregated results onward to Redshift. Both destinations are kept deliberately rather than picking one: raw S3 storage preserves full fidelity, which matters because aggregation is a one-way, irreversible transformation - you can always recompute a different aggregate from raw events later (a different window size, a corrected calculation, a new metric nobody thought of originally), but you can never reconstruct individual events from an aggregate that already discarded them. Redshift's aggregated data, meanwhile, keeps BI/dashboard queries cheap and fast by avoiding the need to scan and re-aggregate raw event volume on every query. For late and out-of-order data specifically, the KDA/Flink layer needs to run on event-time semantics, using the actual timestamp embedded in each device event, not the time it happened to arrive - IoT devices with intermittent connectivity routinely send events late, sometimes well after they occurred. Flink tracks a watermark representing its best estimate of event-time progress, and I'd configure an explicit allowed-lateness tolerance so a window isn't finalized and emitted the instant the watermark passes it; events arriving within that lateness window trigger an updated re-emission of that window's aggregate rather than being silently dropped. There's a real tradeoff in how large to set that lateness tolerance: too short and you lose legitimately late data or compute slightly wrong aggregates; too long and you delay how quickly any aggregate becomes available, hurting dashboard freshness. Because a window's aggregate can be re-emitted after a late correction, the Redshift sink has to upsert/MERGE by window key - device ID plus time bucket - rather than blind-appending, so a corrected re-emission updates the existing row instead of creating a duplicate. The raw S3/Firehose path doesn't need any of this complexity, since it's simply appending events as they arrive with their true event-time field preserved, which is exactly what makes it the right place to go back to later if the aggregation logic itself ever needs to be redone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by explaining why I'm deliberately keeping two destinations instead of just picking one, because that's really the heart of the design decision here, not an afterthought. Once you've aggregated data, you can't get the individual events back - it's a one-way door. So even though the aggregated numbers in Redshift are what the dashboards actually use day to day, I'd always keep the raw event stream landing untouched in S3 too, because the day someone asks for a different window size, or realizes the aggregation logic had a bug, or wants a metric nobody thought to compute originally, the raw data is the only thing that lets you go back and redo it correctly. Firehose handling that raw path is nice because it's basically zero-maintenance - it just buffers and drops events into S3 as Parquet, no aggregation logic to get wrong. The more interesting engineering problem is the aggregation path, specifically because these are IoT devices, and IoT devices are notorious for sending data late - a device loses connectivity for twenty minutes, reconnects, and suddenly a batch of events shows up well after they actually happened. If my aggregation layer just groups things by when they arrived instead of when they actually occurred, I'd end up with wrong numbers - events from an outage landing in whatever window happens to be open when they finally show up, instead of the window they actually belong to. So I'd insist on event-time processing in the Flink application, using the timestamp the device recorded, with a watermark tracking how far event-time has progressed, and critically, an explicit allowed-lateness setting so a window doesn't just slam shut the second the watermark crosses it - data arriving within that grace period still gets folded into the right window and the aggregate gets re-emitted with the correction. That's a real tuning decision, not a free lunch - too generous a lateness window and dashboards feel stale because nothing's final for a while; too strict and you're silently losing or miscounting data from devices that reconnect a bit late. And because a window's number can get revised after a late arrival, I'd make sure the Redshift side is built to handle that gracefully - upserting by a window key, device plus time bucket, instead of just appending new rows every time, otherwise a legitimate correction turns into a duplicate instead of an update. The raw S3 side, by contrast, doesn't need any of this - it's just append whatever arrives, whenever it arrives, with its true timestamp intact, and that simplicity is exactly why it's valuable as the fallback source of truth.
commonMistakes: Running KDA aggregation on processing-time instead of event-time, producing incorrect aggregates for delayed devices
Not setting an appropriate allowed-lateness/watermark tolerance, causing excessive delay or dropped late data
Writing aggregated results to Redshift via blind INSERT instead of upsert/MERGE by window key
Assuming raw S3 storage needs the same windowing and lateness handling as the aggregation path
Silently losing data that arrives after a window has already closed and lateness tolerance has expired
keyPoints: Keeping both raw S3 and aggregated Redshift destinations avoids an irreversible granularity tradeoff
KDA/Flink should use event-time processing with watermarks and a configured allowed lateness for out-of-order IoT data
Late data within the lateness tolerance should trigger an update/re-emit of the affected window, not a new disjoint record
The Redshift sink must upsert/MERGE by window key to handle re-emitted or corrected aggregates idempotently
Raw landing via Firehose is append-only and does not need windowing logic, just accurate event-time capture

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why both raw S3 and aggregated Redshift destinations are kept
Correctly designs event-time, watermark, and allowed-lateness handling in KDA/Flink
Designs an idempotent Redshift sink (upsert/MERGE by window key) for late corrections
Explains the raw S3/Firehose path does not need the same windowing complexity
Addresses handling of data arriving after the lateness tolerance expires

questions.title: Technical Migration Architecture: On-Prem SQL Server Warehouse to AWS via DMS, S3, and Redshift
questions.prompt: Design the technical migration architecture (not the people or timeline side - that's a separate behavioral question) for moving a mid-size on-prem SQL Server data warehouse to AWS using DMS, S3, and Redshift. Cover a phased cutover plan and how you'd validate data parity before decommissioning the source.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start with assessment and schema conversion using the AWS Schema Conversion Tool, which evaluates SQL Server DW objects - tables, views, stored procedures - for Redshift compatibility, flags constructs that need manual rewriting, and converts the DDL to Redshift-compatible schema, at which point I'd also choose sort and distribution keys based on the DW's known query patterns rather than guessing blind. Next, an initial full load: a DMS task extracts existing table data to S3 staging in Parquet, then a load step COPYs it into Redshift tables matching the converted schema, run entirely while the source system remains live and authoritative - nothing user-facing changes yet. Immediately following full load, I'd enable DMS's ongoing CDC replication so Redshift continuously receives changes from the source's transaction log, keeping it trailing the source by a small, measurable lag - this begins the dual-run period where both systems are live and in near-sync simultaneously. Validation is the phase I'd treat as non-negotiable and give real time to: beyond DMS's built-in data validation feature (row count and content checksums), I'd reconcile actual business metrics - daily revenue totals, key report figures - between the legacy DW and Redshift, since row counts can match while aggregate values differ due to type conversion, rounding, or subtle logic differences introduced during schema conversion; I'd also run the organization's existing BI reports against both systems side by side and diff the output. I'd keep this dual-run validation period going for at least one full business cycle - including period-end close processing specifically, since that's often where hidden logic differences surface that a few ordinary days of validation would miss. Only once validation is clean would I begin a phased cutover - moving BI consumers and reports over table-by-table or subject-area-by-subject-area, starting with lower-risk areas, rather than a single big-bang switch - while deliberately keeping CDC running throughout this phase, since the source remaining in sync is exactly what makes rollback possible if a cutover subject area reveals an issue. Only after every consumer has been cut over and a defined post-cutover monitoring window - another full reporting cycle or two - passes with no discrepancies would I stop the CDC task, take a final archival export of the source for compliance retention, and decommission the source infrastructure; decommissioning before that monitoring window closes removes the rollback safety net while there's still real risk of an undiscovered issue.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this as a sequence of gates, because the part I actually care about most in a migration like this isn't the happy path, it's making sure I never lose the ability to roll back until I'm genuinely confident I won't need to. So, first gate: before any data moves, I'd run the Schema Conversion Tool against the existing SQL Server DW to find out what's actually going to be a problem - certain stored procedure logic, certain data types, things that don't translate cleanly to Redshift - and get the DDL converted and the sort and distribution keys chosen based on how the warehouse actually gets queried today, not guessed at. Second gate: do the initial full load into Redshift via DMS and S3 staging while the old system just keeps running exactly as it always has - nobody downstream even knows this is happening yet. Third, and this is really where the interesting part of the migration begins, I'd turn on DMS CDC immediately after the full load so Redshift starts continuously trailing the source, and now I've got both systems live and roughly in sync at the same time - what I'd call the dual-run period. This is the phase I'd actually spend the most real calendar time on, because validating correctly here is what the entire migration's safety depends on. And I'd be specific about what 'validating correctly' actually means - it's not enough to check that row counts match between the two systems, because I've seen migrations where the counts lined up perfectly and the actual dollar figures in a report were subtly wrong because of some rounding or type-conversion quirk that crept in during schema conversion. So I'd reconcile real business numbers - the actual report totals people care about - not just counts, and I'd deliberately let this dual-run period span at least one full close cycle, because period-end processing is exactly where hidden logic differences tend to surface, and a few random weekdays of validation just won't catch that. Once that's clean, I'd cut consumers over gradually - subject area by subject area, starting with the lowest-stakes reports - rather than flipping everyone over in one shot, and critically, I'd keep CDC running the entire time I'm doing that phased cutover, because that's my actual rollback plan if cutting over one subject area reveals a problem I didn't catch in validation. The very last gate, and the one I'd never skip no matter how much pressure there is to save cost by shutting the old system down sooner, is a defined monitoring window after everyone's fully cut over - another reporting cycle or two with zero discrepancies - before I'll agree to actually decommission the source. Decommissioning early is how migrations turn into unrecoverable incidents.
commonMistakes: Attempting a big-bang cutover without a dual-run validation period
Validating only row counts without reconciling actual business metric values
Decommissioning the source immediately after cutover instead of keeping a monitoring and rollback window
Not accounting for stored procedure or view logic differences between SQL Server and Redshift SQL during conversion
Treating the CDC dual-run phase as instant or short, underestimating how long true parity validation takes
keyPoints: Use AWS SCT for schema and code conversion assessment before any data movement begins
DMS full load establishes the initial Redshift dataset; DMS CDC then keeps it continuously in sync during a dual-run validation period
Parity validation must include row counts, checksums, and reconciled business metrics, not counts alone
Cutover should be phased by subject area or consumer rather than all at once, with CDC running as a rollback safety net
The source should only be decommissioned after a defined post-cutover monitoring window with no discrepancies

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sequences schema conversion, full load, and CDC dual-run phases
Designs thorough parity validation (counts, checksums, business metric reconciliation)
Designs a phased, not big-bang, cutover by subject area or consumer
Correctly treats CDC as a rollback safety net during the transition
Specifies a sound decommissioning gate (post-cutover monitoring window)

lessonLink.label: Review: Migrating a Database with DMS

questions.title: Defending a Redshift Recommendation Against a Cost-Focused VP
questions.prompt: You recommended Redshift for a new analytics workload; a VP pushes back, pointing at the sticker-price difference vs. just querying S3 with Athena, and wants you to justify the choice in a room with non-technical leadership. Tell me about a time you had to defend a technical/architecture decision to leadership who weren't convinced by cost alone, or how you'd approach this one.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a translation problem, not a technical-superiority argument. Start with Situation: frame the workload characteristics that drove the Redshift recommendation in the first place — high query concurrency from BI dashboards, repeated scans over the same large tables, predictable business-hours usage, and a need for workload management (WLM) and consistent sub-second response for dozens or hundreds of concurrent users. Task: you need to justify the choice to leadership whose only visible data point is sticker price, in a room where technical jargon won't land.

The core of the Action should be reframing cost from 'price of the service' to 'total cost of ownership and risk.' A strong candidate explains concretely how they built this case: pulling actual or projected query volume and data-scanned-per-query estimates, modeling what Athena's per-TB-scanned pricing would actually cost under realistic concurrent BI usage (not a single ad hoc query), and comparing that against Redshift's flat, predictable cluster cost. They should mention that Athena has no native concurrency throttling or resource isolation the way Redshift's WLM queues do, so a popular dashboard under Athena risks both unpredictable bills and degraded performance for other users — a business risk, not just an engineering preference. Critically, a strong answer does not dismiss the VP's concern; it validates that sticker price is a legitimate lens, then shows the fuller picture with a simple side-by-side number (e.g., 3-year TCO) that a non-technical audience can read at a glance.

Another key element: offering a way to de-risk the decision rather than just asserting it — proposing a short proof-of-concept, a cost-monitoring guardrail (e.g., Redshift reserved instances or Concurrency Scaling to control spend), or a fallback plan if usage patterns change (e.g., moving cold/rarely-queried data to S3 with Redshift Spectrum). This signals maturity: the candidate isn't just defending a decision, they're managing cost risk on an ongoing basis.

Result should show the outcome: did leadership approve with the added cost controls, did the candidate's data change the framing of the conversation, or did they even discover through the exercise that a hybrid approach (Redshift for hot/concurrent workloads, Athena for ad hoc/cold data) was actually the better call. Interviewers are listening for composure under pushback, the ability to speak in business terms (dollars, risk, user experience) rather than technical ones, and willingness to engage the question honestly instead of getting defensive.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This actually happened to me at a previous company. We were building out a BI layer for the finance and sales teams, and I'd recommended Redshift. Our VP of Finance, who was very cost-conscious, pulled up the AWS pricing pages in the meeting and said 'Athena is basically free until you query it — why are we paying for a cluster to sit there 24/7?' It was a fair question and I didn't want to brush it off.

What I did was go back after that meeting and actually pull our Athena query logs from a smaller pilot we'd already run, so I had real numbers instead of guesses. I built a simple one-page comparison: at our projected usage — about 40 concurrent dashboard users during business hours, each dashboard re-running similar aggregation queries against a 2TB fact table multiple times a day — Athena's per-TB-scanned pricing would have cost us more per month than a right-sized Redshift cluster, and that's before counting the fact that Athena has no concurrency control, so during peak hours queries would queue or compete for resources with no way to prioritize the exec dashboard over an analyst's ad hoc query.

When I presented it, I led with 'you're right that the sticker price looks worse, here's why the full picture is different,' and showed the TCO number side by side rather than a wall of technical explanation. I also proposed we use Redshift reserved instances to lock in a lower rate once we were confident in the sizing, and that we'd keep historical, rarely-touched data in S3 and query it via Redshift Spectrum instead of duplicating it — so we weren't paying twice.

The VP's main follow-up was 'how do we know the cluster is sized right and we're not overpaying for headroom we don't use,' which told me the real concern wasn't Redshift versus Athena at all, it was fear of an open-ended AWS bill. So I committed to a monthly cost review for the first quarter with actual utilization numbers, which gave them a concrete checkpoint instead of just trusting my judgment. They approved it, and by month three we'd actually right-sized down one node type, which built a lot of credibility for future architecture calls.
commonMistakes: Leading with technical architecture details (WLM, cluster nodes, concurrency scaling) before establishing the business cost comparison the VP actually cares about
Treating the VP's cost concern as uninformed rather than validating it as a legitimate business question before adding nuance
Presenting only a qualitative argument ('Redshift is faster/better for this') with no actual dollar or usage-based comparison
Getting visibly defensive or over-explaining technical tradeoffs when pushed, instead of acknowledging the tradeoff and offering a mitigation
Failing to offer any ongoing cost control or review mechanism, leaving leadership with the impression the decision is a blank check
keyPoints: Reframes cost from sticker price to total cost of ownership including risk and concurrency
Uses real or realistic query volume and data-scanned numbers rather than hand-waving
Validates the VP's concern before adding nuance instead of dismissing it
Translates technical tradeoffs into business language (dollars, risk, user experience) for a non-technical room
Proposes a concrete way to de-risk or validate the decision (POC, reserved instances, cost review cadence)
Shows composure and stays collaborative rather than defensive under pushback

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quality and rigor of the cost/TCO comparison presented
Ability to translate technical tradeoffs into business language for non-technical leadership
Composure and collaborative tone when handling pushback
Concrete risk-mitigation or follow-up mechanism offered (POC, cost review, reserved pricing)
Clear STAR structure with a believable, specific outcome

questions.title: Handling a Junior Engineer's Costly Unmonitored Glue Job
questions.prompt: A junior engineer's Glue job, left with default settings and no monitoring, ran up a multi-thousand-dollar AWS bill over a weekend before anyone noticed. Tell me about how you'd handle the aftermath with that engineer — the conversation, the fix, and what changes you'd put in place — without making them afraid to ship again.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question is testing whether a senior engineer can separate 'fixing the system' from 'blaming the person,' while still being honest about what went wrong. A strong answer should open with Situation/Task: a junior engineer shipped a Glue job with default worker configuration (e.g., default DPU count, no auto-scaling limits, no job timeout) and no cost or CloudWatch alarming, and it ran unbounded over a weekend, generating a large bill. The senior engineer discovers it Monday and has to respond.

The Action should cover three distinct threads, and a strong answer keeps them separate rather than blending them into vague 'I talked to them' language. First, the immediate technical fix: stopping/bounding the job, understanding why it ran away (e.g., a missing partition filter causing a full table scan, or a retry loop with no backoff), and remediating the specific root cause. Second, the conversation with the junior engineer: a strong answer explicitly describes leading with curiosity ('walk me through what you were seeing') rather than accusation, separating the mistake from the person's competence, and making clear this is a systems gap, not a personal failure — most importantly, pointing out that the reason this wasn't caught wasn't the engineer's fault alone: there was no job timeout, no budget alarm, and no required review step for new production Glue jobs, which are organizational gaps a senior engineer or lead should have had in place already. Third, the structural fix: concrete guardrails such as mandatory job timeouts, AWS Budgets alerts tied to Glue/Cost Explorer tags, a lightweight pre-production checklist or peer review for new job configs, and possibly Service Quotas or SCPs to cap DPU usage for non-critical jobs.

The answer should explicitly address the 'without making them afraid to ship' angle: the senior engineer should describe how they framed the postmortem as blameless, credited the engineer for flagging it honestly or helping debug quickly, and possibly had the engineer co-author the fix (e.g., writing the runbook or the Terraform guardrail) so they leave the experience with more ownership and confidence, not less. A weak answer stops at 'I taught them to check their config' without building durable organizational guardrails — the interviewer should hear that the senior engineer takes institutional responsibility for the gap, not just individual blame.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This is close to something I dealt with directly. A newer engineer on my team had written a Glue ETL job to backfill about a year of historical data, and it had a bug where a join condition caused it to reprocess the same huge partition range in a loop instead of moving forward incrementally. It kicked off Friday afternoon, nobody was watching it over the weekend, and by Monday it had burned through several thousand dollars in DPU-hours.

The first thing I did Monday morning was stop the job and figure out the actual root cause before I said anything to him, because I didn't want to have a conversation based on assumptions. Once I confirmed it was the join logic plus the fact that we had no job timeout set, I went and found him in person rather than messaging, because I didn't want this to feel like a paper trail building against him. I opened with 'hey, I want to walk through the backfill job with you, I think I found what happened, want to make sure I'm right.' I let him explain his thinking first, and honestly his debugging logic for the original backfill was reasonable — the bug was subtle and the kind of thing that happens to everyone eventually.

I told him directly: this isn't on you alone. We had no job timeout, no cost alarm on that job's budget tag, and no second pair of eyes on a backfill job touching that much data before it went to prod. That's a gap in our process that I own as much as he does. We agreed together on three fixes: add a hard timeout to every Glue job as a non-negotiable default in our job-creation template, set up an AWS Budgets alert tied to our Glue cost allocation tags so anything unusual pages someone within hours instead of days, and require a quick peer review specifically for any job touching more than a defined row/partition threshold before it runs unattended.

I had him actually write the Terraform change for the default timeout and the budget alarm himself, partly because he understood the failure mode best, but also because I wanted his takeaway from this to be 'I helped fix something that'll protect the whole team,' not 'I'm the guy who torched the AWS bill.' A few weeks later he caught a similar issue in someone else's PR before it shipped, which told me the lesson landed the right way.
questions.example: Example guardrail set introduced after the incident: Glue job template requires --job-timeout, a mandatory cost-allocation tag enforced via a tagging policy, an AWS Budgets alert at 150% of the job's historical average spend, and a lightweight checklist item in the PR template for any job processing more than N GB or touching a backfill date range.
commonMistakes: Opening the conversation with blame or 'what happened' framed as an accusation instead of leading with curiosity about what they saw
Treating this purely as an individual mistake and fixing only the one job's config without adding systemic guardrails (timeouts, budget alarms)
Skipping the root-cause investigation and assuming the cause before talking to the engineer
Failing to acknowledge the senior engineer/team's own responsibility for missing review steps or alarms that should have existed already
Not giving the junior engineer a path to rebuild confidence (e.g., having them help author the fix) after the incident
keyPoints: Separates the technical root cause investigation from the interpersonal conversation
Leads the conversation with curiosity, not accusation
Explicitly frames the failure as a systems/process gap shared with the team, not solely the junior engineer's fault
Introduces concrete, durable guardrails (job timeouts, budget alarms, review checklist) rather than just a verbal warning
Actively protects the engineer's confidence and sense of ownership going forward
Shows a measurable or observed positive outcome after the fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quality of root-cause technical investigation before acting
Handling of the interpersonal conversation with psychological safety and respect
Shares institutional/process accountability rather than placing blame solely on the junior engineer
Concreteness and durability of the guardrails introduced
Evidence of a real, positive long-term outcome for the engineer and team

questions.title: Negotiating an Unrealistic Migration Timeline With Leadership
questions.prompt: Leadership wants the on-prem-to-AWS data warehouse migration finished in 6 weeks; your technical assessment says a safe migration with proper CDC validation and parallel-run needs 14. Tell me about a time you had to negotiate a timeline you knew was unrealistic, or how you'd handle this one.
questions.modelAnswer:
The interviewer wants to see that the candidate can push back on an unrealistic deadline using evidence and options, not just authority or a flat refusal, and not simply capitulating either. Situation/Task: leadership has set a 6-week deadline for an on-prem-to-AWS warehouse migration; the candidate's own technical assessment, based on CDC (change data capture) validation needs and a parallel-run period to confirm data parity, puts the realistic timeline at 14 weeks.

A strong Action breaks the gap down rather than arguing the headline number. The candidate should describe quantifying exactly where the 8-week gap comes from — e.g., X weeks for CDC pipeline validation against a sample of historical data, Y weeks for running old and new systems in parallel and reconciling discrepancies, Z weeks buffer for the inevitable data-quality surprises that show up only once real production volume hits the new system. This turns an abstract disagreement ('14 vs 6') into a concrete, inspectable breakdown leadership can engage with.

The strongest answers then offer options rather than just risk. For example: proposing a phased migration where a subset of lower-risk tables or a single business domain cuts over in 6 weeks while the full warehouse follows the 14-week plan; or offering to compress timeline by adding resources/parallelizing CDC validation across teams, in exchange for accepting a defined, named risk (e.g., 'we can hit 8 weeks for the core finance tables if we accept running without the full historical reconciliation and treat the first month of new-system numbers as provisional'). This shows the candidate understands that 'no' alone isn't useful to leadership — they need a menu of tradeoffs with the risk attached to each clearly named, usually in terms leadership cares about (customer-facing reporting errors, financial close risk, compliance exposure).

The candidate should also mention documenting the risk explicitly and getting it acknowledged in writing/email if leadership chooses to compress the timeline anyway — not as a CYA move for its own sake, but as a way of making sure the tradeoff was a conscious, informed decision rather than something that quietly got skipped. The Result should show either leadership adjusting the deadline once they saw the broken-down risk, or the team executing a phased/de-risked compromise. A weak answer either just complies with 6 weeks without flagging risk, or digs in on '14 weeks, non-negotiable' without offering any path forward — both fail to show the senior-level skill of negotiating with data and options.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I ran into almost exactly this during a warehouse migration off an on-prem Teradata system onto Redshift. Leadership had committed to a board deadline of six weeks publicly before engineering had even weighed in, which is its own problem, but that's the hand I was dealt.

Instead of just saying 'that's impossible,' I went back and broke down exactly why fourteen weeks was my number. I mapped it to three chunks: three weeks to build and validate the CDC pipeline against a real slice of production data and confirm row counts and checksums matched, six weeks of running the old and new systems in parallel so finance could reconcile month-end close numbers against both systems before cutting over for real, and about five weeks of buffer because in every migration I've done, something in the historical data — usually a timezone handling difference or a type coercion issue — surfaces only once you're running real volume.

I brought that breakdown to the program lead and framed it as 'here's what's driving the number, and here are two ways we could move faster if we're willing to accept specific named risk.' Option one: we migrate the three lowest-risk, non-financial reporting domains in six weeks, and keep the finance and compliance-sensitive tables on the fourteen-week track, since getting those wrong has real regulatory exposure. Option two: we compress by running CDC validation and parallel-run simultaneously instead of sequentially by pulling in a second engineer, which got us to about nine weeks, but meant the first two weeks of finance numbers post-cutover would be labeled provisional until full reconciliation finished.

Leadership actually went with a version of option one — they cut over the marketing and product analytics domains in six weeks, which let them tell the board something shipped on time, and gave the finance warehouse the full fourteen weeks since a single wrong revenue number in a board deck was a much bigger risk than being a few weeks late. I also made sure the agreed risk tradeoff was in a written project doc that the program lead signed off on, not because I was trying to protect myself, but so that if someone later asked 'why didn't finance ship in six weeks,' there was a clear record that it was a deliberate, informed call.
commonMistakes: Flatly refusing the deadline without breaking down where the time actually goes, leaving leadership no way to engage with the real constraints
Simply agreeing to the unrealistic deadline to avoid conflict, quietly planning to cut corners on CDC validation or parallel-run
Presenting only one option (the full 14 weeks) instead of offering phased or risk-traded alternatives leadership can choose between
Failing to name the concrete business risk (financial misstatement, compliance exposure, customer-facing errors) in terms leadership actually weighs
Not documenting the agreed tradeoff, leaving ambiguity later about whether the compressed risk was a conscious decision
keyPoints: Breaks the timeline gap into concrete components rather than arguing the headline number
Offers multiple options or a phased approach instead of a flat yes/no
Names the specific business risk being traded off in terms leadership cares about
Negotiates with data (historical migration experience, validation requirements) rather than authority alone
Documents the agreed tradeoff so the risk decision is explicit and deliberate
Shows a real resolution, not just the disagreement itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clarity and specificity of the timeline breakdown and risk reasoning
Quality of the negotiated options/alternatives offered to leadership
Ability to frame technical risk in business terms leadership can act on
Evidence of documenting or formalizing the agreed-upon tradeoff
Believable, specific outcome resolving the negotiation

questions.title: Owning an Overnight Pipeline Outage That Corrupted Downstream Reports
questions.prompt: A production data pipeline you're the primary owner of went down for several hours overnight, corrupting a day's worth of downstream reports before anyone caught it. Tell me how you handled (or would handle) owning that outage — the incident response, the communication to stakeholders, and the postmortem.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is an ownership and incident-response question, and a strong answer moves through three distinct phases clearly: immediate response, stakeholder communication, and postmortem/prevention — rather than blending them into one vague narrative. Situation/Task: the candidate owns a production pipeline that failed overnight (e.g., an upstream schema change, a failed Lambda/Glue step, or a silent data-quality issue) and bad or incomplete data propagated into downstream reports before anyone noticed, meaning the damage isn't just 'pipeline was down' but 'wrong numbers were consumed by someone.'

For the immediate response, a strong answer shows methodical triage: confirming the scope of the damage first (which tables, which date ranges, which downstream reports/dashboards/consumers were affected) before declaring it fixed, rather than guessing. It should mention concrete diagnostic steps appropriate to the AWS data stack — checking CloudWatch logs/metrics, Step Functions execution history, DLQs, or Glue job run history to find exactly where and why it broke — and distinguishing between 'stop the bleeding' (halting further bad data from propagating, e.g., pausing downstream consumers or flagging the affected date partition) and 'full fix' (correcting and reprocessing the bad data).

For stakeholder communication, the key behavior the interviewer wants to hear is proactive, early, and honest disclosure — not waiting until the fix is complete to say anything. A strong answer describes reaching out to known downstream consumers (e.g., the finance or reporting team using that data) as soon as the scope is understood, even before a fix is ready, with a clear statement of what's wrong, which numbers are affected, and when to expect a correction — and following up when it's actually resolved, including explicitly flagging which already-distributed reports need to be corrected or re-run.

For the postmortem, the answer should go beyond 'what caused it' to 'why didn't we catch it sooner.' The real seniority signal is addressing the detection gap: the pipeline failed and nobody noticed for hours, which points to missing or insufficient monitoring/alerting (e.g., no CloudWatch alarm on job failure, no data-quality check validating row counts or key business metrics before downstream consumption, no freshness SLA alert). The answer should name specific preventive measures — automated data-quality checks (e.g., row count anomaly detection, null-rate checks) gating downstream publication, alerting on pipeline failure within minutes not hours, and a documented runbook for this failure mode. A weak answer focuses only on the technical fix and skips the detection-gap analysis and stakeholder communication entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I had this happen with a pipeline I owned that fed our daily revenue reporting dashboard. An upstream source system changed a field's data type without telling us, our Glue job didn't fail loudly, it just silently dropped records that didn't match the expected schema, and that ran all night. By morning, the daily revenue numbers were understated by about 15%, and the reporting team had already pulled the dashboard into a leadership summary before I found out.

The first thing I did when I got the alert — which honestly came from someone in reporting saying 'these numbers look wrong,' not from our own monitoring, which was itself a problem — was to scope the damage before touching anything. I checked the Glue job run history and CloudWatch logs, found the exact run where records started getting silently dropped, and identified precisely which date partition and which downstream tables were affected, rather than assuming the whole week was bad.

Once I knew the scope, I didn't wait until I had a fix to tell people. I messaged the reporting team lead and my manager within about twenty minutes of confirming the issue: 'we have a data quality problem affecting yesterday's revenue numbers, root cause is a schema change upstream, we're working on a fix now, I'll have corrected numbers within the hour, please hold off distributing that dashboard further.' That mattered because leadership had already seen the wrong number, and the reporting lead was able to proactively flag it rather than someone else catching the discrepancy later and it looking like we tried to hide it.

I fixed the immediate issue by adding a defensive schema check and reprocessing the affected partition, and sent a follow-up with the corrected numbers and exactly which report needed re-pulling. But the postmortem is really where the senior-level fix happened: the real failure wasn't the schema change, upstream systems change schemas, that's expected. The real failure was that our pipeline failed silently and nobody downstream noticed for twelve hours. So I added a data-quality check comparing day-over-day row counts and revenue totals with a tolerance threshold, wired to a CloudWatch alarm that pages us before the dashboard even refreshes if the numbers look anomalous, and I made that a required gate before downstream publication for that pipeline going forward.
commonMistakes: Declaring the issue fixed before confirming the full scope of affected date ranges and downstream consumers
Waiting to communicate with stakeholders until a complete fix is in hand instead of disclosing early with a known-affected scope and timeline
Treating the schema change itself as the root cause instead of identifying the real gap: the failure happened silently with no detection
Fixing the immediate data but not reprocessing or flagging already-distributed downstream reports that consumed the bad data
Skipping concrete, specific postmortem action items in favor of a vague 'we'll be more careful' conclusion
keyPoints: Scopes the full blast radius (tables, date ranges, downstream consumers) before declaring anything fixed
Uses concrete AWS diagnostic tools (CloudWatch, Step Functions history, Glue job runs) to find root cause
Communicates proactively and early with affected stakeholders, before the fix is complete
Explicitly addresses already-distributed bad reports, not just the underlying data
Identifies the detection gap as the real root cause, not just the triggering event
Introduces concrete, durable monitoring/alerting to catch the failure mode faster next time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Methodical incident triage and accurate scoping of impact
Timeliness and honesty of stakeholder communication
Depth of postmortem root-cause analysis, especially the detection gap
Concreteness of preventive measures introduced afterward
Overall sense of ownership and accountability throughout

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Stakeholder's Preference for Kinesis Over Micro-Batching
questions.prompt: A senior stakeholder insists a reporting feed should move to real-time Kinesis streaming; your analysis says a 15-minute micro-batch would meet the actual business need at a fraction of the complexity and cost. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a stakeholder's technical preference and had to make your case, or how you'd handle this one.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question tests whether a senior engineer can separate 'what's technically exciting' from 'what the business actually needs,' and advocate for the simpler solution without being dismissive of the stakeholder's underlying goal. Situation/Task: a senior stakeholder wants to move a reporting feed to real-time streaming via Kinesis; the candidate's analysis shows a 15-minute micro-batch would satisfy the actual business requirement with far less operational complexity (no shard management, no stream processing application to maintain, simpler error handling/replay) and lower cost.

The Action should start with genuinely understanding why the stakeholder wants real-time — a strong answer explicitly describes asking clarifying questions about the actual decision being made off this data (e.g., is someone making a decision within minutes of an event, or is 'real-time' being used loosely to mean 'fresher than our current daily batch'?). This matters because many 'we need real-time' requests are actually proxy requests for 'our data is too stale,' and 15-minute micro-batching may fully solve the real underlying pain.

The candidate should then describe building a concrete comparison grounded in the stakeholder's own use case: what latency does the consuming process/dashboard/alert actually require, what Kinesis would cost and require operationally (shard provisioning or on-demand costs, a consumer application needing its own scaling and failure handling, more complex exactly-once/idempotency handling), versus what a 15-minute EventBridge-scheduled Glue or Lambda micro-batch job would cost and require (far simpler, reuses existing batch tooling, easier to debug and replay). Framing this as 'let's make sure we're solving the real latency requirement, not just adopting the more impressive-sounding architecture' shows maturity.

Critically, a strong answer doesn't just win the argument — it tests the assumption. The candidate should mention proposing to validate directly with the actual downstream consumers (e.g., the analysts or decision-makers who'd use the fresher data) whether 15 minutes actually meets their need, rather than relying on the stakeholder's assumption alone. If the answer reveals that in some future case, true sub-minute latency genuinely was needed (e.g., fraud detection, real-time personalization), the candidate should acknowledge that's exactly when Kinesis is the right call — showing they're not against streaming in principle, just against adopting it without matching it to an actual requirement. Result: ideally the stakeholder either changes their mind once shown the end-user validation, or a middle ground (e.g., a 1-minute micro-batch) satisfies both the business need and avoids unnecessary complexity.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I had a product lead come to me wanting to move our customer engagement reporting feed to Kinesis because another team had just done a flashy real-time personalization project and he wanted 'the same thing' for his reporting. My first move wasn't to argue architecture at all — I asked him directly: 'walk me through what decision someone makes differently if this data is 30 seconds old versus 15 minutes old.' It turned out nobody was making decisions at that speed; the actual pain was that our existing pipeline ran once a day, and by the time the data showed up, it was basically useless for the weekly ops review. The real ask was 'fresher,' not 'instant.'

Once I understood that, I put together a short comparison. Kinesis would mean standing up a consumer application, most likely a Lambda or a KCL-based consumer, handling shard scaling or paying for on-demand mode, building in idempotency so a consumer retry didn't double-count events, and having someone own that always-running piece of infrastructure. A 15-minute micro-batch using EventBridge Scheduler triggering a Glue job, on the other hand, reused tooling we already operated, had simple built-in retry and backfill semantics if something failed, and would cost a small fraction of what a continuously running stream-processing setup would, both in AWS spend and in engineering time maintaining it.

Rather than just telling him my answer, I asked if we could check with two of the actual report consumers — the ops managers who used this daily — about whether 15-minute freshness would solve their actual complaint. Both said yes immediately; what they wanted was to stop looking at yesterday's numbers, not sub-minute latency. I brought that back to the stakeholder along with the cost and complexity comparison, and he agreed to go with the micro-batch, with the explicit caveat that if we ever added a use case that genuinely needed seconds-level latency — he mentioned a fraud-pattern alert someone had floated — we'd revisit Kinesis then, and I agreed that would absolutely be the right call at that point. That last part mattered to him, because it showed I wasn't against streaming, I just wanted it matched to an actual need.
commonMistakes: Arguing architecture preferences directly without first clarifying what latency the stakeholder's actual use case requires
Dismissing the stakeholder's request as simply wrong instead of uncovering the real underlying need (freshness vs. true real-time decisioning)
Presenting only cost as the objection without addressing the added operational complexity (shard management, idempotency, consumer scaling) Kinesis would introduce
Not validating the proposed alternative with actual downstream data consumers before presenting it as settled
Framing the pushback as 'streaming is bad' rather than 'streaming isn't matched to this specific need,' leaving the stakeholder feeling shut down rather than heard
Failing to leave the door open for revisiting streaming if a genuinely low-latency use case emerges later
keyPoints: Clarifies the actual latency requirement behind the request before debating architecture
Distinguishes 'data feels stale' requests from genuine sub-minute decisioning needs
Builds a concrete cost and operational-complexity comparison grounded in the real use case
Validates the proposed alternative directly with downstream consumers rather than asserting it unilaterally
Keeps the stakeholder's underlying goal (fresher data) central rather than just rejecting their proposed solution
Leaves room to adopt streaming later if a genuine low-latency need appears

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Effectiveness of uncovering the real underlying business requirement
Quality and specificity of the technical/cost comparison between approaches
Validating the recommendation with actual downstream consumers rather than asserting it
Respectful, non-dismissive handling of the stakeholder's original preference
Clear, believable resolution to the disagreement

questions.title: Containing Scope Creep on a 'Just Add One Column' Task
questions.prompt: Mid-sprint, what started as "add one column to the Redshift fact table" has grown into reworking the whole Glue transformation and backfilling six months of history, with the same deadline. Tell me about a time scope crept on a data engineering task and how you handled it, or how you'd handle this one.
questions.modelAnswer:
This tests whether a senior engineer manages scope proactively and transparently rather than either silently absorbing the extra work (leading to burnout or a missed deadline nobody saw coming) or rigidly refusing any change. Situation/Task: a simple-sounding task — add one column to a Redshift fact table — turned out to require reworking the Glue transformation logic (likely because the new column needs a derived calculation, a new join, or a schema change upstream) and backfilling six months of historical data to make the column useful, but the original deadline hasn't moved.

A strong Action starts with recognizing and naming the moment scope changed, rather than just quietly doing more work. The candidate should describe pinpointing exactly when and why the task grew (e.g., 'once we looked at it, populating this column correctly for new rows was simple, but making it useful required backfilling history, which touches a transformation step that currently can't be safely re-run idempotently') — showing technical understanding of why the 'small' ask wasn't actually small.

The core of a strong answer is how they communicated the change, not just that they noticed it. This means going back to whoever requested the original one-column change as soon as the real scope became clear — not after missing the deadline — with a clear restatement of original ask vs. actual ask, and options: e.g., ship the column populated correctly for new data now, meeting the original spirit of the deadline, and backfill history as a tracked follow-up with its own estimate; or extend the deadline to cover the full backfill; or descope the backfill to a shorter window (e.g., last 30 days instead of six months) if that meets the real business need. This shows the senior behavior of re-negotiating scope against a fixed deadline rather than silently trying to cram everything in and failing, or burning out trying.

A strong answer also touches on the technical care needed for a historical backfill specifically — idempotency (being able to safely re-run the backfill without duplicating or corrupting data), validating a sample of backfilled rows against expected values before running the full six months, and possibly running the backfill in batches to limit blast radius and Redshift cluster load/cost. Result: ideally the answer shows the requester being glad they were informed early and a mutually agreed resequencing, not resentment about a missed date. A weak answer either silently works overtime to cram it all in, or treats the growing scope as someone else's problem without proposing a path forward.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This happened on a sprint where product asked for 'just add a margin column to the sales fact table.' Sounded like a half-day job. Once I actually looked, calculating margin correctly required a cost field that lived in a different source system and wasn't currently flowing through our Glue job at all, and product wanted the column to be usable in trend reports, which meant it needed to be populated for the last six months of history too, not just going forward.

As soon as I realized that, probably two days into a one-week sprint, I didn't just quietly start reworking the whole transformation and hope I'd finish in time. I went back to the product manager the same day and said, 'here's what I found: the column itself is easy for new data, but making it actually useful for your trend reports means pulling in a new source join and backfilling six months, and that's a meaningfully bigger job than what we scoped.' I laid out three options: ship the column correctly for new data by end of sprint and track the backfill as a follow-up ticket with its own two-to-three day estimate; push the sprint deadline out to cover the full backfill now; or narrow the backfill window to the last 60 days, which would still support his most common trend view, as a middle ground.

He actually preferred the third option, because his most urgent need was a recent-trends dashboard, not a full six-month lookback, so narrowing the backfill window solved his real problem without blowing the deadline. We agreed on that scope change in about a ten-minute conversation instead of me finding out on the last day that I was two weeks behind.

On the technical side, since I was running a historical backfill, I made sure the Glue job change was idempotent, so if something failed partway I could safely re-run it without double-counting margin values, and I validated the new logic against a small sample of known orders before kicking off the full 60-day backfill, batching it by week to keep load on the Redshift cluster manageable. We shipped on the original deadline with the 60-day backfill, and the full six-month backfill went out the following sprint as its own tracked piece of work.
commonMistakes: Silently absorbing the expanded scope and working overtime instead of flagging the change as soon as it's discovered
Waiting until close to the deadline to raise the scope issue instead of surfacing it the moment the real requirements become clear
Presenting the problem without offering concrete options (descope, extend deadline, phase the work) for the requester to choose from
Treating the historical backfill as a simple re-run of the same logic without addressing idempotency or validation risk
Framing the conversation as a complaint about the requester's original ask rather than a collaborative resequencing of the work
keyPoints: Identifies and names the specific technical reason the 'small' task actually grew in scope
Surfaces the scope change to the requester immediately, not near the deadline
Offers concrete options (descope, phase, extend) rather than just describing the problem
Addresses backfill-specific technical risk: idempotency, validation sampling, batching
Reaches a mutually agreed resequencing rather than unilaterally deciding or silently overworking
Delivers something real by the original deadline rather than missing it outright

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Speed and clarity of surfacing the scope change to the requester
Quality of the options offered to resolve the scope/deadline conflict
Technical soundness of the backfill approach (idempotency, validation, batching)
Collaborative, non-defensive framing of the conversation
Concrete, believable resolution that meets both the deadline and the real need

questions.title: Leading a Least-Privilege Cleanup of Wildcard IAM Permissions
questions.prompt: A security review found several IAM roles across your data platform with wildcard S3 permissions ("s3:*" on "*") that had been copy-pasted between Glue jobs for years. Tell me about how you'd lead the team through tightening this to least privilege without breaking production pipelines, or a time you did something similar.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question tests the candidate's ability to lead a cross-cutting technical remediation that carries real risk of breaking production, which requires methodical process and influence skills, not just IAM knowledge. Situation/Task: a security review surfaced multiple Glue job IAM roles with overly broad 's3:*' on '*' permissions, copy-pasted over years, and the candidate needs to drive remediation to least privilege without causing outages.

A strong Action should walk through a deliberate, staged approach rather than 'I just locked it down.' First, discovery and risk triage: inventorying every affected role, and for each, determining what it actually needs by analyzing what buckets/prefixes/actions the job genuinely touches — using tools like AWS IAM Access Analyzer, CloudTrail event history (to see actual S3 API calls made by that role over a meaningful window, e.g., 90 days), or CloudTrail data events if enabled, rather than guessing from code review alone. This grounds the new, tighter policy in actual observed behavior.

Second, a safe rollout mechanism: a strong answer explicitly avoids flipping policies directly to 'deny everything except X' in production. Instead, it describes an approach like drafting the tightened policy, then testing it in a non-production account or against a shadow/staging role first, or using IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation and the 'what-if' simulation (IAM policy simulator) to validate the new policy against known job behavior before applying it. For production rollout, mentioning a staged cutover — e.g., applying the new restrictive policy to one lower-risk job first, monitoring CloudTrail/CloudWatch for AccessDenied errors for a defined window, then proceeding job by job rather than all at once — shows real operational maturity.

Third, the leadership/team dimension: since this spans multiple Glue jobs likely owned by different engineers, the candidate should describe how they got buy-in and shared ownership rather than unilaterally changing everyone's IAM roles — e.g., presenting the security finding and remediation plan to the team, assigning each job's own owner to validate their job's specific required permissions (since they know the job's actual S3 access patterns best), and setting a realistic phased timeline rather than a single risky mass change. The answer should also mention establishing a lasting guardrail afterward — e.g., a policy template/module (IAM policy as Terraform module) enforcing scoped bucket/prefix access by default for all new Glue jobs, and possibly an SCP or automated check (e.g., AWS Config rule) flagging any future wildcard grants — so this doesn't recur. Result: remediation completed in stages with no production incidents, and a preventive control in place.
questions.professionalAnswer:
We had almost this exact finding come out of a security audit — a dozen or so Glue job roles all had 's3:*' on '*' because someone years earlier had copy-pasted a working policy as a template and it just kept propagating. I was asked to lead the cleanup.

The first thing I did was resist the urge to just lock everything down immediately, because I knew that approach was how you cause a production outage on a Friday. Instead, for each role, I pulled ninety days of CloudTrail history filtered to that role's actual S3 API calls, which told me exactly which buckets, prefixes, and actions — GetObject, PutObject, ListBucket, whatever it actually was — each job genuinely used. That gave me a real, evidence-based least-privilege policy to draft for each job instead of guessing from reading old code, which often doesn't reflect what the job actually touches anymore.

I didn't roll these out myself across every job. I brought the finding and the drafted policies to the team and assigned each job's actual owner to review and confirm the proposed scoped policy matched what they knew their job needed, because they understood edge cases in their own pipelines — things like a monthly job that only touches a specific prefix once a month, which ninety days of CloudTrail history might not have fully captured.

For rollout, I picked the lowest-risk job first — an internal reporting job with a small blast radius if something went wrong — applied the new scoped policy, and watched CloudWatch and CloudTrail for AccessDenied errors over a full business week before moving to the next job. We did this one job at a time rather than all at once, which took about five weeks total instead of an afternoon, but we had zero production incidents from the change.

The part I'm most proud of is what we did afterward: I worked with our platform team to build a Terraform module for Glue job IAM roles that only allows scoped bucket/prefix access by default, so anyone creating a new job going forward can't accidentally copy-paste a wildcard policy the way it happened originally. We also added an AWS Config rule that flags any IAM policy attached to a Glue role containing a wildcard S3 action, so if it ever creeps back in, we catch it automatically instead of waiting for the next audit.
commonMistakes: Tightening IAM policies based on a code review guess rather than actual observed access patterns from CloudTrail
Rolling out the restrictive policy to all jobs simultaneously instead of a staged, monitored cutover
Unilaterally changing every job's permissions without involving the individual job owners who understand their own edge cases
Fixing the current violations without introducing any lasting guardrail (policy template, Config rule) to prevent recurrence
Underestimating how long a safe, staged remediation actually takes and rushing it to look fast
keyPoints: Grounds the tightened policy in actual observed access (CloudTrail history, Access Analyzer) rather than guesswork
Uses a staged, monitored rollout (one job at a time) instead of a single risky mass change
Involves individual job owners in validating their own job's real permission needs
Builds team buy-in and shared ownership rather than acting unilaterally
Introduces a durable preventive control (policy template/module, Config rule) after remediation
Achieves the fix with zero or minimal production impact

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Rigor of the discovery/risk-triage process grounded in actual access data
Safety and staging of the production rollout approach
Team leadership: building buy-in and involving job owners appropriately
Introduction of a durable preventive guardrail against recurrence
Clear outcome with no or minimal production impact

questions.title: Weighing a Brewing Pipeline Issue Against a Sprint Deadline
questions.prompt: At 2pm you're deep in a sprint commitment when a production Step Functions pipeline starts failing intermittently, not critical enough to page on-call but clearly getting worse. Tell me about how you decide what to prioritize when a brewing production issue competes with a sprint deadline, with a real example.
questions.modelAnswer:
This tests real-time judgment under competing pressures — a skill that's hard to fake and that interviewers probe specifically because 'everything is top priority' and 'I always finish my sprint commitment' are both wrong answers. Situation/Task: mid-sprint-deadline-work, a production Step Functions pipeline starts throwing intermittent failures — not severe enough to page on-call, but trending worse over time.

A strong Action should describe a quick, structured triage rather than either ignoring it or dropping everything immediately. The candidate should mention pausing briefly to assess actual severity and trajectory: what's actually failing (a specific state/Lambda step, a downstream service throttling, a transient timeout), what's the current blast radius (does it affect a handful of executions or a growing percentage), and crucially, what's the trend — intermittent-and-stable versus intermittent-and-worsening. 'Getting worse' is the key signal in the prompt, and a strong answer explicitly reasons about why a worsening trend changes the calculus even if current severity is low: it suggests something like a retry storm, resource exhaustion, or a throttling threshold about to be crossed, meaning inaction now likely becomes a full outage later, possibly at a worse time (e.g., overnight).

The candidate should describe a time-boxed initial investigation — e.g., 15-20 minutes to check CloudWatch metrics/alarms, Step Functions execution history, and recent related deploys — to decide whether this is a quick, contained fix (e.g., bump a Lambda's reserved concurrency, add a retry/backoff) versus a deeper problem needing dedicated focus. This shows they don't treat 'investigate' and 'drop everything and fix it right now' as the same action.

Critically, the answer should include communication: looping in the sprint stakeholder (e.g., 'heads up, I need 30-60 minutes to contain a worsening production issue, it'll push my sprint task, here's the plan') rather than silently context-switching and letting the sprint commitment slip without explanation, or silently ignoring the brewing issue to protect the deadline. This is the core senior behavior being tested: making the tradeoff explicit and communicated rather than either extreme. Result: the answer should show a specific resolution — either a quick containment that let them return to sprint work with low lingering risk, or a case where the issue proved bigger and they explicitly renegotiated the sprint commitment with reasoning, not silence. A weak answer picks one side reflexively ('production always wins' or 'I always finish what's committed') without showing the triage reasoning.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This happened on a day I was heads-down trying to finish a feature for a sprint demo the next morning. I started getting intermittent failure notifications, not pages, just failed-execution entries, on a Step Functions pipeline that handled order enrichment. At first it was maybe one in twenty executions failing, which on its own wasn't alarming.

I gave myself about fifteen minutes to actually look rather than just noting it and going back to my feature work. I checked the Step Functions execution history and saw the failures were all timing out on the same Lambda step, and when I pulled up CloudWatch metrics for that function, I could see its duration crawling upward over the last two hours and the failure rate climbing from 5% to about 15% in that window. That trend was the thing that changed my mind — a steady 5% blip I might have logged and come back to later, but a climbing trend on the same step told me this was heading toward something like throttling or a memory leak that would likely become a real outage overnight if I didn't act, and overnight is a much worse time to be debugging it.

I messaged my manager and the PM right then: 'I found a worsening production issue on the order enrichment pipeline, it's not bad enough to page on-call yet but it's trending toward one, I need to spend the next hour containing it, which will likely push my sprint task past today.' I didn't just vanish and let the deadline silently slip.

The actual fix ended up being quick once I found it: the Lambda's memory allocation was undersized for a recent increase in payload size from an upstream change, causing it to run close to its timeout and occasionally tip over. I bumped the memory allocation, which also gave it proportionally more CPU, redeployed, and watched the failure rate drop back to zero over the next thirty minutes. That whole detour took about an hour.

I went back to my sprint task, and because I'd flagged the delay proactively, the PM and I had already agreed I'd ship the feature that evening instead of by end of day, which is what happened. The alternative, where I either ignored the trend and it became an overnight outage, or silently dropped my sprint task without saying anything, would have been worse either way.
commonMistakes: Reflexively treating any production signal as the top priority regardless of actual severity or trend, abandoning sprint work unnecessarily
Ignoring the brewing issue entirely to protect the sprint deadline, missing the worsening trend that predicts a bigger outage later
Jumping straight to a deep fix without a quick time-boxed triage to understand actual severity and trajectory first
Silently context-switching to the production issue without communicating the tradeoff or the delay to the sprint stakeholder
Fixing the issue but failing to re-communicate the revised sprint plan or timeline afterward
keyPoints: Does a quick, time-boxed triage to assess actual severity and trend before deciding how to react
Treats a worsening trend as a distinct signal from current severity, recognizing deferred risk
Separates 'contained quick fix' from 'needs dedicated focus' rather than treating all production issues identically
Proactively communicates the tradeoff and time cost to the sprint stakeholder instead of silently context-switching
Uses concrete AWS diagnostics (CloudWatch metrics, Step Functions execution history) to ground the decision
Closes the loop afterward with a renegotiated, explicit plan rather than letting the deadline just quietly slip

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quality of the triage reasoning (severity vs. trend) before acting
Appropriate use of AWS diagnostics to ground the decision in evidence
Proactive communication of the tradeoff to the sprint stakeholder
Avoids reflexive all-or-nothing prioritization in either direction
Concrete, specific outcome with a closed loop on the sprint commitment

questions.title: Giving Hard PR Feedback on Security Gaps to a Sensitive Contributor
questions.prompt: You're reviewing a teammate's Terraform pull request for a new Redshift cluster and spot a real problem — no deletion protection, a publicly-open security group, and a hardcoded password — but they're a strong contributor who's sensitive to criticism. Tell me about how you'd give that feedback, or a similar time you had to push back hard on a PR.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question tests whether a senior engineer can hold a hard line on real security issues without damaging the relationship or discouraging a valued contributor, which is a different skill from simply knowing the issues are wrong. Situation/Task: reviewing a teammate's Terraform PR for a new Redshift cluster, the candidate finds three distinct, serious issues — missing deletion protection (risking accidental data loss), a security group open to the public internet (direct exposure risk), and a hardcoded password (a secrets-management and compliance violation) — and the teammate is known to take critical feedback personally.

A strong Action should first show the candidate distinguishing severity rather than treating all three as equally 'this is bad' comments — the hardcoded password and open security group are blocking, non-negotiable security issues; deletion protection might be a 'should fix' depending on context. This shows judgment, not just a checklist reaction.

The feedback delivery itself is the core of the answer. A strong candidate describes specific tactics: leading with something genuinely positive and specific about the PR (not generic flattery) to establish the review isn't a referendum on their competence; separating the 'what' from the 'why' for each issue — explaining the actual risk in concrete terms (e.g., 'a hardcoded password in the Terraform state file or git history means anyone with repo access, or anyone who ever gets a leaked state file, has a live credential — this is specifically why we use Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store with dynamic references') rather than just saying 'don't do this'; and asking questions rather than issuing commands where appropriate ('what was the thinking on the open security group — do we actually need broad access here, or can we scope it to the VPC/specific CIDR?') to invite dialogue rather than dictate.

The candidate should also address tone and medium: considering whether a sensitive teammate would respond better to the issues being raised in a quick synchronous conversation first (especially for the security-critical ones) rather than a cold, public PR comment thread that others can see, while still documenting the resolution in the PR for the record. They should make clear they're not compromising on the actual fix — a hardcoded password and an open security group must be fixed before merge, full stop — while being flexible and collaborative about how the fix gets made. Result: a strong answer shows the PR getting fixed, the relationship staying intact, and ideally the teammate internalizing the lesson (e.g., later catching a similar issue themselves) rather than becoming defensive or avoidant of future reviews.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I had this almost exactly: a strong engineer on my team, really good at getting things shipped fast, submitted a Terraform PR for a new Redshift cluster, and he's someone who in the past had gotten visibly deflated by blunt review comments, to the point I'd seen him avoid asking for review on things he wasn't confident about. So I knew how I delivered this mattered as much as what I said.

The PR had a hardcoded master password in the resource definition, a security group with ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 on the Redshift port, and no deletion protection enabled. The first two are non-negotiable blockers to me; the deletion protection I considered a strong recommendation but less urgent.

Instead of leaving a wall of PR comments, I messaged him directly and said, 'hey, nice work getting this cluster module together so fast, good use of variables for the sizing — I found a couple of things in there I want to walk through with you before this merges, got five minutes?' That framing mattered: it was true, the module structure was genuinely well done, and it signaled this wasn't a takedown.

On the call, I didn't just say 'fix the password.' I explained the actual mechanism: 'if this password is in the Terraform config, it's in our state file and probably in git history forever, even if we rotate it later — anyone with repo access or a leaked state file has a live credential into this cluster.' I asked him if he'd used Secrets Manager elsewhere, and he had on a different project, so I suggested pulling the password from there with a dynamic reference instead, which he immediately saw the logic of once it wasn't framed as 'you did this wrong' but 'here's the actual exposure.' Same approach on the security group — I asked what the thinking was, and it turned out he'd just copied a pattern from an older module that predated our VPC security group standards, so we scoped it to our internal CIDR range together.

I did make clear, kindly but firmly, that these two couldn't merge as-is — I wasn't going to approve with a hardcoded credential or a publicly open database port, no matter how good the rest of the module was. He fixed both within the hour, added deletion protection on his own without me having to ask again, and a few weeks later he actually flagged a similar hardcoded-secret pattern in someone else's PR before I even saw it, which told me the conversation landed as coaching rather than criticism.
commonMistakes: Treating all three issues as equally severe instead of clearly distinguishing non-negotiable blockers from lower-priority recommendations
Leaving blunt, public PR comments without any softer, synchronous conversation first for a teammate known to be sensitive to criticism
Softening the feedback so much that the actual security requirement becomes ambiguous or optional
Explaining 'what to change' without explaining 'why it's actually risky,' missing the teaching opportunity
Avoiding the hard conversation altogether to prevent friction, letting a real security issue merge unaddressed
keyPoints: Distinguishes true security blockers from lower-priority recommendations rather than treating everything as equally urgent
Chooses a delivery method (synchronous conversation vs. public comment thread) suited to the teammate's sensitivity
Explains the concrete mechanism of risk for each issue, not just that it's wrong
Asks questions to invite dialogue and understand the reasoning behind the gap, rather than only issuing directives
Holds a firm, non-negotiable line on the actual security fix while staying collaborative on how it gets resolved
Preserves the relationship and ideally produces a lasting behavior change in the teammate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking security issues from lower-priority recommendations
Thoughtfulness of delivery approach given the teammate's sensitivity
Technical clarity in explaining the actual risk/mechanism of each issue
Firmness on the non-negotiable fix without becoming harsh or dismissive
Evidence of a preserved relationship and lasting positive outcome

questions.title: Making the Case for Observability Investment Over New Features
questions.prompt: Nobody on the team has invested in CloudWatch alarms or pipeline observability because it's never been anyone's assigned ticket, and leadership keeps prioritizing new feature requests over it — until the near-miss outage last month. Tell me about how you've made the case for investing in technical debt/observability over new features, or how you would here.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question tests whether a candidate can translate an invisible, unglamorous investment (observability) into terms leadership will actually fund, and whether they can use a recent near-miss as leverage without being alarmist or 'I told you so.' Situation/Task: the team has no CloudWatch alarms or real pipeline observability because it's never been anyone's explicit ticket, leadership has consistently deprioritized it in favor of visible feature work, and a recent near-miss outage has created a window of attention.

A strong Action should first describe making the invisible cost of the gap visible and concrete, rather than arguing abstractly that 'observability is important.' This means quantifying what the near-miss actually cost or risked — e.g., how long it took to detect, how close it came to affecting customers/revenue, how many engineer-hours were spent firefighting blind because there was no alarm or dashboard to immediately show what was wrong — and ideally connecting it to a believable 'next time' scenario if nothing changes, grounded in specifics rather than fear-mongering.

The candidate should describe framing the investment in the same language used to justify feature work: cost, risk, and time, not a vague appeal to engineering hygiene. For example, estimating the actual AWS cost of a baseline observability layer (CloudWatch alarms on key pipeline failure/freshness metrics, a simple dashboard, SNS-based paging) against the cost of the last incident in engineer-hours and business risk, making clear this is a comparatively cheap insurance policy relative to the near-miss.
