A strong answer explicitly avoids an all-or-nothing pitch — proposing a small, scoped first increment (e.g., alarms on the three most critical pipelines, not 'rebuild all observability') that can be delivered alongside ongoing feature work rather than requiring the team to halt everything, making it easier for leadership to say yes.

The candidate should also mention building a coalition rather than relying on their voice alone — getting the engineer who was paged/firefighting during the near-miss, or whoever felt the pain most directly, to co-present or back the ask, since a shared team voice lands differently than one engineer's opinion. And they should propose a concrete follow-up mechanism — e.g., a standing small percentage of each sprint (not a one-time ask) dedicated to observability/reliability work, so this doesn't slide back to zero once the memory of the near-miss fades. Result: ideally leadership approves a scoped first increment and some ongoing allocation, using the near-miss as leverage without being punitive or alarmist about it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
We'd had almost no alerting on our core ingestion pipelines for a long time — if something broke, we found out because someone downstream complained, not because anything paged us. Then we had a near-miss: a DMS replication task fell behind for about six hours overnight, and we only caught it the next morning because an analyst noticed stale numbers in a dashboard. It didn't actually cause customer-facing damage that time, but it easily could have.

I didn't go to leadership right away with 'we need to invest in observability,' because that's the kind of ask that's easy to nod at and then deprioritize again next sprint. Instead, I put together a short writeup quantifying what actually happened: six hours of undetected lag, about ninety minutes of two engineers' time the next morning tracing it back, and a believable scenario of what it would have looked like if it had happened during a financial close week instead of a quiet one — stale customer records flowing into a billing report, which is a very concrete, leadership-relevant risk versus a vague 'something could break' pitch.

Then I scoped a small, specific ask rather than 'rebuild all our monitoring': CloudWatch alarms on replication lag and row-count anomalies for our three highest-business-impact pipelines, wired to an SNS topic that pages on-call, which I estimated would take about a week of one engineer's time and a few dollars a month in CloudWatch costs. I framed that explicitly against the six-hours-of-blind-exposure cost from the near-miss, so it wasn't 'engineering wants to gold-plate things,' it was 'here's a cheap insurance policy against a risk we just saw firsthand.'

I also didn't present this alone — I asked the analyst who'd actually caught the stale data to describe in the meeting what it looked like from her side, since hearing it from someone outside engineering carried more weight than me describing it abstractly. Leadership approved the scoped alarm work immediately, and I also asked for, and got, a standing agreement that 10% of each sprint going forward would be reserved for reliability and observability work rather than a one-time favor, specifically so this didn't quietly disappear again once the memory of the near-miss faded in a month or two.
commonMistakes: Pitching observability investment abstractly ('it's good practice') instead of quantifying the actual cost and risk of the recent near-miss
Asking for a large, open-ended observability overhaul instead of a small, scoped first increment that's easy to approve
Relying solely on their own voice instead of bringing in whoever was directly affected by the near-miss to help make the case
Treating the near-miss punitively or using it to assign blame rather than as neutral leverage for the investment case
Winning a one-time approval without securing any standing, ongoing allocation, letting the priority slide back to zero once attention fades
keyPoints: Quantifies the concrete cost and risk of the recent near-miss rather than arguing abstractly
Frames the investment in cost/risk/time terms comparable to how feature work gets justified
Proposes a small, scoped first increment rather than an all-or-nothing overhaul
Brings in a firsthand witness or affected stakeholder to strengthen the case beyond one voice
Uses the near-miss as leverage without being alarmist or blame-oriented
Secures a standing ongoing allocation, not just a one-time approval, to prevent the priority sliding back to zero

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quality of quantifying the near-miss's real cost and risk
Effectiveness of framing observability investment in business/cost terms
Scoping a small, approvable first increment rather than an all-or-nothing ask
Building coalition/support beyond the candidate's own voice
Securing a lasting, ongoing commitment rather than a one-time fix

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem for a Silent CDC Failure
questions.prompt: A broken DMS CDC task silently fell behind for two days before anyone noticed, and a batch of customer records ended up stale in Redshift, affecting a downstream billing report. Tell me about how you'd lead a blameless postmortem for a data-quality incident like this, including how you'd actually determine and communicate root cause.
questions.modelAnswer:
This question tests the candidate's ability to run a genuinely blameless postmortem process — not just say the word 'blameless' — and their technical rigor in actually nailing down root cause for a CDC-specific failure rather than a surface-level explanation. Situation/Task: an AWS DMS change data capture task silently fell behind by two days (likely without alarming because nobody had freshness/lag monitoring on it), leading to stale customer records in Redshift that corrupted a downstream billing report, and the candidate is leading the postmortem.

A strong Action should first describe establishing the postmortem's tone and ground rules explicitly at the start of the meeting: this is about understanding the system and timeline, not assigning blame to whoever was on call or whoever built the original DMS task; actions and systems are discussed, not people's competence. The candidate should mention inviting everyone who touched the incident (the person who noticed it, whoever investigated, whoever owns the DMS task and the billing report) rather than a narrow group, so the full timeline is accurate.

For determining root cause specifically, a strong answer shows real DMS/CDC technical knowledge: walking the actual timeline using CloudWatch metrics for the DMS task (e.g., CDCLatencySource/CDCLatencyTarget metrics, which directly measure replication lag), DMS task logs, and the task's state history to pinpoint exactly when lag started growing and why (e.g., a long-running transaction on the source blocking log reading, insufficient replication instance sizing causing it to fall behind under load, or a network/connectivity blip that didn't trigger a task failure, just stalled progress). The key senior insight to voice is the '5 whys' style drill-down: the proximate cause (DMS fell behind) is not the real root cause — the real root cause is almost always 'why didn't anyone know for two days,' pointing at the missing CDCLatencyTarget alarm, meaning the detection gap is itself a root cause, not just the triggering technical event.

The answer should describe producing concrete, owned, dated action items (not vague 'improve monitoring') — e.g., a specific CloudWatch alarm on DMS replication lag exceeding a defined threshold, a freshness check on the Redshift target table gating the billing report from running on stale data, and a clear owner and due date for each. Finally, the candidate should describe how they communicated this to affected stakeholders (the billing team) — transparently explaining what happened, the corrected data, and the concrete fix — distinct from the internal engineering postmortem. Result: a documented postmortem with real preventive action items completed, not just a conversation that happened and was forgotten.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I led a postmortem very close to this. We had a DMS CDC task replicating customer data into Redshift, and it quietly fell behind for almost two days because a long-running transaction on the source database was holding open a transaction log segment DMS needed to read past, and the task didn't fail, it just slowed to a crawl. Nobody noticed until the billing team flagged that a batch of accounts showed stale subscription statuses in their report.

I scheduled the postmortem within a couple of days, while details were still fresh, and opened by setting the tone directly: 'this is about understanding what happened in the system and our processes, not about who should have caught it — if anyone feels like they're being blamed at any point, stop me.' I made sure to invite the DMS task owner, the engineer who first investigated once billing flagged it, and someone from the billing team so we had the full picture, not just the engineering side.

For root cause, I didn't stop at 'DMS fell behind.' I pulled the CloudWatch CDCLatencyTarget metric for that task and could see the lag climbing steadily starting exactly when a specific batch job on the source system kicked off a long transaction. That told us the proximate technical cause. But the real question I pushed the room on was: why did this run for two days before anyone knew? The honest answer was that we had no alarm on CDCLatencyTarget at all — we were relying on someone noticing bad data downstream, which is the worst possible detection mechanism. I was explicit in the meeting that the two-day detection gap was the actual root cause we needed to fix, not just the source transaction, because source transactions like that will happen again regardless.

We came out of it with three specific action items, each with a named owner and a date: a CloudWatch alarm on CDCLatencyTarget exceeding 30 minutes, owned by the DMS task's engineer, due that week; a freshness check added before the billing report job runs, so it refuses to run against data older than a defined threshold rather than silently reporting stale numbers, owned by the billing pipeline owner; and a review of whether that specific source batch job's transaction pattern could be adjusted to avoid holding logs open so long, owned by the source database team, as a longer-term item.

Separately from the internal postmortem, I worked with the billing team to communicate plainly to their stakeholders what had happened, which records were affected, and that the corrected data had been reprocessed, so that conversation stayed factual and solution-focused rather than becoming a blame exercise aimed at engineering.
questions.example: Root-cause chain surfaced in the postmortem: proximate cause — long-running source transaction held open a log segment, stalling DMS CDC replication; contributing cause — replication instance had no auto-scaling or capacity headroom for sustained lag recovery; true systemic root cause — no CDCLatencyTarget CloudWatch alarm existed, so the two-day detection gap, not the stall itself, was what allowed stale data to reach the billing report.
commonMistakes: Treating the postmortem as a venue to identify who should have caught the issue rather than focusing on systems and timeline
Stopping root-cause analysis at the proximate technical trigger without asking why it took two days to detect
Failing to use concrete DMS/CloudWatch evidence (CDCLatencyTarget, task logs) to establish an accurate timeline, relying on memory or assumption instead
Producing vague action items like 'improve monitoring' without a specific metric, threshold, owner, and due date
Not distinguishing internal postmortem communication from the separate, plain-language explanation owed to affected business stakeholders like the billing team
keyPoints: Explicitly sets a blameless tone and ground rules at the start of the postmortem
Includes everyone involved across the incident timeline, not just the engineering owner
Uses concrete DMS/CloudWatch evidence (CDCLatencyTarget, task logs) to establish an accurate root-cause timeline
Drills past the proximate technical cause to the real systemic root cause, usually the detection gap
Produces specific, owned, dated action items rather than vague commitments
Communicates transparently and separately with affected business stakeholders about what happened and what was corrected

Technical rigor in using DMS/CloudWatch evidence to determine accurate root cause
Correctly identifying the detection gap as a systemic root cause, not just the triggering event

Appropriate, transparent communication with affected business stakeholders
